items.stem: The wave speed v on a guitar string obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ with a unit constant. A student measures the tension as 216 N ± 4 N and the mass per unit length as 16 g m⁻¹ ± 0.08 g m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates SI base dimensions kg, m, s to deduce a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.
Converts linear density to 0.016 kg m⁻¹ and substitutes into √(T/μ).
Obtains v = 116 m s⁻¹.
Multiplies both %ΔT and %Δμ by 1/2 before adding.
Obtains 1.18%.
Obtains Δv = 1.37 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By equating SI base units on both sides of v = Tᵃ μᵇ, determine a and b and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: [T] = kg m s⁻² and [μ] = kg m⁻¹ ⇒ kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, so a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in v.
Determine the absolute uncertainty Δv in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A cyclist rides around a flat circular bend of radius 0.5 m ± 0.05 m at speed 16 m s⁻¹ ± 0.5 m s⁻¹. The centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes v and r into a = v² / r.
Obtains a = 512 m s⁻².
Uses 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) and converts to a percentage.
Obtains 16.3%.
Obtains Δa = 83.2 m s⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the nominal centripetal acceleration a.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a.
Determine the absolute uncertainty Δa.

items.stem: A flare is fired vertically upward with initial velocity +22 m s⁻¹ and negligible air drag. Take upward as positive with g = 9.81 m s⁻², and consider its motion at t = 1.4 s. Calculate its vertical displacement from the launch point at t = 1.4 s.
items.workedSolution: With upward positive, u = +22 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻². Vertical displacement s = ut + ½at² = (22)(1.4) − 0.5(9.81)(1.4)² = 21.2 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses s = ut − ½gt² with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 21.2 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses +g instead of −g when initial velocity is upward, adding ½gt² to ut.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 1/2 in the gravitational displacement term −½gt².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the motion as release from rest and omits the upward initial-velocity term ut.

items.stem: A steel piano wire has diameter d = 1 mm ± 0.02 mm and experiences a tension of F = 24 N ± 0.6 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 with d converted from mm to m.
Obtains σ = 3.06 × 10⁷ Pa.
Doubles %Δd and adds to %ΔF.
Obtains 6.50%.
Obtains Δσ = 1.99 × 10⁶ Pa.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in σ.
Hence state the absolute uncertainty Δσ in pascals.

items.stem: A horizontal flat plate of area 1 m² rests 39 m below the open surface of seawater. The liquid density is 1025 kg m⁻³, atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Result (a): Δp = ρgh = 3.922 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 3.92 × 10⁵ Pa. Result (b): p_abs = 1.01 × 10⁵ + Δp = 4.932 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 4.93 × 10⁵ Pa. Result (c): F = p_abs A = 4.932 × 10⁵ N ≈ 4.93 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Δp = ρgh with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Adds atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa to Δp.
p_abs = 4.93 × 10⁵ Pa.
Uses F = p_abs A.

parts.prompt: Calculate the hydrostatic pressure increase Δp due to the column of liquid alone.
Determine the total absolute pressure acting at this depth.
Calculate the total downward force exerted on the flat surface.

items.stem: Physical measurements in mechanics are grouped into scalar and vector quantities.
items.workedSolution: Step (a): Scalar quantity is completely specified by magnitude alone such as mass energy speed or temperature. Step (b): Vector quantity possesses both magnitude and direction such as displacement velocity force momentum or acceleration.

markScheme.criterion: Scalar quantity is completely specified by magnitude alone such as mass energy speed or temperature.
Vector quantity possesses both magnitude and direction such as displacement velocity force momentum or acceleration.

parts.expectedAnswer: Scalar quantity is completely specified by magnitude alone such as mass energy speed or temperature.
workingSteps: Key point: Scalar quantity is completely specified by magnitude alone such as mass energy speed or temperature.

parts.prompt: Define a vector quantity and give two examples. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Vector quantity possesses both magnitude and direction such as displacement velocity force momentum or acceleration.
workingSteps: Link (direction distinguishes vector quantities from scalar quantities): Vector quantity possesses both magnitude and direction such as displacement velocity force momentum or acceleration.

items.stem: With g = 9.81 m s⁻², a hoist check shows a water pump drawing 1916 W for 16 s while lifting 250 kg of salt water vertically through 10 m at steady speed.

items.stem: When checking a metal alloy cube in a lab practical, the measured edge length is 7.5 cm ± 0.06 cm. The recorded mass is 2280 g ± 2 g.

markScheme.criterion: Converts mass to kg (× 10⁻³) and cubes converted side length (× 10⁻⁶ m³).

items.stem: Heating a sealed fluid changes the microscopic energies of its particles.
items.workedSolution: Compute (a): Sum of random distribution of kinetic energies of all molecules in the system. Compute (b): Plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules.

Plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules.

parts.expectedAnswer: Plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules.
workingSteps: Link (internal energy combines microscopic random kinetic energy and molecular potential energy): Plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules.

items.stem: A rigid glass bulb connected to a pressure gauge is placed in a water bath.
items.workedSolution: Solution: (a) Pressure is directly proportional to thermodynamic temperature measured in kelvin. Then (b) Requires a fixed mass of gas kept at constant volume.

workingSteps: Key point: Pressure is directly proportional to thermodynamic temperature measured in kelvin.

parts.expectedAnswer: Requires a fixed mass of gas kept at constant volume.
workingSteps: Link (direct proportionality requires absolute kelvin temperature at constant volume and fixed mass): Requires a fixed mass of gas kept at constant volume.

items.stem: At an angle of 36.87° above the horizontal, a steady 24 N force pulls a glider across a smooth horizontal air track for 8 s. Its mass is 12 kg and starting speed is 2 m s⁻¹. Work out the speed along the horizontal after 8 s.
items.workedSolution: Forward pull F_x = 24 cos(36.87°) = 19.200000000000003 N ⇒ a_x = 1.6 m s⁻². Resulting speed v = u + a_x t = 2 + (1.6)(8) = 14.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a_x = 1.6 m s⁻² via F cos 36.87° / m and obtains v = 14.8 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the vertical component F sin θ instead of F cos θ to compute horizontal acceleration.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies F/m directly without resolving the angled force vector horizontally.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the velocity change Δv = a_x t and forgets to add the initial speed u.

items.stem: Initially 4.50 m long and 0.400 mm in diameter, a cylindrical metal resistance wire (resistivity 4.90 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) is redrawn at fixed volume so its diameter is halved to 0.200 mm. Find its new resistance.
items.workedSolution: Initial area A = πd²/4 = 1.257 × 10⁻⁷ m² and R = ρL/A = 17.55 Ω. Scaling diameter by factor k = 0.5 scales area by k² and length by 1/k² at constant volume, so R₂ = R / k⁴ = 280.7 Ω ≈ 281 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 281 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Only scaled area by k² and forgot that constant volume also changes length by 1/k².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumed resistance varies inversely with diameter rather than diameter to the fourth power.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted the scaling factor k⁴ when computing the redrawn resistance.

items.stem: In a head-on bounce off a rubber stop, a trolley of mass 0.12 kg arrives at +30 m s⁻¹ and leaves straight back at 16 m s⁻¹. Contact time is 4 ms.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for opposite signs of u and v in Δp = m(v − u).
Obtains J = -5.52 N s.
Divides |J| by contact time in seconds (0.004 s).
Obtains F_avg = 1.38 × 10³ N.
Uses ½m(v² − u²).
Obtains ΔE_k = -38.6 J.

parts.prompt: Taking the incoming direction as positive, calculate the signed impulse J delivered to the object.
Calculate the magnitude of the average contact force during the impact.
Determine the signed change in kinetic energy ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i.

items.stem: Open-circuit measurement across a car battery using a high-resistance voltmeter gives 12.0 V. When a 15.0 Ω resistor is placed across the terminals, the reading falls to 10.8 V. Find the terminal potential difference if the 15.0 Ω resistor is changed to a 5.00 Ω resistor.
items.workedSolution: Open-circuit reading gives ε = 12.0 V. With R₁ = 15 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 0.7200 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.667 Ω. With R₂ = 5 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 9.000 V ≈ 9.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 1.67 Ω and computes V₂ = 9.00 V.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumed terminal potential difference stays unchanged when load resistance changes.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: Over 9 min, a small electric fan operates at 6.00 V with a constant current of 420 mA.
items.workedSolution: Method: (a) One coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second. Second, (b) Q = It = 226.8 C, so N = Q/e = 1.417 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.42 × 10²¹ electrons. Third, (c) W = QV = 1.361 × 10³ J ≈ 1.36 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: States that one coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
Converts time to 540 s, computes Q = It = 226.8 C, and divides by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Correct electron count 1.42 × 10²¹.
Correct electrical work W = QV = 1.36 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Define the coulomb.
parts.expectedAnswer: The coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
workingSteps: Recall the SI definition linking electric charge, steady current, and time.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of conduction electrons passing through the device during the test.
workingSteps: Convert t = 9 × 60 = 540 s and I = 0.4200 A.
Number of electrons N = Q / e = 226.8 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 1.417 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.42 × 10²¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total electrical work done by the supply during the test.

Obtains Δk = 50.7 N m⁻¹.

items.stem: A resistance of 3.75 Ω is measured along the 25 mm length of a rectangular silicon bar. Its dimensions are 25 mm by 0.8 mm wide by 0.4 mm thick. What is the material's resistivity?

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Rearranged resistivity wrongly as ρ = R L / A.

items.stem: What current flows through a camping floodlight rated "12 V, 36 W" when operating at its rated potential difference?

options.label: C

items.stem: Two ohmic metallic conductors X and Y are plotted on the same graph with current on the vertical axis and potential difference on the horizontal axis. Line X is steeper than line Y. Which conclusion follows?
items.workedSolution: With current on the y-axis, gradient = I / V = 1 / R; therefore a steeper ohmic line corresponds to a smaller resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Therefore a steeper ohmic line corresponds to a smaller resistance.

options.label: A
options.text: Since gradient is reciprocal resistance, a steeper ohmic line corresponds to a larger resistance
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the inverse relationship between I–V slope and resistance.

options.label: B
options.text: Since gradient is reciprocal resistance, both conductors have identical resistance because both pass through the origin
options.distractorRationale: Passing through the origin shows ohmic behaviour, not equal resistance values.

options.label: C
options.text: Since gradient is reciprocal resistance, conductor X must be operating at a higher temperature than conductor Y
options.distractorRationale: Slope alone compares resistance values, not temperature directly.

options.label: D
options.text: Since gradient is reciprocal resistance, therefore a steeper ohmic line corresponds to a smaller resistance

Determine the energy wasted during the lift.

items.stem: A pressure probe is lowered to depth h = 15 m ± 0.3 m in a lake of density ρ = 1020 kg m⁻³ ± 12 kg m⁻³. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ as exact. Calculate the gauge pressure p = ρgh at this depth in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure p = ρgh = 1020 × 9.81 × 15 = 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates p = ρgh = 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes ρh and omits gravitational field strength g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reports the numerical value in kilopascals while labelling the unit as pascals.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides ρg by depth h instead of multiplying ρgh.

items.stem: Dimensions of a rectangular alloy sample are 6 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm. It consists by volume of 65% silver of density 10500 kg m⁻³ and 35% aluminium of density 2700 kg m⁻³. Determine the block's mass in kg.
items.workedSolution: Volume V = (6 × 3 × 5) × 10⁻⁶ = 9.000 × 10⁻⁵ m³. Volume-weighted density ρ = (0.65 × 10500) + (0.35 × 2700) = 7770 kg m⁻³ ≈ 7.77 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Total mass m = ρ V = 0.6993 kg ≈ 0.699 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 0.699 kg.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the harmonic mean density instead of the volume-weighted mean.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses 10⁻⁴ instead of 10⁻⁶ when converting cm³ to m³.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Includes only the mass of the first metal.

items.stem: A calorimetry check shows 1.2 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) warming by 18 K in 200 s with a heating coil at 605 W.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into Q = mcΔT.
Obtains Q = 9.07 × 10⁴ J.
Subtracts Q from total electrical energy P_in t.
Obtains E_lost = 3.03 × 10⁴ J.
Obtains η = 75.0%.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy Q absorbed by the sample.
Calculate the thermal energy lost to the surroundings during the heating interval.
Determine the percentage efficiency of the heating arrangement.

items.stem: In a buoyancy practical, a solid steel block of mass 7.5 kg and density 7870 kg m⁻³ hangs on a spring balance fully inside freshwater (density 1000 kg m⁻³), clear of the bottom (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Evaluate (a): buoyancy pushing upward equals the weight of fluid displaced. Evaluate (b): V = 9.530 × 10⁻⁴ m³ ⇒ F_B = 9.349 N ≈ 9.35 N. Evaluate (c): W_app = W − F_B = 64.23 N ≈ 64.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Upthrust equals weight of displaced fluid.
Finds V = m / ρ_obj and applies F_B = ρ_fluid V g.
Subtracts upthrust from weight in air.
Apparent weight = 64.2 N.

parts.prompt: State Archimedes' principle.
parts.expectedAnswer: Archimedes' principle states that the upward buoyancy force equals the weight of fluid displaced by the body.
workingSteps: State that upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced by the body in the fluid.

parts.prompt: Calculate the upthrust acting on the fully under water block.
Hence calculate the reading on the spring balance while the block remains fully under water.
workingSteps: Spring balance tension = W − F_B = 64.23 N ≈ 64.2 N.

items.stem: Potential difference is measured in volts ($\mathrm{V}$). A student checks its units in terms of SI base units.
items.workedSolution: (a) $V = W/Q = (Fs)/(It)$, giving $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}} / (\mathrm{A\,s}) = \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$ (kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere). (b) A micrometer gives finer resolution ($0.01\text{ mm}$) and smaller percentage uncertainty. Take repeated measurements at different positions and perpendicular angles and find the mean (do not accept vague 'repeat experiment').

markScheme.criterion: Recall $W = Fs$ yields $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$ for the joule.
Recall $Q = It$ yields $\mathrm{A\,s}$ for the coulomb.
Correctly simplify to $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$ (kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere).
Micrometer has higher resolution giving lower percentage uncertainty on a thin wire (reject Vernier callipers).
Repeat diameter measurements at several points/perpendicular orientations and calculate the mean (reject bare 'repeat experiment').

parts.prompt: Using the defining equations $V = W/Q$, $W = Fs$, and $Q = It$, derive the coherent SI base units of the volt.
parts.expectedAnswer: Starting from $V = W/Q$, substitute work in joules ($\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$) and charge in ampere seconds ($\mathrm{A\,s}$) to obtain kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere ($\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$).
workingSteps: Write $V = W / Q$ and replace force $F = ma$ so $W = Fs$ has base units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$.
Replace charge $Q = It$ with base units $\mathrm{A\,s}$.

parts.prompt: State why a thin copper wire's diameter should be measured with a micrometer screw gauge rather than Vernier callipers. Explain how to reduce random uncertainty in the diameter.
parts.expectedAnswer: A micrometer screw gauge has finer resolution ($0.01\text{ mm}$ vs $0.1\text{ mm}$) giving smaller percentage uncertainty on a thin wire; repeat diameter measurements at several positions and perpendicular orientations along the wire and calculate the mean.
workingSteps: Compare micrometer resolution with Vernier callipers for a sub-millimetre wire.
Specify repeat measurements along length and perpendicular orientations plus calculating the mean.

items.stem: A ductile brass wire is loaded progressively until its unloading curve no longer returns to the origin.
items.workedSolution: Result (a): Maximum force or stress a material can bear and still return completely to its original length upon unloading. Result (b): Exceeding the elastic limit leaves a permanent extension due to plastic deformation.

Exceeding the elastic limit leaves a permanent extension due to plastic deformation.

parts.prompt: Define the elastic limit of a material. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Maximum force or stress a material can bear and still return completely to its original length upon unloading.
workingSteps: Key point: Maximum force or stress a material can bear and still return completely to its original length upon unloading.

parts.prompt: State what happens to the wire when unloaded after exceeding the elastic limit. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Exceeding the elastic limit leaves a permanent extension due to plastic deformation.
workingSteps: Link (elastic behaviour means complete recovery of original dimensions on removing load): Exceeding the elastic limit leaves a permanent extension due to plastic deformation.

items.stem: Which statement accurately defines the electrical resistivity of a conducting material?
items.workedSolution: From ρ = R A / L, resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.

markScheme.criterion: Resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.

options.label: A
options.text: Resistivity is the resistance per unit length of a wire regardless of its thickness
options.distractorRationale: Omits cross-sectional area; resistance per unit length depends on wire diameter.

options.label: B
options.text: Resistivity is the resistance divided by both length and cross sectional area
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the geometric factor A / L in ρ = R A / L.

options.label: C
options.text: Resistivity is the total resistance of a cylindrical wire measured at its melting point
options.distractorRationale: Confuses a material constant defined for unit geometry with total wire resistance.

options.label: D
options.text: Resistivity is the resistance of a specimen of unit length and unit cross sectional area

items.stem: A pressure probe is lowered to depth h = 45 m ± 0.8 m in a lake of density ρ = 1020 kg m⁻³ ± 25 kg m⁻³. Take g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ as exact. Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δp in the gauge pressure in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Nominal gauge pressure p = ρgh = 4.50 × 10⁵ Pa. Fractional uncertainty Δp/p = Δρ/ρ + Δh/h = 25/1020 + 0.8/45 = 0.0423. Hence Δp = 1.90 × 10⁴ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes p(Δρ/ρ + Δh/h) to obtain Δp = 1.90 × 10⁴ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the fractional uncertainties |Δρ/ρ − Δh/h| instead of adding them.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies absolute uncertainties Δρ × g × Δh directly instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Propagates fractional uncertainties correctly but forgets the factor of g in p = ρgh.

items.stem: Derived electrical units can be expressed in multiple equivalent SI forms.
items.workedSolution: Answers: (a) Energy transferred per unit charge gives joule per coulomb. Next (b) Replacing joule with newton metre and coulomb with ampere second yields joule per ampere second.

markScheme.criterion: Energy transferred per unit charge gives joule per coulomb.
Replacing joule with newton metre and coulomb with ampere second yields joule per ampere second.

parts.prompt: Express the volt in terms of energy and charge units. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Energy transferred per unit charge gives joule per coulomb.
workingSteps: Key point: Energy transferred per unit charge gives joule per coulomb.

parts.prompt: Explain how this leads to an equivalent unit involving joule, ampere, and second. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Replacing joule with newton metre and coulomb with ampere second yields joule per ampere second.
workingSteps: Link (potential difference equals work done per unit charge): Replacing joule with newton metre and coulomb with ampere second yields joule per ampere second.

items.stem: A flare is fired vertically upward with initial velocity +25 m s⁻¹ and negligible air drag. Take upward as positive with g = 9.8 m s⁻², and consider its motion at t = 1.4 s. Calculate its signed vertical velocity at t = 1.4 s.
items.workedSolution: Using v = u + at with u = +25 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.8 m s⁻² gives v = 25 − (9.8)(1.4) = 11.3 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds gt to u instead of subtracting gt when upward is defined as positive.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the algebraic sign of the vertical velocity vector.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes the mean vertical velocity u − ½gt rather than the instantaneous velocity u − gt.

items.stem: An ammeter is inserted into a laboratory lighting circuit to measure branch current.
items.workedSolution: Answers: (a) Connected in series with the branch carrying the current. Next (b) Zero internal resistance ensures no potential difference is dropped across the ammeter.

markScheme.criterion: Connected in series with the branch carrying the current.
Zero internal resistance ensures no potential difference is dropped across the ammeter.

parts.prompt: State how the ammeter must be connected in the branch. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Connected in series with the branch carrying the current.
workingSteps: Key point: Connected in series with the branch carrying the current.

parts.prompt: Explain why an ideal ammeter must have zero resistance. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Zero internal resistance ensures no potential difference is dropped across the ammeter.
workingSteps: Link (series connection with zero resistance introduces no extra voltage drop): Zero internal resistance ensures no potential difference is dropped across the ammeter.

items.stem: Which option accurately states Kirchhoff's second law together with the fundamental conservation law from which it follows?
items.workedSolution: Kirchhoff's second law states that the sum of electromotive forces equals sum of potential differences around a closed loop expressing conservation of energy.

markScheme.criterion: Sum of electromotive forces equals sum of potential differences around a closed loop expressing conservation of energy.

options.label: A
options.text: In any DC network, the sum of electromotive forces equals sum of potential differences around a closed loop expressing conservation of energy

options.label: B
options.text: In any DC network, the sum of electromotive forces equals sum of potential differences around a closed loop expressing conservation of charge
options.distractorRationale: Links the closed-loop voltage law to charge conservation rather than energy conservation.

options.label: C
options.text: In any DC network, the sum of branch currents around a closed loop is zero expressing conservation of energy
options.distractorRationale: Applies a junction-current idea to a loop instead of summing emfs and potential differences.

options.label: D
options.text: In any DC network, every resistor in a closed loop drops the same potential difference expressing conservation of energy
options.distractorRationale: Potential drops depend on individual resistances and currents, not equal sharing.

items.stem: A dry cell drives current through a metallic wire joined between its positive and negative terminals.
items.workedSolution: Result (a): Conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current. Result (b): Electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.

markScheme.criterion: Conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.
Electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.

parts.prompt: State the direction of free electron drift relative to conventional current. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.
workingSteps: Key point: Conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.

parts.prompt: State which battery terminal conduction electrons drift toward through the external wire. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.
workingSteps: Link (conventional current tracks positive charge flow so negative electrons move the opposite way): Electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.

items.stem: Which statement gives the complete principle of conservation of linear momentum?
items.workedSolution: Total linear momentum before equals total linear momentum after provided no external resultant force acts.

markScheme.criterion: Total linear momentum before equals total linear momentum after provided no external resultant force acts.

options.label: A
options.text: In any collision or explosion, total linear momentum before equals total linear momentum after under all external forces
options.distractorRationale: Omits the mandatory isolated-system condition: a net external force changes total system momentum.

options.label: B
options.text: In any collision or explosion, total linear momentum before equals total linear momentum after provided no external resultant force acts

options.label: C
options.text: In any collision or explosion, total speed before equals total speed after provided no friction acts
options.distractorRationale: Confuses scalar speed with vector linear momentum (mass times velocity).

options.label: D
options.text: In any collision or explosion, momentum is conserved only when kinetic energy is also conserved
options.distractorRationale: Momentum is conserved in both elastic and inelastic isolated collisions.

items.stem: A battery with non-negligible internal resistance drives a variable resistor. Without calculation, what happens to the voltmeter reading across the battery terminals when the variable resistance is reduced?
items.workedSolution: Because V = ε − Ir, lower external resistance increases circuit current raising lost volts across internal resistance so terminal potential difference decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Lower external resistance increases circuit current raising lost volts across internal resistance so terminal potential difference decreases.

options.label: A
options.text: Reducing load resistance means circuit current drops so terminal potential difference rises above the electromotive force
options.distractorRationale: Reducing load resistance raises current and can never push terminal pd above emf.

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing load resistance means terminal potential difference stays fixed because battery electromotive force never changes
options.distractorRationale: Ignores internal lost volts Ir, which grows as current rises.

options.label: C
options.text: Reducing load resistance means internal resistance decreases proportionally so lost volts remain constant
options.distractorRationale: Internal resistance is a physical property of the cell and does not track the external load.

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing load resistance means lower external resistance increases circuit current raising lost volts across internal resistance so terminal potential difference decreases

items.stem: A calibrated cathode-ray oscilloscope displays a sinusoidal voltage from a signal generator. Settings are time-base 2.0 ms div⁻¹ and Y-gain 1.5 V div⁻¹. One full cycle covers 4.0 horizontal divisions, and peak-to-peak height is 5.2 vertical divisions.
items.workedSolution: (a) $T = 8.00 × 10⁻³ s$, so $f = 1/T = 125 Hz$. (b) $V_0 = 3.90 V$, giving $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = 2.76 V$. (c) Reduce the time-base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty. Switching the time-base off gives a vertical line of height equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates period $T = 8.00 × 10⁻³ s$ from divisions × time-base.
Frequency $f = 125 Hz$.
Finds peak voltage $V_0 = 3.90 V$ and divides by $\sqrt{2}$.
Root-mean-square voltage $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = 2.76 V$.
Reduce time-base setting (ms div⁻¹) to stretch waveform horizontally and lower % uncertainty.
Time-base OFF collapses AC waveform to a vertical line of height equal to peak-to-peak voltage.

parts.prompt: Determine the frequency $f$ of the alternating signal.
Calculate the root-mean-square voltage $V_{\mathrm{rms}}$ of the signal.
Explain how adjusting the time-base improves period precision and describe the screen trace if the time-base is switched off.
parts.expectedAnswer: Reduce the time-base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty. Switching the time-base off gives a vertical line of height equal to the peak-to-peak voltage
workingSteps: Lower ms div⁻¹ stretches one cycle across more divisions, cutting % uncertainty.
With time-base OFF, AC forms a centred vertical line of length peak-to-peak voltage.

items.stem: A student measures a metal resistance wire using a 0.01 mm resolution micrometer screw gauge with a closed-jaw zero error of +0.04 mm. The sleeve reads 2.5 mm and thimble division 23 aligns with the reference line.
items.workedSolution: (a) Corrected diameter $d = 2.73 - 0.04 = 2.69$ mm. (b) $\%\Delta d = 0.372\%$, so $\%\Delta A = 2 \times \%\Delta d = 0.743\%$. (c) use the ratchet to avoid over tightening or compressing the wire and repeat perpendicular diameter measurements along the length.

markScheme.criterion: Reads sleeve + thimble correctly and subtracts positive zero error.
Corrected diameter $d = 2.69$ mm.
Computes $\%\Delta d = 0.372\%$ and doubles for $d^2$.
Percentage uncertainty in area $= 0.743\%$.
Close spindle using the ratchet to avoid compressing/deforming the wire.
Take repeat measurements in perpendicular directions at >= 3 positions along the wire.

items.stem: Which expression defines the SI unit of power, the watt?
items.workedSolution: One watt is a rate of energy transfer of one joule per second.

markScheme.criterion: Rate of energy transfer of one joule per second.

options.label: A
options.text: A rate of energy transfer of one joule per second

options.label: B

options.label: C

items.stem: A student checks the thickness of an acrylic optical block using manual Vernier callipers of resolution 0.02 mm. With the jaws closed, the scale reads -0.04 mm. On the block, the vernier zero lies past 26 mm and mark 9 aligns with the main scale.
items.workedSolution: (a) Raw reading $= 26.18$ mm; subtracting $-0.04$ mm gives 26.22 mm. (b) Percentage uncertainty $= (0.02 / 26.22) \times 100\% = 0.0763\%$. (c) record any zero error with the jaws closed and view the coinciding vernier division perpendicularly to eliminate parallax.

markScheme.criterion: Combines main scale and Vernier coincidence, then subtracts negative zero error.
Corrected thickness $= 26.22$ mm.
Divides instrument resolution by corrected thickness and multiplies by 100%.
Percentage uncertainty $= 0.0763\%$.
Check and correct for closed-jaw zero error.
View the aligned scale mark perpendicularly at eye level to eliminate parallax.

parts.expectedAnswer: Record any zero error with the jaws closed and view the coinciding vernier division perpendicularly to eliminate parallax
workingSteps: Inspect and record closed-jaw zero error before measuring.

items.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor is charged to a higher potential difference without exceeding its breakdown rating. What happens to its capacitance?
items.workedSolution: Both Q and V scale proportionally, so capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.

options.label: A
options.text: Its capacitance stays constant because charge stored stays fixed as voltage increases
options.distractorRationale: Charge increases proportionally with voltage (Q = CV) so the ratio Q/V stays constant.

options.label: B
options.text: Its capacitance doubles because doubling potential difference doubles the farad rating
options.distractorRationale: Capacitance is fixed by plate geometry and dielectric, not applied voltage.

options.label: C
options.text: Its capacitance stays constant because capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage

options.label: D
options.text: Its capacitance halves because potential difference appears in the denominator of charge per volt
options.distractorRationale: Forgets that Q also doubles when V doubles, keeping C = Q/V invariant.

items.stem: A student takes repeat readings of wire diameter with a micrometer that has a zero error when closed.
items.workedSolution: Solution: (a) Random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging. Then (b) Averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error. Key idea: repeat averaging reduces random scatter while calibration removes systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: Random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging.
Links to principle: Repeat averaging reduces random scatter while calibration removes systematic offset.
Averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error.
Systematic errors such as zero offset bias every measurement consistently in the same direction.

parts.prompt: Distinguish between random errors and systematic errors in experimental measurements. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging.
workingSteps: Main point: Random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging.
Key idea: Repeat averaging reduces random scatter while calibration removes systematic offset.

parts.prompt: Explain what taking repeated readings and averaging achieves and why it cannot remove the micrometer zero error. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error.
workingSteps: Explanation: Averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error.
Avoid the common error of claiming that repeating measurements and computing a mean removes a zero error on a meter.

items.stem: Starting from the same initial voltage, a charged capacitor is discharged through a fixed resistor and then through a smaller resistor. Without calculation, how does the second discharge differ?
items.workedSolution: From τ = RC and I = V/R, a smaller resistance reduces the time constant so initial current is larger and capacitor potential difference falls more rapidly.

markScheme.criterion: Smaller resistance reduces the time constant so initial current is larger and capacitor potential difference falls more rapidly.

options.label: A
options.text: A smaller resistance increases the time constant so initial current drops and voltage stays higher for longer
options.distractorRationale: Time constant τ = R C decreases, not increases, when R is reduced.

options.label: B
options.text: A smaller resistance reduces the time constant so initial current is larger and capacitor potential difference falls more rapidly

options.label: C
options.text: A smaller resistance keeps the time constant unchanged because capacitance alone controls discharge speed
options.distractorRationale: Time constant depends on the product of BOTH resistance and capacitance.

options.label: D
options.text: A smaller resistance reduces initial current while doubling the total charge initially stored on the plates
options.distractorRationale: Initial charge Q = C V depends only on capacitance and initial voltage, not the discharge resistor.

items.stem: A dense sphere is released from rest at the top of a deep tank filled with viscous oil.
items.workedSolution: Compute (a): Initially weight exceeds drag so the object accelerates downward and speed increases. Compute (b): Drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero. Key idea: balance between speed dependent drag and constant weight yields zero acceleration.

markScheme.criterion: Initially weight exceeds drag so the object accelerates downward and speed increases.
First causal step: initially weight exceeds drag so the object accelerates downward and speed increases.
Intermediate physical mechanism: resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration.
Final physical conclusion: when upward drag equals downward weight resultant force becomes zero so velocity stays constant at terminal velocity.

parts.prompt: Describe the initial force balance immediately after release and the initial slope of a velocity–time sketch graph. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Initially weight exceeds drag so the object accelerates downward and speed increases.
workingSteps: Main point: Initially weight exceeds drag so the object accelerates downward and speed increases.
Key idea: Balance between speed dependent drag and constant weight yields zero acceleration.

parts.prompt: Explain in terms of changing drag force and resultant force how the sphere reaches a constant terminal velocity and how the sketch graph flattens. [3]
parts.expectedAnswer: Drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero.
workingSteps: Explanation: Drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero.
Avoid the common error of believing gravity decreases during the fall or that forces drop to zero at terminal velocity.

items.stem: Under a central centripetal force, a satellite orbits at constant speed along a circular path.
items.workedSolution: First, (a) Velocity is a vector so constant speed along a circular path still involves continuous velocity change and acceleration. Next, (b) Resultant centripetal force and acceleration always point perpendicular to instantaneous velocity toward the centre of the circle.

markScheme.criterion: Velocity is a vector so constant speed along a circular path still involves continuous velocity change and acceleration.
Resultant centripetal force and acceleration always point perpendicular to instantaneous velocity toward the centre of the circle.

parts.prompt: Explain why the satellite is accelerating even though its speed is constant. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Velocity is a vector so constant speed along a circular path still involves continuous velocity change and acceleration.
workingSteps: Key point: Velocity is a vector so constant speed along a circular path still involves continuous velocity change and acceleration.

parts.prompt: Explain why the centripetal force does zero work on the satellite. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Resultant centripetal force and acceleration always point perpendicular to instantaneous velocity toward the centre of the circle.
workingSteps: Link (centripetal force alters direction of velocity without changing speed): Resultant centripetal force and acceleration always point perpendicular to instantaneous velocity toward the centre of the circle.

items.stem: When illuminated smoke trapped in a glass cell is observed through a microscope, bright specks dance along erratic zig-zag paths. What causes this motion?
items.workedSolution: Brownian motion arises because uneven rapid collisions from much smaller invisible randomly moving air molecules transfer momentum to smoke specks.

markScheme.criterion: Uneven rapid collisions from much smaller invisible randomly moving air molecules transfer momentum to smoke specks.

options.label: A
options.text: It occurs because visible air molecules collide directly with one another under the microscope lamp
options.distractorRationale: Air molecules are far too small to be seen under an optical microscope; only smoke specks are visible.

options.label: B
options.text: It occurs because uneven rapid collisions from much smaller invisible randomly moving air molecules transfer momentum to smoke specks

options.label: C
options.text: It occurs because steady upward convection currents sweep all specks smoothly in one direction
options.distractorRationale: Convection produces smooth collective drift, not random individual zig-zag jitter.

options.label: D
options.text: It occurs because the microscope lamp pushes the specks randomly with intense radiation pressure
options.distractorRationale: Radiation pressure from a bench lamp is negligible and directional rather than randomly fluctuating.

items.stem: Which statement accurately expresses Lenz's law of electromagnetic induction?
items.workedSolution: Lenz's law states that the direction of induced electromotive force opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it.

markScheme.criterion: Direction of induced electromotive force opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it.

options.label: A
options.text: The direction of induced electromotive force opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it

options.label: B
options.text: The magnitude of induced electromotive force is always equal to the steady magnetic flux through the coil
options.distractorRationale: Confuses Faraday's rate-of-change law with steady flux and omits direction.

options.label: C
options.text: The direction of induced current always assists the motion of the magnet to conserve charge
options.distractorRationale: Assisting motion would create energy from nothing, violating conservation of energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The induced current always flows clockwise regardless of magnet polarity
options.distractorRationale: Induced current direction reverses whenever magnet polarity or direction of motion reverses.

items.stem: What defining condition must hold for an oscillating mass to perform simple harmonic motion?
items.workedSolution: In simple harmonic motion, acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from a fixed equilibrium position and always directed toward it.

markScheme.criterion: Acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from a fixed equilibrium position and always directed toward it.

options.label: A
options.text: Its velocity is directly proportional to displacement and directed away from equilibrium
options.distractorRationale: Velocity is maximum at equilibrium and zero at turning points, not proportional to displacement.

options.label: B
options.text: Its acceleration stays constant in magnitude and reverses sign only at the endpoints
options.distractorRationale: Constant acceleration produces parabolic motion, not sinusoidal simple harmonic motion.

options.label: C
options.text: Its periodic oscillation repeats with constant amplitude regardless of force law
options.distractorRationale: Not every periodic motion is simple harmonic; acceleration must be proportional and opposite to displacement.

options.label: D
options.text: Its acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from a fixed equilibrium position and always directed toward it

items.stem: The wave speed v on a stretched wire obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ with a unit constant, where T is tension (in N, or kg m s⁻²) and μ is mass per unit length. In a lab test, T = 48 N ± 1.2 N and μ = 3 g m⁻¹ ± 0.1 g m⁻¹. Use base units to find a and b, and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Matching SI base units: [v] = m s⁻¹, [T] = kg m s⁻², [μ] = kg m⁻¹. For kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, −2a = −1 ⇒ a = 0.5 and b = −0.5, so v = √(T/μ). With μ = 3 × 10⁻³ = 0.003 kg m⁻¹, v = √(48 / 0.003) = 126 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a = 1/2, b = −1/2, converts μ to 0.003 kg m⁻¹, and obtains v = 126 m s⁻¹.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Deduces v = √(T/μ) correctly but forgets to convert μ from g m⁻¹ into kg m⁻¹ (off by √1000).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a = 1, b = −1 (computing T/μ with units m² s⁻²) without taking the square root required by dimensional homogeneity.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the dimensional ratio to √(μ/T), yielding s m⁻¹ instead of m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A point on a spinning blade moves in a circle of radius 4 m ± 0.03 m at speed 9 m s⁻¹ ± 0.2 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the centripetal acceleration a.
items.workedSolution: For a = v² / r, Δa/a = 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) = 2(0.2/9) + (0.03/4). Multiplying by 100% gives 5.19%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses %Δa = 2(%Δv) + (%Δr) to obtain 5.19%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 on the fractional uncertainty of v despite v being squared in v²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainty of r from 2(%Δv) because r is in the denominator.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the percentage uncertainties instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: A small capsule is launched vertically upward at 36 m s⁻¹ with negligible air resistance. Take upward as positive and g = 9.81 m s⁻², and consider its motion at t = 1.8 s.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes u = +36 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻² into v = u + at.
Obtains v = 18.3 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½gt² with consistent signs.
Obtains s = 48.9 m.
Obtains v_avg = 27.2 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the signed vertical velocity at the stated time.
Calculate the vertical displacement relative to the launch point.
Determine the average vertical velocity over this time interval.

items.stem: A steel wire of circular diameter d = 0.8 mm ± 0.01 mm is held under a tension of F = 135 N ± 0.5 N. Calculate the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = π(0.8 × 10⁻³)² / 4 = 5.03 × 10⁻⁷ m². Tensile stress σ = F / A = 4F / (πd²) = 2.69 × 10⁸ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 in m² to obtain σ = 2.69 × 10⁸ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses A = πd² instead of A = πd²/4 (treating diameter d as if it were radius r, off by a factor of 4).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter in millimetres directly without converting d² from mm² to 10⁻⁶ m².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by circumference πd instead of cross-sectional area πd²/4.

items.stem: Take atmospheric pressure as 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². A flat horizontal plate of area 2 m² lies 28.5 m deep in open freshwater (density 1000 kg m⁻³). What is the total downward force acting on the plate?
items.workedSolution: Fluid gauge pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1000 × 9.81 × 28.5 = 2.796 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 2.80 × 10⁵ Pa. Combined pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 2.796 × 10⁵ = 3.806 × 10⁵ Pa = 380.6 kPa ≈ 381 kPa. Resultant force F = p_abs A = 3.806 × 10⁵ × 2 = 7.612 × 10⁵ N ≈ 7.61 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 7.61 × 10⁵ N.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides absolute pressure by area instead of multiplying F = p A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure, omitting atmospheric force.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes fluid mass instead of total downward force.

items.stem: Two equal and opposite parallel forces act at opposite ends of a steering wheel (a couple). The resultant force is zero, yet the wheel is NOT in equilibrium. Why?
items.workedSolution: Complete rigid body equilibrium also requires zero resultant force in any direction alongside zero resultant moment about any point.

markScheme.criterion: Complete rigid body equilibrium also requires zero resultant force in any direction.

options.label: A
options.text: Because equilibrium only requires resultant force to be zero and never depends on turning moments
options.distractorRationale: A couple has zero resultant force yet produces a net turning torque.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the two forces must act in the same direction to establish static equilibrium
options.distractorRationale: Same-direction forces yield a non-zero resultant force and accelerate the centre of mass.

options.label: C
options.text: Because complete rigid body equilibrium also requires zero resultant force in any direction

options.label: D
options.text: Because rigid body equilibrium requires both resultant force and resultant moment to be non zero
options.distractorRationale: Equilibrium requires both resultant force and resultant moment to be ZERO.

items.stem: Find the percentage efficiency when an electric winch lifts a cage of mass 500 kg through 10 m vertically in 16 s at steady speed. The input power is 3832 W and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Gravitational energy gained ΔE_p = mgh = 500 × 9.81 × 10 = 4.91 × 10⁴ J. Total electrical input E_in = 3832 × 16 = 61312 J. Hoist efficiency η = (ΔE_p / E_in) × 100% = 80.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgh / (P_in t) × 100% with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 80.0%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits gravitational field strength g when computing gravitational potential energy mgh.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input energy wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides useful energy mgh in joules directly by input power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

items.stem: Work out the absolute uncertainty Δρ, expressed in kg m⁻³, for the density of a small ceramic cube. The measured values are edge 4.5 cm ± 0.03 cm and mass 656 g ± 4 g.
items.workedSolution: Start by computing ρ = (0.656) / (0.045)³ = 7.20 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Combined fractional uncertainty Δρ/ρ = (4/656) + 3(0.03/4.5) = 0.0261. Thus Δρ = ρ × (Δρ/ρ) = 188 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Combines SI density with fractional uncertainty Δm/m + 3ΔL/L to obtain Δρ = 188 kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 3 from L³ when propagating the fractional uncertainty of the edge length.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the absolute uncertainty in g cm⁻³ rather than converting to kg m⁻³.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the fractional uncertainty of L³ from that of mass in the quotient m / L³.

items.stem: A pure crystalline wax sample is heated steadily by an electrical heater. During melting, the thermometer reading stays flat on a horizontal plateau. What happens at the molecular scale during this plateau?
items.workedSolution: During melting, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while supplied energy increases internal potential energy by breaking bonds.

markScheme.criterion: Mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while supplied energy increases internal potential energy by breaking bonds.

options.label: A
options.text: Along the plateau, both molecular kinetic energy and molecular potential energy remain completely constant
options.distractorRationale: Energy is continually supplied by the heater, so internal potential energy must increase.

options.label: B
options.text: Along the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy rises steadily while molecular potential energy decreases
options.distractorRationale: A rise in mean molecular kinetic energy would raise the temperature rather than keeping a plateau.

options.label: C
options.text: Along the plateau, all heater energy escapes immediately into the room so internal energy cannot change
options.distractorRationale: Even with negligible heat loss, melting requires latent heat to weaken intermolecular bonds.

options.label: D

items.stem: Which statement gives the exact form of the Pressure Law for an ideal gas?
items.workedSolution: The Pressure Law states that for a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin.

markScheme.criterion: For a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin.

options.label: A
options.text: It states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to temperature in degrees Celsius
options.distractorRationale: Pressure vs Celsius has a non-zero intercept at freezing point; direct proportionality requires kelvin.

options.label: B
options.text: It states that for a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin

options.label: C
options.text: It states that for any mass of gas at constant pressure volume is inversely proportional to kelvin temperature
options.distractorRationale: Mixes up Charles's law variables and inverts proportionality.

options.label: D
options.text: It states that pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature regardless of vessel expansion
options.distractorRationale: Omits the controlled variable of constant volume.

items.stem: An electric car runs at a steady speed of 36 km h⁻¹ on a flat road against a resistive force of 800 N. It draws 9524 W of DC power for 40 s. Calculate the percentage efficiency of the motor system.
items.workedSolution: At constant velocity, tractive force F = 800 N and v = 36/3.6 = 10 m s⁻¹. Useful power P_out = Fv = 800 × 10 = 8000 W. Efficiency η = (8000/9524) × 100% = 84.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Converts speed to 10 m s⁻¹, computes P_out = Fv = 8000 W, and obtains η = 84.0%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies drag force in N by speed in km h⁻¹ without dividing speed by 3.6 to obtain watts.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical power dissipated as heat rather than motor system efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by velocity (F/v) instead of multiplying P = Fv.

items.stem: Three NAND gates form the circuit shown. The first ties both inputs to A, and the second ties both to B. Their outputs D and E drive the third gate. Which single logic gate is equivalent?
items.workedSolution: Each tied NAND acts as a NOT gate ($D = \bar{A}$, $E = \bar{B}$). The output NAND computes $Q = \overline{\bar{A} \cdot \bar{B}} = \overline{\bar{A}} + \overline{\bar{B}} = A + B$, a single two-input OR gate.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that single two-input OR gate.

items.stem: A 4.20 m piece of cylindrical metal resistance wire (diameter 0.220 mm, resistivity 9.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) serves as a heating element across a steady 48.0 V DC supply.
items.workedSolution: Evaluate (a): A = 3.801 × 10⁻⁸ m², R = 105.0 Ω ≈ 105 Ω. Evaluate (b): P = V²/R = 22.0 W. Evaluate (c): V = AL = 1.597 × 10⁻⁷ m³, so s = ∛V = 5.42 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates A = πd²/4 = 3.80 × 10⁻⁸ m² and substitutes into R = ρL/A.
Correct resistance 105 Ω.
Correct power P = V²/R = 22.0 W.
Computes conserved volume V = AL = 1.60 × 10⁻⁷ m³ and sets s³ = V.
Correct cube edge length 5.42 mm.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical resistance of the wire.
Calculate the thermal power output of the heating element at 48.0 V.
The wire is later melted down without loss and cast into a solid cube. Calculate the edge length of the cube in mm.
workingSteps: Volume conserved: V = AL = 3.801 × 10⁻⁸ m² × 4.2 = 1.597 × 10⁻⁷ m³.

items.stem: Find the signed change in kinetic energy ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i. Striking a rubber stop at +18 m s⁻¹ for 12.5 ms, a trolley (mass 0.06 kg) rebounds straight back at 16 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Applying the relation: ΔE_k = ½m(v² − u²) = 0.5(0.06)((−16)² − 18²) = -2.04 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ½m(v² − u²) including negative sign to obtain -2.04 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes positive energy lost (E_k,i − E_k,f) instead of the signed change E_k,f − E_k,i.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates ½m(v − u)² instead of ½mv² − ½mu².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds the two kinetic energies because the velocity reversed sign, forgetting v² is always positive.

items.stem: Measurements on a rechargeable battery using an ideal voltmeter give 4.80 V on open circuit. A 6.00 Ω load reduces the terminal potential difference to 4.00 V. The load is then switched to a 2.40 Ω resistor.
items.workedSolution: Compute (a): I₁ = 0.6667 A, so r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.200 Ω ≈ 1.20 Ω. Compute (b): I₂ = 1.333 A, so V₂ = I₂R₂ = 3.200 V ≈ 3.20 V.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 0.667 A and substitutes into r = (ε − V₁) / I₁.
Correct internal resistance 1.20 Ω.
Uses V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) (or finds I₂ then I₂R₂).
Correct terminal potential difference 3.20 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.
workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 4 / 6 = 0.6667 A.
Internal resistance r = (ε − V₁) / I₁ = (4.8 − 4) / 0.6667 A = 1.200 Ω ≈ 1.20 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new terminal potential difference across the 2.40 Ω resistor.
workingSteps: Terminal pd V₂ = I₂ R₂ = 1.333 A × 2.4 = 3.200 V ≈ 3.20 V.

items.stem: For 8 min, a 4.50 V supply drives a steady current of 1.45 A through an electrolysis cell. Determine the total number of electrons flowing past a point in the wire.
items.workedSolution: SI time t = 8 × 60 = 480 s and current I = 1.450 A. Total charge Q = It = 696.0 C. Total electrons N = Q / e = 696.0 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 4.350 × 10²¹ ≈ 4.35 × 10²¹.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 4.35 × 10²¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert time from minutes to seconds (factor of 60 error).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applied the wrong unit conversion factor for current or time.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied charge by e instead of dividing Q by e.

items.stem: Two ruler readings are recorded for a flat steel spring: x₁ = 15 mm ± 1 mm unloaded and x₂ = 95 mm ± 1 mm loaded. The applied force is F = 60 N ± 0.6 N. Given Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx₁ + Δx₂, determine the percentage uncertainty in k = F / (x₂ − x₁).
items.workedSolution: Stretch length e = x₂ − x₁ = 95 − 15 = 80 mm and spread Δe = Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 1 + 1 = 2 mm. Thus %Δk = (%ΔF) + (%Δe) = (0.6/60 + 2/80) × 100% = 3.50%.

markScheme.criterion: Finds e = 80 mm, Δe = 2 mm, and obtains %Δk = 3.50%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the uncertainty of a single ruler reading Δx rather than summing Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 2Δx for the difference x₂ − x₁.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumes Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx − Δx = 0 by subtracting absolute uncertainties in a difference.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the fractional uncertainty of extension from %ΔF in the quotient F / e.

items.stem: An electrical supply delivers 2813 W to a motor for 50 s. It moves a model boat along a water tank at 6 m s⁻¹, with 600 N in the tow line at 60° to the path. How much energy is wasted during the 50 s interval?
items.workedSolution: Mechanical power P_out = Fv cos(60°) = 1800 W. Power wasted = 2813 − 1800 = 1013 W. Over 50 s, E_wasted = (1013)(50) = 5.07 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts Fv cos 60° from 2813 W and multiplies by 50 s to get 5.07 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes wasted power in watts (P_in − P_out) and forgets to multiply by the time interval.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the useful mechanical work done Fvt cos θ instead of the wasted energy.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to resolve cable tension by cos θ before subtracting from input power.

items.stem: Across the 0.9 mm × 0.35 mm end faces of a rectangular metal-oxide bar, a 6.00 V potential difference gives a resistance of 2.23 Ω. The bar measures 32 mm in length, 0.9 mm in width, and 0.35 mm in height.
items.workedSolution: Step (a): A = 3.150 × 10⁻⁷ m², which gives 2.20 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m. Step (b): P = V² / R = 16.14 W ≈ 16.1 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates A = w × h = 3.15 × 10⁻⁷ m² and substitutes into R = ρL/A.
Correct value 2.20 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m.
Substitutes V and R into P = V² / R.
Correct power dissipated 16.1 W.

Calculate the electrical power dissipated in the bar at this potential difference.
workingSteps: Use P = V² / R with V = 6.000 V and R = 2.230 Ω.

items.stem: An alloy wire of length 3 m and cross-sectional area 1.2 mm² extends elastically by 1.8 mm under a pulling force of 201.6 N. The uncertainties are ±3% in stress and ±2.5% in strain. Calculate the Young modulus E of the wire in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Tensile stress σ = F / A = 201.6 / (1.2 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.68 × 10⁸ Pa. Tensile strain ε = ΔL / L = (1.8 × 10⁻³) / 3 = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴. Young modulus E = σ / ε = 2.80 × 10¹¹ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates σ = F/A and ε = ΔL/L in SI units to obtain E = 2.80 × 10¹¹ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Converts mm² to m² using 10⁻³ instead of (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁶, underestimating stress and Young modulus by 10³.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets both mm² → 10⁻⁶ m² and mm → 10⁻³ m unit prefix powers properly.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies tensile stress by tensile strain (σ × ε) instead of dividing σ / ε.

items.stem: Increasing the potential difference across a filament bulb increases its electrical resistance.
items.workedSolution: Answers: (a) Greater current heats the metal filament raising its temperature. Next (b) Metal lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude so conduction electrons suffer more frequent collisions.

markScheme.criterion: Greater current heats the metal filament raising its temperature.
Metal lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude so conduction electrons suffer more frequent collisions.

parts.prompt: State what happens to the filament temperature as current increases. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Greater current heats the metal filament raising its temperature.
workingSteps: Key point: Greater current heats the metal filament raising its temperature.

parts.prompt: Explain in terms of lattice ions and electrons why resistance rises. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Metal lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude so conduction electrons suffer more frequent collisions.
workingSteps: Link (larger lattice ion vibrations impede electron drift and raise metallic resistance): Metal lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude so conduction electrons suffer more frequent collisions.

items.stem: In a uniform silver wire (free-electron density 5.80 × 10²⁸ m⁻³), the diameter is 0.800 mm. A steady current of 2.40 A passes through it. Determine the average electron drift speed in the wire.
items.workedSolution: Diameter in metres: d = 8.000 × 10⁻⁴ m. Wire area A = πd²/4 = 5.027 × 10⁻⁷ m². Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives v = I / (nAe) = 5.145 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 5.15 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 5.15 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in A = πr² (four times too large an area).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied by 4 instead of dividing by 4 in A = πd²/4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π when calculating the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: At 90 km h⁻¹ on a straight track, the driver of a test train applies the brakes. A steady deceleration of 3.5 m s⁻² lasts for 4.5 s.

items.stem: Measured values for a metal heating coil are R = 12 Ω ± 0.2 Ω and V = 30 V ± 0.5 V under a steady DC supply. Determine the power dissipated by the component.
items.workedSolution: Quick calculation: P = V² / R = 30² / 12 = 75.0 W.

items.stem: With no loss of material, a solid copper block (0.8 kg, density 8930 kg m⁻³) is drawn into a uniform wire of diameter 0.8 mm, or else cast as a solid cube. Determine the length of this drawn wire in m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value = 178 m.

options.distractorRationale: Uses diameter d instead of radius d/2 in A = πr², giving one quarter of the true length.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits π from the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: With dimensions 12 cm × 5 cm × 4.5 cm, an alloy cuboid contains 30% copper (density 8930 kg m⁻³) and 70% titanium (density 4510 kg m⁻³) by volume.

items.stem: For 0.4 kg of oil (specific heat capacity 1800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), a student switches on an electric heater at 144 W. After 100 s, the temperature rises by 15 K. Determine the energy lost to the surroundings over the 100 s interval.

items.stem: Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Lowered fully into freshwater of density 1000 kg m⁻³ without touching the bottom, a solid titanium block (22.5 kg, density 4510 kg m⁻³) hangs from a spring balance. Determine the apparent weight read on the spring balance.

items.stem: Which statement gives the full definition of Young's modulus for a solid material?
items.workedSolution: Young's modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the linear elastic region.

markScheme.criterion: Ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the linear elastic region.

options.label: A
options.text: It is the ratio of applied load to extension for a specific wire sample
options.distractorRationale: Defines the spring constant k = F / x (geometry dependent), not the material constant Young modulus.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the ratio of tensile strain to tensile stress across the plastic region
options.distractorRationale: Inverts stress over strain and uses the plastic region instead of the linear elastic region.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the maximum tensile stress a specimen can sustain before breaking
options.distractorRationale: Defines ultimate tensile strength rather than Young's modulus.

options.label: D
options.text: It is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the linear elastic region

items.stem: A tall tank holds oil of density ρ = 1100 kg m⁻³ ± 25 kg m⁻³ to a depth of h = 8.5 m ± 0.3 m. Take g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ with negligible uncertainty.

Obtains p = 9.16 × 10⁴ Pa.
Adds percentage uncertainties in ρ and h.
Obtains 5.80%.
Obtains Δp = 5.32 × 10³ Pa.

items.stem: Which pair of derived SI unit expressions are both equivalent to the volt?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference is work done per unit charge (V = W / Q), so one volt equals joule per coulomb and newton metre per coulomb (J C⁻¹ = N m C⁻¹ = J A⁻¹ s⁻¹).

markScheme.criterion: Joule per coulomb and newton metre per coulomb.

options.label: A
options.text: Both newton per coulomb and joule coulomb (N C⁻¹ and J C)
options.distractorRationale: Confuses electric field strength (N C⁻¹) and multiplied work-charge (J C) with potential difference.

options.label: B
options.text: Both joule per coulomb and newton metre per coulomb (J C⁻¹ and N m C⁻¹)

options.label: C
options.text: Both coulomb per joule and watt ampere (C J⁻¹ and W A)
options.distractorRationale: Inverts energy per unit charge and multiplies power by current instead of dividing.

options.label: D
options.text: Both joule per second and ampere second (J s⁻¹ and A s)
options.distractorRationale: Lists units for electrical power (watt) and charge (coulomb) rather than potential difference.

items.stem: A small sphere is launched vertically upward from a platform with initial velocity +40 m s⁻¹. Neglect air drag, take upward as positive with g = 9.8 m s⁻², and consider its motion 2.6 s later.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes u = +40 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.8 m s⁻² into v = u + at.
Obtains v = 14.5 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½gt² with consistent signs.
Obtains s = 70.9 m.
Obtains v_avg = 27.3 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A student measures the voltage across a large resistor in a potential divider. Why does a high-resistance digital voltmeter give a more accurate reading than a low-resistance analogue one?
items.workedSolution: Ideally, infinite internal resistance ensures negligible current is diverted through the voltmeter so the divider ratio stays unperturbed.

markScheme.criterion: Infinite internal resistance ensures negligible current is diverted through the voltmeter.

options.label: A
options.text: Because lower internal resistance allows extra current to boost the voltmeter coil deflection
options.distractorRationale: Extra meter current loads the divider and depresses the measured potential difference.

options.label: B
options.text: Because infinite resistance increases the electromotive force supplied by the power pack
options.distractorRationale: A voltmeter cannot alter the chemical electromotive force of the power supply.

options.label: C
options.text: Because higher meter resistance eliminates the internal resistance of the DC power pack
options.distractorRationale: The source internal resistance is fixed inside the supply regardless of the voltmeter.

options.label: D
options.text: Because infinite internal resistance ensures negligible current is diverted through the voltmeter

items.stem: In electrical physics, which statement defines one volt?
items.workedSolution: One volt is the potential difference when one joule of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge.

markScheme.criterion: Potential difference when one joule of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge.

options.label: A
options.text: The current flowing through a conductor when one joule of heat is produced each second
options.distractorRationale: Confuses potential difference with electric current and power.

options.label: B
options.text: The electrostatic force exerted on one coulomb of charge in a uniform electric field
options.distractorRationale: Defines electric field strength (N C⁻¹) rather than potential difference (J C⁻¹).

options.label: C
options.text: The total electrical energy stored inside a battery regardless of charge delivered
options.distractorRationale: Omits division by charge; voltage is energy per unit charge.

options.label: D
options.text: The potential difference when one joule of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge

items.stem: Wired in series with a fixed resistor across a constant-voltage battery, an NTC thermistor is placed in hot water. Without calculation, what changes in the circuit?
items.workedSolution: In an NTC thermistor divider, heating frees more charge carriers and lowers the thermistor resistance. Its share of potential difference falls while the fixed resistor voltage rises.

markScheme.criterion: Heating releases more charge carriers lowering thermistor resistance so its share of potential difference falls while the fixed resistor voltage rises.

options.label: A
options.text: As temperature increases, lattice vibration raises thermistor resistance so the fixed resistor receives a smaller voltage share
options.distractorRationale: Confuses a semiconductor NTC thermistor with a metal filament lamp.

options.label: B
options.text: As temperature increases, thermistor resistance drops to zero while total circuit current decreases
options.distractorRationale: Lowering series resistance increases, rather than decreases, circuit current.

options.label: C
options.text: As temperature increases, heating releases more charge carriers lowering thermistor resistance so its share of potential difference falls while the fixed resistor voltage rises

options.label: D
options.text: As temperature increases, potential difference across both the thermistor and fixed resistor increases simultaneously
options.distractorRationale: The two potential differences must sum to the constant battery electromotive force.

items.stem: Eight tightly crowded sine waves appear across an oscilloscope screen. How should the time-base be adjusted to measure the period more precisely, and what appears if the time-base is switched off?
items.workedSolution: Reduce the time-base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty. Switching the time-base off gives a vertical line of height equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Reduce the time-base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty. Switching the time-base off gives a vertical line of height equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce the time base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty and switching time base off produces a vertical line of height peak to peak voltage.

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the time-base setting to pack more cycles onto the screen, while switching time-base off turns the trace into a single stationary dot.
options.distractorRationale: Increasing ms div⁻¹ compresses cycles further; an AC signal with time-base off produces a vertical line of height V_pp (only DC makes a dot).

options.label: C
options.text: Increase Y-gain to stretch the trace horizontally, while switching time-base off displays a horizontal line at V_rms.
options.distractorRationale: Y-gain scales vertical voltage, not horizontal time; time-base off collapses horizontal sweep to zero.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce Y-gain to expand the horizontal period and switching time-base off clears the screen completely.
options.distractorRationale: Time-base controls horizontal sweep; with sweep off the electron beam oscillates vertically across V_pp.

items.stem: A parallel-plate air capacitor is charged first to a low voltage and later to a higher voltage.
items.workedSolution: Check (a): Capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. Check (b): Capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage. Key idea: capacitance equals charge stored divided by potential difference.

markScheme.criterion: Capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Links to principle: Capacitance equals charge stored divided by potential difference.
Capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.
One coulomb of charge stored when potential difference across the plates is one volt.

parts.prompt: Define the farad. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Main point: Capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Key idea: Capacitance equals charge stored divided by potential difference.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain whether raising the charging voltage alters the capacitance of the capacitor. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.
workingSteps: Explanation: Capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.
Avoid the common error of defining the farad as energy stored per volt rather than charge stored per volt.

items.stem: A student repeats a timing measurement several times using a stopwatch with a constant start-delay offset. Which statement correctly compares random and systematic errors?
items.workedSolution: Random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging.

markScheme.criterion: Random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging.

options.label: A
options.text: In experimental physics, systematic errors scatter unpredictably and are eliminated by taking a large mean
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the properties of random and systematic errors; averaging cannot fix a constant offset.

options.label: B
options.text: In experimental physics, random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging

options.label: C
options.text: In experimental physics, both random and systematic errors are completely removed by repeating readings
options.distractorRationale: Repeating and averaging reduces random scatter only and leaves systematic bias untouched.

options.label: D
options.text: In experimental physics, random errors shift every reading by the same fixed amount in one direction
options.distractorRationale: Describes a constant systematic zero error rather than random variation.

items.stem: In a lab trial, a charged capacitor discharges across a resistor. The test is repeated from the same voltage using a lower resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) Time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant. (b) Initial discharge current increases because initial voltage is divided by a smaller resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant.
Initial discharge current increases because initial voltage is divided by a smaller resistance.
