workingSteps: Link (shorter time constant produces a steeper exponential decay curve): Initial discharge current increases because initial voltage is divided by a smaller resistance.

items.stem: A skydiver leaps from a stationary balloon and falls vertically before opening the parachute. Why does the gradient of the skydiver's velocity–time graph decrease gradually toward zero?
items.workedSolution: The gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration: resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration.

markScheme.criterion: Resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration.

options.label: A
options.text: During the fall, gravitational field strength drops rapidly toward zero as altitude decreases
options.distractorRationale: Gravity stays virtually constant over skydiving altitudes.

options.label: B
options.text: During the fall, resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration

options.label: C
options.text: During the fall, air resistance stays constant while the skydiver loses mass
options.distractorRationale: Air drag grows strongly with speed while mass remains constant.

options.label: D
options.text: During the fall, upward drag decreases with speed so acceleration climbs smoothly
options.distractorRationale: Drag increases with speed, reducing acceleration.

items.stem: Swung on a string, a small stone travels at constant speed in a horizontal circle. Which option correctly explains both its acceleration and the work done by the centripetal force?
items.workedSolution: In uniform circular motion, velocity direction changes continuously so resultant centripetal force and acceleration act perpendicular to velocity toward the centre doing zero work.

markScheme.criterion: Velocity direction changes continuously so resultant centripetal force and acceleration act perpendicular to velocity toward the centre doing zero work.

options.label: A
options.text: Throughout the orbit, velocity direction changes continuously so resultant centripetal force and acceleration act perpendicular to velocity toward the centre doing zero work

options.label: B
options.text: Throughout the orbit, acceleration is zero because speed stays constant while an outward centrifugal force balances tension
options.distractorRationale: Velocity changes direction continuously so acceleration is non-zero; no outward centrifugal force acts on the stone.

options.label: C
options.text: Throughout the orbit, the centripetal force acts along the tangent and continually increases the kinetic energy
options.distractorRationale: Centripetal force points radially inward perpendicular to velocity, so speed and kinetic energy stay constant.

options.label: D
options.text: Throughout the orbit, acceleration points radially outward away from the centre while doing positive work
options.distractorRationale: Acceleration points toward the centre and perpendicular force does zero work.

items.stem: The wave speed v on a stretched wire obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ with a unit constant, where T is tension and μ is mass per unit length. A student measures T = 144 N ± 2.4 N and μ = 6 g m⁻¹ ± 0.3 g m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates SI base dimensions kg, m, s to deduce a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.
Converts linear density to 0.006 kg m⁻¹ and substitutes into √(T/μ).
Obtains v = 155 m s⁻¹.
Multiplies both %ΔT and %Δμ by 1/2 before adding.
Obtains 3.33%.
Obtains Δv = 5.16 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By equating SI base units on both sides of v = Tᵃ μᵇ, determine a and b and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: [T] = kg m s⁻² and [μ] = kg m⁻¹ ⇒ kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, so a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in v.
Determine the absolute uncertainty Δv in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A small mass moves in a circle of radius r = 1.6 m ± 0.08 m at speed v = 14 m s⁻¹ ± 0.3 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration is given by a = v² / r.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes v and r into a = v² / r.
Obtains a = 123 m s⁻².

Obtains 9.29%.
Obtains Δa = 11.4 m s⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the nominal centripetal acceleration a.

items.stem: A small sphere is launched vertically upward from a platform with initial velocity +18 m s⁻¹. Neglect air drag, take upward as positive with g = 9.81 m s⁻², and consider its motion 2.6 s later. Calculate its signed vertical velocity at t = 2.6 s.
items.workedSolution: Using v = u + at with u = +18 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻² gives v = 18 − (9.81)(2.6) = -7.51 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds gt to u instead of subtracting gt when upward is defined as positive.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the algebraic sign of the vertical velocity vector.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the mean vertical velocity u − ½gt rather than the instantaneous velocity u − gt.

items.stem: Melted with no loss of metal and cast into a solid cube, a cylindrical metal resistance wire had length 3.00 m, diameter 0.250 mm, and resistivity 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Calculate the edge length of the cube.
items.workedSolution: Wire area A = πd²/4 = 4.909 × 10⁻⁸ m², so volume V = AL = 1.473 × 10⁻⁷ m³. For a solid cube of equal volume, edge s = ∛V = 5.281 × 10⁻³ m = 5.28 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 5.28 mm.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in V = πr²L.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Took the square root rather than the cube root of the volume.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π from the cylindrical wire volume.

items.stem: A 0.4 kg steel block hits a flat metal plate head-on with velocity +12 m s⁻¹. After 20 ms of contact, it rebounds straight back at 9 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for opposite signs of u and v in Δp = m(v − u).
Obtains J = -8.40 N s.
Divides |J| by contact time in seconds (0.02 s).
Obtains F_avg = 420 N.

Obtains ΔE_k = -12.6 J.

items.stem: Terminal voltage across a lab battery is 4.50 V on open circuit (measured by a high-resistance voltmeter) and 3.60 V with a 6.00 Ω resistor. Calculate the new terminal voltage when the 6.00 Ω resistor is swapped for a 3.00 Ω resistor.
items.workedSolution: No-load reading yields ε = 4.50 V. With R₁ = 6 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 0.6000 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.500 Ω. With R₂ = 3 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 3.000 V ≈ 3.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 1.50 Ω and computes V₂ = 3.00 V.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumed terminal potential difference stays unchanged when load resistance changes.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: A steady current of 2.60 A flows through a soldering iron for 2 min across an 18.0 V supply.
items.workedSolution: Evaluate (a): A coulomb equals the electric charge transferred by a steady one-ampere current in one second. Evaluate (b): Q = It = 312.0 C, so N = Q/e = 1.950 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.95 × 10²¹ electrons. Evaluate (c): W = QV = 5.616 × 10³ J ≈ 5.62 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: States that one coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
Converts time to 120 s, computes Q = It = 312.0 C, and divides by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Correct electron count 1.95 × 10²¹.
Correct electrical work W = QV = 5.62 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Define the coulomb.
parts.expectedAnswer: The coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
workingSteps: Recall the SI definition linking electric charge, steady current, and time.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of conduction electrons passing through the device during the test.
workingSteps: Convert t = 2 × 60 = 120 s and I = 2.600 A.
Number of electrons N = Q / e = 312.0 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 1.950 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.95 × 10²¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total electrical work done by the supply during the test.

items.stem: Without a load, a metal spring in a lab press has pointer mark x₁ = 28 mm ± 0.5 mm. A force F = 18 N ± 0.8 N extends the metal spring in a lab press to x₂ = 128 mm ± 0.5 mm.

Obtains k = 180 N m⁻¹.

Obtains Δk = 9.80 N m⁻¹.

items.stem: A heavy trolley travels at steady speed 4 m s⁻¹ along a straight track for 50 s. It is pulled by an electric winch drawing 2560 W, with 600 N in the cable at 36.87° to the track.

items.stem: Made of graphite (resistivity 3.20 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m), a rectangular bar has length 45 mm, width 1.5 mm, and thickness 0.6 mm. Calculate its resistance between the opposite 1.5 mm × 0.6 mm end faces.
items.workedSolution: End-face area: A = w × h = (1.5 × 10⁻³ m) × (0.6 × 10⁻³ m) = 9.000 × 10⁻⁷ m², and L = 45 × 10⁻³ m. Using R = ρL/A yields 1.60 Ω.

items.stem: Marked "12 V, 24 W", a halogen work lamp operates at its rated potential difference. Calculate its resistance.
items.workedSolution: Step-by-step: Using P = V² / R gives R = V² / P = 12² / 24 = 6.000 Ω ≈ 6.00 Ω.

items.stem: A thin metal wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 0.75 mm² extends elastically by 1.2 mm under a tension of 126 N. The uncertainties are ±2.5% in stress and ±3% in strain.

items.stem: How is the electrical resistance of any two-terminal circuit component universally defined?
items.workedSolution: Quick calculation: For both ohmic and non-ohmic components, resistance is the ratio of potential difference across a component to the current flowing through it.

markScheme.criterion: Ratio of potential difference across a component to the current flowing through it.

options.label: A
options.text: It is the gradient of the tangent drawn to its current against potential difference graph
options.distractorRationale: Tangent gradient gives incremental conductance dI/dV, not static resistance V/I.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the product of potential difference across the component and current through it
options.distractorRationale: The product VI defines electrical power rather than resistance.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the ratio of potential difference across a component to the current flowing through it

options.label: D
options.text: It is the reciprocal of the area enclosed under its current against voltage characteristic
options.distractorRationale: Area under an I–V curve has no physical correspondence to resistance.

items.stem: Through a 1.00 mm diameter uniform metal alloy wire, a steady conventional current of 2.80 A flows from left to right. Take the free-electron density as 8.10 × 10²⁸ m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Evaluate (a): A = 7.854 × 10⁻⁷ m² ≈ 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². Evaluate (b): v = 2.75 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. Evaluate (c): Negatively charged conduction electrons drift opposite to conventional current (right to left).

markScheme.criterion: Converts diameter from mm to m and substitutes into A = πd²/4 (or πr²).
Correct cross-sectional area 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m² (4 s.f. 7.854 × 10⁻⁷ m²).
Rearranges I = nAve to v = I / (nAe) and substitutes values.
Correct final value 2.75 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.
States electrons drift opposite to conventional current (from right to left).

parts.expectedAnswer: Electrons drift from right to left, opposite to conventional current.
workingSteps: Conduction electrons carry negative charge, so they move opposite to conventional current.

items.stem: On a straight track, a braking interval of 3 s at 2.5 m s⁻² slows a test train from an initial speed of 90 km h⁻¹. Determine the braking distance, in metres, covered in 3 s.
items.workedSolution: Rewrite initial speed: u = 90 / 3.6 = 25 m s⁻¹. With a = −2.5 m s⁻², s = ut + ½at² = (25)(3) − 0.5(2.5)(3)² = 63.8 m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts 90 km h⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ and evaluates s = ut − ½|a|t² = 63.8 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Mixes km h⁻¹ and m s⁻¹ by substituting the speed in km h⁻¹ directly into s = ut + ½at² without dividing by 3.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Converts speed to m s⁻¹ correctly but uses +½at² instead of −½|a|t² during braking deceleration.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in the ½at² term.

items.stem: The voltage across a heater element is held steady at V = 8 V ± 0.3 V. Its resistance measures R = 10 Ω ± 0.2 Ω.

items.stem: Machined from solid aluminium of density 2700 kg m⁻³, a flat ring is 14 mm thick with an outer diameter of 48 mm and an inner hole of diameter 20 mm.
items.workedSolution: Solution: (a) V = π(R² − r²)h = 20.94 cm³ ≈ 20.9 cm³. Then (b) m = ρ V = 0.05653 kg ≈ 0.0565 kg. Lastly, (c) density remains constant and no mass is lost when remelting or redrawing the metal.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = π(R² − r²)h with radii and consistent unit conversion.
V = 20.9 cm³.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of the component in kg.

items.stem: To raise a load of mass 80 kg vertically through 20 m, an electric lift runs at steady speed for 24 s. It draws 907 W from the supply. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgh with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Obtains 1.57 × 10⁴ J.

Obtains 72.0%.

items.stem: A tall tank holds salt water of density ρ = 1200 kg m⁻³ ± 12 kg m⁻³ to a depth of h = 12 m ± 0.8 m. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ as exact. Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δp in the gauge pressure in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Nominal gauge pressure p = ρgh = 1.41 × 10⁵ Pa. Fractional uncertainty Δp/p = Δρ/ρ + Δh/h = 12/1200 + 0.8/12 = 0.0767. Hence Δp = 1.08 × 10⁴ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes p(Δρ/ρ + Δh/h) to obtain Δp = 1.08 × 10⁴ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the fractional uncertainties |Δρ/ρ − Δh/h| instead of adding them.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies absolute uncertainties Δρ × g × Δh directly instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Propagates fractional uncertainties correctly but forgets the factor of g in p = ρgh.

items.stem: Melting 60% gold (density 19300 kg m⁻³) with 40% silver (density 10500 kg m⁻³) by mass produces an alloy block of mass 4.4 kg. Assume the volumes add directly. Calculate the density of the alloy in g cm⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Masses: m₁ = 2.640 kg, m₂ = 1.760 kg. Volumes: V₁ = m₁/ρ₁ = 1.368 × 10⁻⁴ m³, V₂ = m₂/ρ₂ = 1.676 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Total volume V = V₁ + V₂ = 3.044 × 10⁻⁴ m³ (304.4 cm³). Alloy density ρ = m / V = 4.4 / 3.044 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.445 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.45 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ (14.5 g cm⁻³).

markScheme.criterion: Correct harmonic-mean alloy density = 14.5 g cm⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses an incorrect geometric factor or lever-arm ratio.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the volume-weighted arithmetic average instead of harmonic mean for a mass-fraction mix.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the mass percentages assigned to the two metals.

items.stem: The temperature of 2 kg of glycerol rises by 30 K after 80 s of heating at 2118 W. Its specific heat capacity is 2400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into Q = mcΔT.

items.stem: A spring balance supports a solid copper block of mass 22.5 kg and density 8930 kg m⁻³ completely inside freshwater (density 1000 kg m⁻³), clear of the base. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Method: (a) upthrust on a body matches the weight of displaced fluid. Second, (b) V = 2.520 × 10⁻³ m³ ⇒ F_B = 24.72 N ≈ 24.7 N. Third, (c) W_app = W − F_B = 196.0 N ≈ 196 N.

markScheme.criterion: Upthrust equals weight of displaced fluid.
Finds V = m / ρ_obj and applies F_B = ρ_fluid V g.
Subtracts upthrust from weight in air.
Apparent weight = 196 N.

parts.expectedAnswer: Archimedes' principle states that the upward buoyancy force equals the weight of fluid displaced by the body.
workingSteps: State that upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced by the body in the fluid.

parts.prompt: Calculate the upthrust acting on the fully under water block.
Hence calculate the reading on the spring balance while the block remains fully under water.
workingSteps: Spring balance tension = W − F_B = 196.0 N ≈ 196 N.

items.stem: Two students calibrate a digital balance using a certified reference mass. Student A obtains readings shown in the target diagram, tightly clustered but all shifted above the true value.
items.workedSolution: (a) Precision describes small spread between repeated measurements; accuracy describes closeness to the true value; the dataset shows high precision with systematic error and low accuracy. (b) Repeating and averaging only reduces random scatter; to fix systematic offset, identify and subtract zero error or recalibrate the instrument.

markScheme.criterion: Precision: closeness of repeated readings to each other / mean (small random spread).
Accuracy: closeness of measurement to the true value.
Identify high precision with systematic error and low accuracy.
Explain that systematic error shifts every reading identically so repeats/mean do not remove it.
State remedy: tare/zero, identify and subtract zero error or recalibrate the instrument.

items.stem: Under what condition is the current through a metal conductor directly proportional to the voltage across it?
items.workedSolution: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.

markScheme.criterion: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.

options.label: A
options.text: Specifically, Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant

options.label: B
options.text: Specifically, Ohm law applies to every circuit component regardless of temperature or heating
options.distractorRationale: Non-ohmic components and heated filaments violate direct proportionality.

options.label: C
options.text: Specifically, Ohm law applies only when current flows through a vacuum rather than a solid metal
options.distractorRationale: Metallic conductors at constant temperature are the primary ohmic devices.

options.label: D
options.text: Specifically, Ohm law applies only when a variable resistor increases circuit temperature smoothly
options.distractorRationale: Changing temperature changes metal resistivity and breaks linearity.

items.stem: A pressure gauge sits at depth h = 8.5 m ± 0.8 m in a deep water tank of density ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ ± 10 kg m⁻³. Take g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ as exact. Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δp in the gauge pressure in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Nominal gauge pressure p = ρgh = 8.33 × 10⁴ Pa. Fractional uncertainty Δp/p = Δρ/ρ + Δh/h = 10/1000 + 0.8/8.5 = 0.104. Hence Δp = 8.67 × 10³ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes p(Δρ/ρ + Δh/h) to obtain Δp = 8.67 × 10³ Pa.

options.label: A

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Propagates fractional uncertainties correctly but forgets the factor of g in p = ρgh.

items.stem: Unit consistency checks confirm whether electrical formulae are dimensionally homogeneous.

items.stem: A small probe is thrown vertically upward with initial velocity +18 m s⁻¹. Neglect air resistance, take upward as positive, and use g = 9.8 m s⁻² over 4.2 s. Calculate its signed vertical velocity at t = 4.2 s.

items.stem: Two ideal cells are connected in series with their positive terminals facing each other inside a single closed loop with two resistors. How does Kirchhoff's second law treat their electromotive forces?
items.workedSolution: In Kirchhoff's loop rule, opposing cells subtract algebraically when going around the loop in a consistent direction.

markScheme.criterion: Opposing cells subtract algebraically when going around the loop in a consistent direction.

options.label: A
options.text: When summing around the loop, opposing cells always add together to double the net circuit electromotive force
options.distractorRationale: Opposing polarities push charge in opposite directions around the loop, so their emfs subtract.

options.label: B
options.text: When summing around the loop, opposing cells subtract algebraically when traversing the loop in a consistent direction

options.label: C
options.text: When summing around the loop, the smaller cell is ignored completely while the larger cell drives the entire current
options.distractorRationale: Both cells contribute algebraically to the net emf around the loop.

options.label: D
options.text: When summing around the loop, current cannot flow unless both cells have identical electromotive force
options.distractorRationale: If the emfs differ, the difference drives current around the loop; equal opposing cells give zero net emf.

items.stem: Closing the switch on a bench lamp turns it on almost at once, even though conduction electrons drift very slowly.
items.workedSolution: Step (a): Conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current. Step (b): Mean drift velocity is very small even though the electric field establishes rapidly along the wire. Key idea: conventional current tracks positive charge flow so negative electrons move the opposite way.

markScheme.criterion: Conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.
Links to principle: Conventional current tracks positive charge flow so negative electrons move the opposite way.
Mean drift velocity is very small even though the electric field establishes rapidly along the wire.
Electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.

parts.prompt: State and explain the direction of conduction electron drift relative to conventional current. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.
workingSteps: Main point: Conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.
Key idea: Conventional current tracks positive charge flow so negative electrons move the opposite way.

parts.prompt: Contrast the magnitude of mean electron drift velocity with the rapid establishment of the electric field in the wire. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Mean drift velocity is very small even though the electric field establishes rapidly along the wire.
workingSteps: Explanation: Mean drift velocity is very small even though the electric field establishes rapidly along the wire.
Avoid the common error of assuming free electrons move in the same direction as conventional current at the speed of light.

items.stem: Two gliders collide on a frictionless horizontal air track with no external horizontal forces acting. Which comparison between an elastic and an inelastic collision is always correct?
items.workedSolution: In an isolated collision, linear momentum is conserved in both whereas total kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.

markScheme.criterion: Linear momentum is conserved in both whereas total kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.

options.label: A
options.text: In isolated collisions, kinetic energy is conserved in both whereas momentum is conserved only when gliders bounce apart
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the conservation rules: momentum is always conserved, while kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic impacts.

options.label: B
options.text: In isolated collisions, neither linear momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved when gliders stick together
options.distractorRationale: Even a completely inelastic sticking collision conserves linear momentum if no external force acts.

options.label: C
options.text: In isolated collisions, both momentum and kinetic energy increase after an elastic rebound
options.distractorRationale: Total energy and momentum cannot spontaneously increase in an isolated collision.

options.label: D
options.text: In isolated collisions, linear momentum is conserved in both whereas total kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision

items.stem: Which comparison correctly distinguishes electromotive force (emf) from potential difference (pd) in a DC circuit?
items.workedSolution: Electromotive force transfers energy to charge in a source whereas potential difference transfers electrical energy from charge to components.

markScheme.criterion: Electromotive force transfers energy to charge in a source whereas potential difference transfers electrical energy from charge to components.

options.label: A
options.text: Fundamentally, electromotive force transfers energy to charge in a source whereas potential difference transfers electrical energy from charge to components

options.label: B
options.text: Fundamentally, electromotive force is a mechanical pushing force in newtons whereas potential difference is measured in volts
options.distractorRationale: Misinterprets the word force in emf; both emf and pd are energy per unit charge measured in volts.

options.label: C
options.text: Fundamentally, electromotive force is always smaller than terminal potential difference whenever a cell supplies current
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the internal-resistance inequality: under load V = ε − Ir < ε.

options.label: D
options.text: Fundamentally, electromotive force measures charge delivered per second whereas potential difference measures resistance
options.distractorRationale: Confuses emf with electric current and pd with resistance.

items.stem: In an automatic lamp sensor, a potential divider combines a fixed resistor with a light-dependent resistor.
items.workedSolution: Working: (a) Greater incident light intensity liberates more mobile charge carriers lowering resistance of the light dependent resistor. For (b), Total series resistance falls causing current in the divider chain to increase.

markScheme.criterion: Greater incident light intensity liberates more mobile charge carriers lowering resistance of the light dependent resistor.
Total series resistance falls causing current in the divider chain to increase.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state how bright sunlight affects the resistance of the light-dependent resistor. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Greater incident light intensity liberates more mobile charge carriers lowering resistance of the light dependent resistor.
workingSteps: Key point: Greater incident light intensity liberates more mobile charge carriers lowering resistance of the light dependent resistor.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, explain how the potential difference across the light-dependent resistor changes. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Total series resistance falls causing current in the divider chain to increase.
workingSteps: Link (light lowers semiconductor resistance and redistributes series voltage share): Total series resistance falls causing current in the divider chain to increase.

items.stem: On a calibrated cathode-ray oscilloscope set to Y-gain 2.0 V div⁻¹ and time-base 0.5 ms div⁻¹, a signal generator produces a sine wave. The waveform measures 4.6 vertical divisions peak-to-peak and 3.2 horizontal divisions per cycle.
items.workedSolution: (a) $T = 1.60 × 10⁻³ s$, so $f = 1/T = 625 Hz$. (b) $V_0 = 4.60 V$, giving $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = 3.25 V$. (c) Reduce the time-base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty. Switching the time-base off gives a vertical line of height equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates period $T = 1.60 × 10⁻³ s$ from divisions × time-base.
Frequency $f = 625 Hz$.
Finds peak voltage $V_0 = 4.60 V$ and divides by $\sqrt{2}$.
Root-mean-square voltage $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = 3.25 V$.
Reduce time-base setting (ms div⁻¹) to stretch waveform horizontally and lower % uncertainty.
Time-base OFF collapses AC waveform to a vertical line of height equal to peak-to-peak voltage.

parts.prompt: Determine the frequency $f$ of the alternating signal.
Calculate the root-mean-square voltage $V_{\mathrm{rms}}$ of the signal.
Explain how adjusting the time-base improves period precision and describe the screen trace if the time-base is switched off.
parts.expectedAnswer: Reduce the time-base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty. Switching the time-base off gives a vertical line of height equal to the peak-to-peak voltage
workingSteps: Lower ms div⁻¹ stretches one cycle across more divisions, cutting % uncertainty.
With time-base OFF, AC forms a centred vertical line of length peak-to-peak voltage.

items.stem: With a closed-jaw zero error of +0.04 mm, a micrometer screw gauge (0.5 mm pitch, 50 thimble divisions) checks a metal resistance wire. The last visible sleeve mark is 2.5 mm and thimble division 23 aligns with the reference line. Determine the corrected diameter.
items.workedSolution: Raw reading $= 2.5 + 23 \times 0.01 = 2.73$ mm. Subtracting the signed zero error (+0.04 mm) gives corrected diameter $= 2.73 - (+0.04) = 2.69$ mm (2.69 mm).

markScheme.criterion: Corrected micrometer reading $= 2.69$ mm (2.69 mm).

items.stem: Which statement gives the complete definition of the joule in mechanics?
items.workedSolution: One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves its point of application one metre in the direction of the force.

markScheme.criterion: One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves its point of application one metre in the direction of the force.

options.label: A
options.text: Strictly, one joule is the force needed to move one kilogram through a distance of one metre
options.distractorRationale: Confuses force with work and mass with force.

options.label: B
options.text: Strictly, one joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves its point of application one metre in the direction of the force

options.label: C
options.text: Strictly, one joule is the work done whenever a force of one newton acts perpendicular to a displacement of one metre
options.distractorRationale: A force perpendicular to displacement does zero mechanical work.

options.label: D

items.stem: A micrometer screw gauge has a constant positive zero error that the experimenter forgets to subtract. Repeating the wire diameter measurement many times produces closely clustered readings. What is the effect of averaging?
items.workedSolution: Averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error.

markScheme.criterion: Averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error.

options.label: A
options.text: In this situation, averaging repeated measurements eliminates the zero error and makes the mean completely accurate
options.distractorRationale: Every reading shares the same positive offset, so the mean still carries the exact zero error.

options.label: B
options.text: In this situation, repeating measurements worsens random scatter without improving precision
options.distractorRationale: Repeating and averaging reduces random scatter and improves precision.

options.label: C
options.text: In this situation, averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error

options.label: D
options.text: In this situation, zero error automatically cancels because half the readings are too high and half too low
options.distractorRationale: Symmetric scatter describes random error, not a one-sided systematic zero offset.

items.stem: Voltage–time decay curves are plotted while a fully charged capacitor empties through a fixed resistor. A second run starts from equal potential difference across a smaller resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) Time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant. (b) Charge leaves the plates more rapidly so after any given elapsed interval the remaining potential difference is lower. Key idea: shorter time constant produces a steeper exponential decay curve.

markScheme.criterion: Time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant.
Links to principle: Shorter time constant produces a steeper exponential decay curve.
Charge leaves the plates more rapidly so after any given elapsed interval the remaining potential difference is lower.
Initial discharge current increases because initial voltage is divided by a smaller resistance.

items.stem: A steel ball bearing is released from rest at the surface of a tall column of viscous glycerol. Why does it eventually move downward at a constant terminal velocity?
items.workedSolution: Initially weight exceeds drag, then drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero.

markScheme.criterion: Drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero.

options.label: A
options.text: As the sphere accelerates, gravitational pull weakens with depth until the weight vanishes completely
options.distractorRationale: Weight stays constant near Earth's surface; acceleration stops because forces balance, not because gravity drops to zero.

options.label: B
options.text: As the sphere accelerates, upward viscous drag stays constant while kinetic energy reaches a fluid ceiling
options.distractorRationale: Viscous drag is speed-dependent and grows until it balances weight (and upthrust).

items.stem: At constant speed, a racing car drives around a flat circular track.
items.workedSolution: (a) Velocity is a vector so constant speed along a circular path still involves continuous velocity change and acceleration. (b) Because force is always perpendicular to instantaneous displacement the centripetal force does zero work and kinetic energy remains constant. Key idea: centripetal force alters direction of velocity without changing speed.

markScheme.criterion: Velocity is a vector so constant speed along a circular path still involves continuous velocity change and acceleration.
Links to principle: Centripetal force alters direction of velocity without changing speed.
Because force is always perpendicular to instantaneous displacement the centripetal force does zero work and kinetic energy remains constant.
Resultant centripetal force and acceleration always point perpendicular to instantaneous velocity toward the centre of the circle.

items.stem: The wave speed v on a stretched wire obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ with a unit constant, where T is tension (in N, or kg m s⁻²) and μ is mass per unit length. In a lab test, T = 216 N ± 1.5 N and μ = 12 g m⁻¹ ± 0.15 g m⁻¹. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the wave speed v.
items.workedSolution: Dimensional homogeneity gives v = T^(1/2) μ^(−1/2). Hence %Δv = ½(%ΔT) + ½(%Δμ) = 0.5(1.5/216 + 0.15/12) × 100% = 0.972%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses exponents |1/2| and |−1/2| to obtain %Δv = 0.972%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Sums %ΔT + %Δμ without multiplying by the 1/2 power factor from the square-root exponents.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainties because μ appears in the denominator of √(T/μ).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the combined percentage uncertainty by 2 instead of 1/2 for a square-root power.

items.stem: A small ball moves on a circular path of radius 1.2 m ± 0.05 m at speed 6 m s⁻¹ ± 0.5 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r. Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δa in the centripetal acceleration.
items.workedSolution: Nominal acceleration a = v²/r = 6² / 1.2 = 30.0 m s⁻². Fractional uncertainty Δa/a = 2(0.5/6) + (0.05/1.2) = 0.208. Absolute uncertainty Δa = a(Δa/a) = 6.25 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Calculates a = v²/r and multiplies by 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) to obtain Δa = 6.25 m s⁻².

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to double Δv/v for the squared v² factor before multiplying by a.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes absolute uncertainties (Δv)² / Δr directly into the formula v² / r.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Stops at the dimensionless fractional uncertainty Δa/a without multiplying by a = v²/r.

items.stem: In a school lab practical, a student measures a wire of diameter d = 0.6 mm ± 0.02 mm under a tension of F = 90 N ± 2 N. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the tensile stress σ = 4F / (πd²).
items.workedSolution: In σ = 4F / (πd²), the constant 4/π has zero uncertainty, so %Δσ = %ΔF + 2(%Δd) = (2/90 + 2 × 0.02/0.6) × 100% = 8.89%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates %ΔF + 2(%Δd) = 8.89%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the power exponent 2 on d² when propagating uncertainty in A = πd²/4.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts 2(%Δd) from %ΔF because d² sits in the denominator of 4F/(πd²).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies %Δd by the constant factor 4 in 4F/(πd²) instead of by the exponent 2.

items.stem: What is the total absolute pressure in kPa on a flat horizontal plate of area 2.2 m² at depth 31.5 m in open seawater (density 1025 kg m⁻³)? Take atmospheric pressure as 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: Column pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1025 × 9.81 × 31.5 = 3.167 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 3.17 × 10⁵ Pa. Absolute pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 3.167 × 10⁵ = 4.177 × 10⁵ Pa = 417.7 kPa ≈ 418 kPa. Total force F = p_abs A = 4.177 × 10⁵ × 2.2 = 9.190 × 10⁵ N ≈ 9.19 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 418 kPa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only gauge pressure ρgh and omits atmospheric pressure.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to multiply by g = 9.81 m s⁻².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts atmospheric pressure instead of adding it.

items.stem: How is the centre of gravity of a rigid object defined?

items.stem: A 20 m vertical rise takes 12 s at steady speed using a crane motor. Load is a steel beam of mass 300 kg, power input is 7664 W, and g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the percentage efficiency of the system.
items.workedSolution: Lift energy output ΔE_p = mgh = 300 × 9.81 × 20 = 5.89 × 10⁴ J. Motor input energy E_in = 7664 × 12 = 91968 J. Overall efficiency η = (ΔE_p / E_in) × 100% = 64.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgh / (P_in t) × 100% with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 64.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits gravitational field strength g when computing gravitational potential energy mgh.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input energy wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides useful energy mgh in joules directly by input power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

items.stem: A student writes down an edge length of 8 cm ± 0.08 cm and a mass of 2760 g ± 2 g for a solid plastic cube. Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δρ of the density, expressed in kg m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Start by computing ρ = (2.76) / (0.08)³ = 5.39 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Proportionate error: Δρ/ρ = (2/2760) + 3(0.08/8) = 0.0307. Therefore Δρ = ρ × (Δρ/ρ) = 166 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Combines SI density with fractional uncertainty Δm/m + 3ΔL/L to obtain Δρ = 166 kg m⁻³.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 3 from L³ when propagating the fractional uncertainty of the edge length.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the absolute uncertainty in g cm⁻³ rather than converting to kg m⁻³.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the fractional uncertainty of L³ from that of mass in the quotient m / L³.

items.stem: A collision with a flat plate reverses the motion of an ice ball of mass 1.5 kg. Incoming velocity is +15 m s⁻¹, rebound speed is 12 m s⁻¹ (v = −12 m s⁻¹), and contact lasts 5 ms. What is the magnitude of the average force acting during the 5 ms collision?
items.workedSolution: With incoming velocity +15 m s⁻¹ and rebound velocity as −12 m s⁻¹, |Δp| = 1.5(15 + 12) = 40.5 N s. With Δt = 5 × 10⁻³ = 0.005 s, F_avg = |Δp| / Δt = 8.10 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Computes |Δp| = m(u + v_reb) and divides by 0.005 s to obtain 8.10 × 10³ N.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts speed magnitudes m(u − v_reb)/Δt instead of accounting for velocity reversal m(u + v_reb)/Δt.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides by contact time in milliseconds without converting ms to seconds (off by 10³).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the impulse magnitude |Δp| in N s and forgets to divide by contact time Δt.

items.stem: Open-circuit testing of a lab battery with an ideal voltmeter gives 8.00 V. Connecting a 7.00 Ω load resistor lowers the terminal voltage to 7.00 V, after which it is changed to 3.00 Ω.
items.workedSolution: Method: (a) I₁ = 1.000 A, so r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.000 Ω ≈ 1.00 Ω. Second, (b) I₂ = 2.000 A, giving V₂ = I₂R₂ = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 1.00 A and substitutes into r = (ε − V₁) / I₁.
Correct internal resistance 1.00 Ω.
Uses V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) (or finds I₂ then I₂R₂).
Correct terminal potential difference 6.00 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.
workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 7 / 7 = 1.000 A.
Internal resistance r = (ε − V₁) / I₁ = (8 − 7) / 1.000 A = 1.000 Ω ≈ 1.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new terminal potential difference across the 3.00 Ω resistor.
workingSteps: New current I₂ = ε / (R₂ + r) = 8 / (3 + 1.000 Ω) = 2.000 A.
Terminal pd V₂ = I₂ R₂ = 2.000 A × 3 = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V.

items.stem: When a light sensor operates at 5.00 V for 6 min, it carries a steady current of 85 mA. Find how many conduction electrons pass a cross-section of the wire in this time.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 1.91 × 10²⁰.

items.stem: On a stiff spring, a student reads x₂ = 74 mm ± 0.8 mm when loaded by F = 36 N ± 0.5 N, compared with x₁ = 14 mm ± 0.8 mm unloaded. Find the absolute uncertainty Δk, expressed in N m⁻¹, for the spring constant.
items.workedSolution: Stretch length e = (74 − 14) × 10⁻³ = 0.06 m with Δe = 2(0.8) × 10⁻³ = 0.0016 m. Nominal k = 36 / 0.06 = 600 N m⁻¹. Proportionate error: Δk/k = 0.5/36 + 0.0016/0.06 = 0.0406, so Δk = 24.3 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines Δe = 2Δx with ΔF/F + Δe/e to obtain Δk = 24.3 N m⁻¹.

workingSteps: Link (resistance is defined by the direct ratio of voltage to current): Evaluated from the coordinate ratio rather than the reciprocal of the tangent gradient on a curved graph.

items.stem: Carrying a steady current of 1.80 A, a uniform copper wire has diameter 0.600 mm. Its free-electron density is 8.50 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the mean drift speed of the electrons.
items.workedSolution: Diameter in metres: d = 6.000 × 10⁻⁴ m. Wire area A = πd²/4 = 2.827 × 10⁻⁷ m². Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives v = I / (nAe) = 4.681 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 4.68 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 4.68 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in A = πr² (four times too large an area).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied by 4 instead of dividing by 4 in A = πd²/4.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π when calculating the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: Slowing uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² for 5 s, a train had an initial speed of 54 km h⁻¹ along a straight level track.

markScheme.criterion: Divides 54 by 3.6 to obtain u = 15 m s⁻¹ and applies v = u − |a|t.
Obtains v = 2.50 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½|a|t² or ½(u + v)t with SI units.
Obtains s = 43.8 m.
Obtains v_mean = 8.75 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Convert the initial speed into m s⁻¹ and calculate the speed at the end of the braking interval.
Calculate the distance travelled during the braking interval.
Determine the mean speed over this interval in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Calculate the electrical power dissipated when a school lab resistor has R = 6 Ω ± 0.4 Ω and V = 48 V ± 0.2 V.
items.workedSolution: Formula substitution: P = V² / R = 48² / 6 = 384 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates P = V²/R = 384 W.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes current I = V / R instead of electrical power P = V² / R.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies V × R (confusing V = IR with P = VI).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes V²R (confusing I²R with V²/R).

items.stem: Made of solid stainless steel (density 7870 kg m⁻³), a flat metal ring has thickness 22 mm, outer diameter 44 mm, and central hole diameter 30 mm. Calculate the mass of the ring in grams.
items.workedSolution: Outer radius R = 22 mm = 0.02200 m; inner radius r = 15 mm = 0.01500 m; thickness h = 0.02200 m. Volume V = π(R² − r²)h = 1.790 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (17.90 cm³). Mass m = ρ V = 0.1409 kg = 140.9 g ≈ 141 g.

markScheme.criterion: Correct mass = 141 g.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses outer and inner diameters instead of radii in π(R² − r²), inflating area by 4×.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats the washer as a solid cylinder and omits the central hole.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes π(R − r)² instead of π(R² − r²).

items.stem: A load of mass 80 kg is raised vertically through 20 m at steady speed by an electric lift. The lift takes 24 s at 907 W input power. Assume g = 9.8 m s⁻². Find the percentage efficiency of this arrangement.
items.workedSolution: Lift energy output ΔE_p = mgh = 80 × 9.8 × 20 = 1.57 × 10⁴ J. Motor input energy E_in = 907 × 24 = 21768 J. Overall efficiency η = (ΔE_p / E_in) × 100% = 72.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgh / (P_in t) × 100% with g = 9.8 m s⁻² to obtain 72.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits gravitational field strength g when computing gravitational potential energy mgh.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input energy wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides useful energy mgh in joules directly by input power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

items.stem: A sensor is lowered to depth h = 6 m ± 0.8 m in seawater of density ρ = 1250 kg m⁻³ ± 25 kg m⁻³. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ as exact.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into p = ρgh with g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.
Obtains p = 7.36 × 10⁴ Pa.
Adds percentage uncertainties in ρ and h.
Obtains 15.3%.
Obtains Δp = 1.13 × 10⁴ Pa.

parts.prompt: Calculate the hydrostatic gauge pressure p at depth h in pascals.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in p.
Hence state the absolute uncertainty Δp in pascals.

items.stem: A 4.8 kg metal alloy mixes 60% tungsten (19250 kg m⁻³) with 40% iron (7870 kg m⁻³) by mass, with total volume equal to the sum of both volumes.
items.workedSolution: Working: (a) A substance's density is its mass per unit volume. For (b), V₁ + V₂ = 393.6 cm³ ≈ 394 cm³. For (c), ρ = m / V = 1.220 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.22 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Defines density as mass per unit volume.
Finds both masses and sums V₁ = m₁/ρ₁ and V₂ = m₂/ρ₂.
Total volume = 394 cm³.
Converts cm³ to m³ (× 10⁻⁶) and divides total mass by total volume.
Alloy density = 1.22 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³.

parts.prompt: Define the density of a substance.
parts.expectedAnswer: Density is defined as mass per unit volume of a material.
workingSteps: State that density is mass divided by volume.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total volume of the cast alloy sample in cm³.
Hence calculate the overall density of the alloy in kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Over 80 s, a heating element drawing 1800 W supplies energy to 2 kg of oil. The sample (c = 1800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) warms by 30 K. Work out the heat lost to the surroundings during the 80 s.
items.workedSolution: Heater input energy E_in = P_in t = 1800 × 80 = 144000 J. Useful heat stored Q = mcΔT = 2 × 1800 × 30 = 108000 J. Escaped heat = E_in − Q = 3.60 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mcΔT (108000 J) from P_in t (144000 J) to obtain 3.60 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the thermal energy absorbed by the sample Q = mcΔT rather than the heat lost to the surroundings.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the total electrical energy supplied P_in t instead of subtracting mcΔT.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the rate of heat loss in watts without multiplying by the heating time t.

items.stem: Suspended from a spring balance, a solid titanium block (mass 22.5 kg, density 4510 kg m⁻³) is lowered completely into seawater of density 1025 kg m⁻³. It does not touch the base. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the upthrust acting on the block.
items.workedSolution: Object volume V = m / ρ_obj = 22.5 / 4510 = 4.989 × 10⁻³ m³. Upthrust F_B = ρ_fluid V g = 1025 × 4.989 × 10⁻³ × 9.81 = 50.16 N ≈ 50.2 N. Measured weight W_app = m g − F_B = 220.7 − 50.16 = 170.6 N ≈ 171 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value = 50.2 N.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses object density instead of fluid density, recovering the object's own weight.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reports apparent weight instead of upthrust.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes displaced mass in kg without multiplying by g = 9.81 m s⁻².

items.stem: What is the approximate order of magnitude of the kinetic energy of an adult sprinter running at top speed?
items.workedSolution: Taking typical adult mass $m \approx 75\text{ kg}$ and sprint speed $v \approx 9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives $E_{\text{k}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \approx 0.5 \times 75 \times 81 \approx 3.0 \times 10^3\text{ J}$, which is of order $1.00 \times 10^3\text{ J}$. Option C (1.00 × 10³ J) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Order of magnitude estimate matches $10^3\text{ J}$ (1.00 × 10³ J, option C).

items.stem: Which statement correctly defines tensile stress in a stretched metal wire?
items.workedSolution: Tensile stress is the tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area.

markScheme.criterion: Tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area.

options.label: A
options.text: It is the tensile force acting per unit total outer surface area of the wire
options.distractorRationale: Uses cylindrical surface area instead of cross-sectional area perpendicular to the load.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the extension produced per unit original length of the stretched wire
options.distractorRationale: Defines tensile strain rather than tensile stress.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area

options.label: D
options.text: It is the product of tensile force and cross sectional area of the wire
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies force by area instead of dividing force by cross-sectional area.

items.stem: A student measures current and potential difference for a uniform resistance wire to verify Ohm's law.
items.workedSolution: Method: (a) Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant. Second, (b) Keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.

markScheme.criterion: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.
Keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.

parts.prompt: State the physical condition required for Ohm's law to remain valid. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.
workingSteps: Key point: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.

parts.prompt: State one practical precaution to prevent heating of the wire during measurements. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.
workingSteps: Link (limiting current prevents self heating from distorting a linear ohmic plot): Keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.

Obtains p = 1.59 × 10⁵ Pa.

Obtains 5.78%.
Obtains Δp = 9.17 × 10³ Pa.

items.stem: Which combination correctly gives two SI unit forms equivalent to the ohm?
items.workedSolution: Resistance equals potential difference divided by current, yielding volt per ampere and joule second per coulomb squared.

markScheme.criterion: Volt per ampere and joule second per coulomb squared.

options.label: A
options.text: Both ampere per volt and coulomb squared per joule second (A V⁻¹ and C² J⁻¹ s⁻¹)
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the definition R = V / I into electrical conductance.

options.label: B
options.text: Both volt ampere and joule per coulomb second (V A and J C⁻¹ s⁻¹)
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies voltage and current instead of taking their ratio.

options.label: C
options.text: Both joule per ampere and newton metre per ampere (J A⁻¹ and N m A⁻¹)
options.distractorRationale: Omits the time factor converting charge into current squared.

options.label: D

items.stem: A steel ball is launched vertically upward in a vacuum tube at +22 m s⁻¹. Take upward as positive and g = 9.8 m s⁻² as the motion is recorded after 2.9000000000000004 s.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes u = +22 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.8 m s⁻² into v = u + at.
Obtains v = -6.42 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½gt² with consistent signs.
Obtains s = 22.6 m.
Obtains v_avg = 7.79 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the signed vertical velocity at the stated time.
Calculate the vertical displacement relative to the launch point.
Determine the average vertical velocity over this time interval.

items.stem: A student uses an ideal voltmeter to measure the potential difference across a resistor. How should it be connected, and what resistance should it have?
items.workedSolution: An ideal voltmeter is connected in parallel with infinite resistance so zero current bypasses the resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Connected in parallel with infinite resistance.

options.label: A
options.text: It must be connected in series with infinite resistance
options.distractorRationale: Wiring an infinite-resistance meter in series would block circuit current completely.

options.label: B
options.text: It must be connected in parallel with infinite resistance

options.label: C
options.text: It must be connected in parallel with zero resistance
options.distractorRationale: A zero-resistance parallel meter would short-circuit the resistor.

options.label: D
options.text: It must be connected in series with zero resistance
options.distractorRationale: Describes the wiring and resistance of an ideal ammeter instead of a voltmeter.

items.stem: Three branches meet at a soldered node in a direct-current circuit.
items.workedSolution: Part (a) — Algebraic sum of currents meeting at any circuit junction is zero. Part (b) — Consequence of conservation of electric charge because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.

markScheme.criterion: Algebraic sum of currents meeting at any circuit junction is zero.
Consequence of conservation of electric charge because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.

parts.prompt: State Kirchhoff's first law. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Algebraic sum of currents meeting at any circuit junction is zero.
workingSteps: Key point: Algebraic sum of currents meeting at any circuit junction is zero.

parts.prompt: State the fundamental conservation law that it represents. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Consequence of conservation of electric charge because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.
workingSteps: Link (junction current rule follows directly from charge conservation): Consequence of conservation of electric charge because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.

items.stem: A steady direct current travels from left to right along a copper wire. How do the free conduction electrons move inside the wire?
items.workedSolution: Because conduction electrons are negatively charged, electrons drift slowly opposite to conventional current (from right to left here).

markScheme.criterion: Electrons drift slowly opposite to conventional current.

options.label: A
options.text: Free electrons drift slowly opposite to conventional current

options.label: B
options.text: Free electrons travel rapidly in the same direction as conventional current at the speed of light
options.distractorRationale: Confuses electromagnetic field propagation speed with slow electron drift and reverses the direction.

options.label: C
options.text: Free electrons drift slowly in the same direction as conventional current from positive to negative
options.distractorRationale: Forgets that electrons carry negative charge so they drift opposite to conventional current.

options.label: D
options.text: Free electrons remain stationary while positive copper lattice ions migrate along the wire
options.distractorRationale: Lattice ions in a solid metal vibrate about fixed positions and do not drift as current carriers.

items.stem: Two pucks collide on a frictionless air table in an isolated laboratory demonstration.
items.workedSolution: Compute (a): Total linear momentum is conserved in every isolated collision regardless of elasticity. Compute (b): Total kinetic energy before equals total kinetic energy after only in an elastic collision.

markScheme.criterion: Total linear momentum is conserved in every isolated collision regardless of elasticity.
Total kinetic energy before equals total kinetic energy after only in an elastic collision.

parts.prompt: State what happens to total linear momentum in both elastic and inelastic impacts. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Total linear momentum is conserved in every isolated collision regardless of elasticity.
workingSteps: Key point: Total linear momentum is conserved in every isolated collision regardless of elasticity.

parts.prompt: State the kinetic energy criterion that distinguishes an elastic impact from an inelastic one. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Total kinetic energy before equals total kinetic energy after only in an elastic collision.
workingSteps: Link (comparing total kinetic energy before and after tests whether a collision is elastic): Total kinetic energy before equals total kinetic energy after only in an elastic collision.

items.stem: Both electromotive force and potential difference are expressed in volts, yet they describe opposite energy transfers.
items.workedSolution: (a) Electromotive force is energy converted from chemical or non electrical forms into electrical energy per unit charge. (b) Potential difference is electrical energy transferred into thermal or other forms per unit charge across a component.

markScheme.criterion: Electromotive force is energy converted from chemical or non electrical forms into electrical energy per unit charge.
Potential difference is electrical energy transferred into thermal or other forms per unit charge across a component.

parts.prompt: Define electromotive force (emf). [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Electromotive force is energy converted from chemical or non electrical forms into electrical energy per unit charge.
workingSteps: Key point: Electromotive force is energy converted from chemical or non electrical forms into electrical energy per unit charge.

parts.prompt: Define potential difference (pd) across a circuit component. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Potential difference is electrical energy transferred into thermal or other forms per unit charge across a component.
workingSteps: Link (direction of energy conversion distinguishes a source from a load): Potential difference is electrical energy transferred into thermal or other forms per unit charge across a component.

items.stem: A bright lamp is switched on above a light-dependent resistor wired in series with a fixed resistor across an ideal DC supply. Without calculation, how does the circuit respond immediately?
items.workedSolution: For an illuminated LDR, brighter light releases more charge carriers reducing light dependent resistor resistance so circuit current rises and its voltage share decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Brighter light releases more charge carriers reducing light dependent resistor resistance so circuit current rises and its voltage share decreases.

options.label: A
options.text: Under illumination, incident photons block electron motion increasing light dependent resistor resistance and lowering current
options.distractorRationale: Light frees additional charge carriers in an LDR, lowering rather than raising its resistance.

options.label: B
options.text: Under illumination, resistance falls so potential difference across the light dependent resistor increases
options.distractorRationale: A smaller resistance receives a smaller fraction of the fixed supply voltage.

options.label: C
options.text: Under illumination, circuit current stays constant because the fixed resistor governs the whole loop
options.distractorRationale: Total series resistance equals the sum of both resistances, so reducing LDR resistance raises total current.

options.label: D
options.text: Under illumination, brighter light releases more charge carriers reducing light dependent resistor resistance so circuit current rises and its voltage share decreases

items.stem: While viewing an AC signal on a CRO, a student varies the time-base control. Which statement correctly describes what the time-base setting changes?
items.workedSolution: Reduce the time-base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty. Switching the time-base off gives a vertical line of height equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Reduce the time-base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty. Switching the time-base off gives a vertical line of height equal to the peak-to-peak voltage.

options.label: A
options.text: Switching time-base off produces a vertical line of height equal to peak voltage V₀ rather than peak-to-peak voltage.
options.distractorRationale: The beam swings from −V₀ to +V₀, giving total vertical length 2V₀ = V_pp.

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing the time-base setting decreases the actual frequency of the alternating generator.
options.distractorRationale: Adjusting CRO time-base changes only the display horizontal scale, never the source frequency.

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce the time base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty and switching time base off produces a vertical line of height peak to peak voltage.

options.label: D
options.text: Switching time-base off converts the alternating supply into a constant direct current voltage.
options.distractorRationale: The supply remains alternating; only the horizontal sweep voltage inside the CRO stops.

items.stem: What is the corrected diameter of a thin steel guitar string checked with a micrometer screw gauge (0.5 mm pitch, 50 thimble divisions)? The sleeve shows 4.0 mm, thimble division 37 aligns with the reference line, and the zero error is -0.03 mm.
items.workedSolution: Raw reading $= 4.0 + 37 \times 0.01 = 4.37$ mm. Subtracting the signed zero error (-0.03 mm) gives corrected diameter $= 4.37 - (-0.03) = 4.40$ mm (4.40 mm).

markScheme.criterion: Corrected micrometer reading $= 4.40$ mm (4.40 mm).

items.stem: Using Vernier callipers (resolution 0.05 mm), a student measures the outer diameter of a brass pendulum bob. The closed-jaw zero error is +0.05 mm. The vernier zero passes 18 mm and vernier division 7 aligns with a main-scale mark. Calculate the corrected diameter.
items.workedSolution: Raw Vernier reading $= 18 + 7 \times 0.05 = 18.35$ mm. Correcting for zero error (+0.05 mm): $18.35 - (+0.05) = 18.30$ mm.

markScheme.criterion: Corrected Vernier reading $= 18.30$ mm (18.30 mm).

items.stem: Capacitors store separated electric charge on conducting plates across a dielectric.
items.workedSolution: Answers: (a) The farad is the capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. Key points: Charge stored on one plate per unit potential difference across the capacitor. One coulomb of charge stored when potential difference across the plates is one volt.

markScheme.criterion: Charge stored on one plate per unit potential difference across the capacitor.
One coulomb of charge stored when potential difference across the plates is one volt.

parts.prompt: Define the farad. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: The farad is the capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Key idea: Capacitance equals charge stored divided by potential difference.
Include both points: Charge stored on one plate per unit potential difference across the capacitor and one coulomb of charge stored when potential difference across the plates is one volt.

items.stem: The wave speed v on a stretched wire obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ with a unit constant, where T is tension (in N, or kg m s⁻²) and μ is mass per unit length. In a lab test, T = 120 N ± 2 N and μ = 4 g m⁻¹ ± 0.2 g m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates SI base dimensions kg, m, s to deduce a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.
Converts linear density to 0.004 kg m⁻¹ and substitutes into √(T/μ).
Obtains v = 173 m s⁻¹.
Multiplies both %ΔT and %Δμ by 1/2 before adding.
Obtains 3.33%.
Obtains Δv = 5.77 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By equating SI base units on both sides of v = Tᵃ μᵇ, determine a and b and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: [T] = kg m s⁻² and [μ] = kg m⁻¹ ⇒ kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, so a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in v.
Determine the absolute uncertainty Δv in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A small ball moves on a circular path of radius 1.5 m ± 0.08 m at speed 18 m s⁻¹ ± 0.15 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes v and r into a = v² / r.
Obtains a = 216 m s⁻².
Uses 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) and converts to a percentage.
Obtains 7.00%.
Obtains Δa = 15.1 m s⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the nominal centripetal acceleration a.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a.
Determine the absolute uncertainty Δa.

items.stem: A steel ball is launched vertically upward in a vacuum tube at +28 m s⁻¹. Take upward as positive and g = 9.81 m s⁻² as the motion is recorded after 2.2 s. Calculate its vertical displacement from the launch point at t = 2.2 s.
items.workedSolution: With upward positive, u = +28 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻². Vertical displacement s = ut + ½at² = (28)(2.2) − 0.5(9.81)(2.2)² = 37.9 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses s = ut − ½gt² with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 37.9 m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses +g instead of −g when initial velocity is upward, adding ½gt² to ut.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 1/2 in the gravitational displacement term −½gt².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the motion as release from rest and omits the upward initial-velocity term ut.

Obtains σ = 3.98 × 10⁷ Pa.

Obtains 3.44%.
Obtains Δσ = 1.37 × 10⁶ Pa.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in σ.
Hence state the absolute uncertainty Δσ in pascals.

items.stem: Consider a 2.2 m² flat horizontal plate 30 m below an open ethanol surface of density 790 kg m⁻³. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻² and 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.
items.workedSolution: Evaluate (a): Δp = ρgh = 2.325 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 2.32 × 10⁵ Pa. Evaluate (b): p_abs = 1.01 × 10⁵ + Δp = 3.335 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 3.33 × 10⁵ Pa. Evaluate (c): F = p_abs A = 7.337 × 10⁵ N ≈ 7.34 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Δp = ρgh with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Adds atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa to Δp.
p_abs = 3.33 × 10⁵ Pa.
Uses F = p_abs A.

parts.prompt: Calculate the hydrostatic pressure increase Δp due to the column of liquid alone.
Determine the total absolute pressure acting at this depth.
Calculate the total downward force exerted on the flat surface.

items.stem: A horizontal footbridge beam rests on two masonry piers and carries a stationary pedestrian.
items.workedSolution: Solution: (a) For a body in equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot. Then (b) Choosing the pivot at an unknown reaction eliminates that force from the moment equation. Key idea: rotational equilibrium balances clockwise and anticlockwise turning effects.

markScheme.criterion: For a body in equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot.
Links to principle: Rotational equilibrium balances clockwise and anticlockwise turning effects.
Choosing the pivot at an unknown reaction eliminates that force from the moment equation.
Complete rigid body equilibrium also requires zero resultant force in any direction.

parts.prompt: State the principle of moments for a rigid body in rotational equilibrium. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: For a body in equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot.
workingSteps: Main point: For a body in equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot.
Key idea: Rotational equilibrium balances clockwise and anticlockwise turning effects.

parts.prompt: State the second condition for static equilibrium and explain why choosing a support as pivot simplifies reaction calculations. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Choosing the pivot at an unknown reaction eliminates that force from the moment equation.
workingSteps: Explanation: Choosing the pivot at an unknown reaction eliminates that force from the moment equation.
Avoid the common error of assuming zero resultant moment alone guarantees equilibrium even when resultant force is non zero.

items.stem: At steady speed, a warehouse lift raises a crate of mass 300 kg vertically through 15 m in 20 s. The electrical power input is 3449 W. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgh with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Obtains 4.41 × 10⁴ J.
Divides ΔE_p by P_in t and multiplies by 100%.
Obtains 64.0%.
Obtains E_wasted = 2.48 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained by the load.
Calculate the percentage efficiency of the hoisting system.
Determine the energy wasted during the lift.

items.stem: Measurements on a solid rock cube show that its mass is 4300 g ± 2.5 g. Each side has length 8 cm ± 0.08 cm.
items.workedSolution: Method: (a) m = 4.3 kg and L = 0.08 m, so ρ = m / L³ = 8.40 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Second, (b) %Δρ = (2.5/4300 + 3 × 0.08/8) × 100% = 3.06%. Third, (c) Δρ = ρ × (Δρ/ρ) = 257 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Converts mass to kg (× 10⁻³) and cubes converted side length (× 10⁻⁶ m³).
Obtains ρ = 8.40 × 10³ kg m⁻³.
Sums percentage uncertainty in mass with three times the percentage uncertainty in side length.
Obtains 3.06%.
Multiplies nominal density by fractional uncertainty to obtain Δρ = 257 kg m⁻³.

parts.prompt: Calculate the nominal density ρ of the cube in coherent SI units (kg m⁻³).
workingSteps: Convert inputs to SI base units: m = 4300 × 10⁻³ = 4.3 kg, L = 8 × 10⁻² = 0.08 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the percentage uncertainty in the calculated density.
Hence state the absolute uncertainty Δρ in kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Ice melts at zero Celsius and water boils at one hundred Celsius under standard atmospheric pressure.
items.workedSolution: Step (a): Thermal energy required per unit mass to change state at constant temperature. Step (b): Specific latent heat of vaporisation exceeds fusion because intermolecular bonds are completely broken and work is done expanding against atmospheric pressure. Key idea: latent heat changes molecular potential energy without changing temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Thermal energy required per unit mass to change state at constant temperature.
Links to principle: Latent heat changes molecular potential energy without changing temperature.
Specific latent heat of vaporisation exceeds fusion because intermolecular bonds are completely broken and work is done expanding against atmospheric pressure.
State change occurs completely at constant temperature.

parts.prompt: Define specific latent heat. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Thermal energy required per unit mass to change state at constant temperature.
workingSteps: Main point: Thermal energy required per unit mass to change state at constant temperature.
Key idea: Latent heat changes molecular potential energy without changing temperature.

parts.prompt: Explain why specific latent heat of vaporisation is much larger than specific latent heat of fusion for the same substance. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Specific latent heat of vaporisation exceeds fusion because intermolecular bonds are completely broken and work is done expanding against atmospheric pressure.
workingSteps: Explanation: Specific latent heat of vaporisation exceeds fusion because intermolecular bonds are completely broken and work is done expanding against atmospheric pressure.
Avoid the common error of including a temperature rise in the definition of specific latent heat.

items.stem: A capillary tube containing dry air trapped behind a movable bead of oil is warmed in a beaker.
items.workedSolution: Solution: (a) Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature measured in kelvin. Then (b) Requires both a fixed mass of gas and constant pressure.

markScheme.criterion: Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature measured in kelvin.
Requires both a fixed mass of gas and constant pressure.

parts.prompt: State Charles's law relating gas volume and temperature. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature measured in kelvin.
workingSteps: Key point: Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature measured in kelvin.

parts.prompt: State the two controlled variables required for Charles's law to hold. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Requires both a fixed mass of gas and constant pressure.
workingSteps: Link (isobaric expansion scales volume directly with absolute kelvin temperature): Requires both a fixed mass of gas and constant pressure.

items.stem: An electric train travels along level rails at a steady speed of 36 km h⁻¹ against a resistive force of 2400 N. It draws 28571 W of electrical power for 80 s.

markScheme.criterion: Converts speed to 10 m s⁻¹ and uses E_useful = Fvt.
Obtains 1.92 × 10⁶ J.
Divides useful mechanical power/energy by electrical input.
Obtains 84.0%.
Obtains E_wasted = 3.66 × 10⁵ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the useful mechanical energy delivered against drag over the interval.
Determine the percentage efficiency of the motor system.
Calculate the energy wasted as heat during the interval.

items.stem: Pulled for 8 s by a strap at 60° above the horizontal, a heavy crate of mass 20 kg accelerates along smooth rollers. The force is 120 N and initial speed is 3 m s⁻¹. Find the horizontal speed reached after these 8 s.
items.workedSolution: Horizontal component F_x = 120 cos(60°) = 60 N ⇒ a_x = 3 m s⁻². Final speed v = u + a_x t = 3 + (3)(8) = 27.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a_x = 3 m s⁻² via F cos 60° / m and obtains v = 27.0 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the vertical component F sin θ instead of F cos θ to compute horizontal acceleration.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies F/m directly without resolving the angled force vector horizontally.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the velocity change Δv = a_x t and forgets to add the initial speed u.

items.stem: A two-input, five-gate comparator network is shown, with internal nodes D and E feeding final output Q.
items.workedSolution: (a) $Q = (\bar{A} \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})$ (not A and B or A and not B forming an EOR gate). (b) 2 rows of the 4-row truth table give $Q = 1$. (c) Equivalent to a single two-input EOR gate.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly expresses intermediate nodes D and E in terms of inputs.
Writes exact unsimplified Boolean expression for Q ($Q = (\bar{A} \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})$).
Correctly simplifies expression: not A and B or A and not B forming an EOR gate.
Evaluates all 4 input rows accurately.
States 2 rows give $Q = 1$.
Identifies equivalent single two-input EOR gate.
