items.stem: With resistivity 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, a cylindrical metal resistance wire measures 2.50 m in length and 0.300 mm in diameter. After melting with no loss, it is cast as a solid cube. Determine the cube edge length.
items.workedSolution: Wire area A = πd²/4 = 7.069 × 10⁻⁸ m², so volume V = AL = 1.767 × 10⁻⁷ m³. For a solid cube of equal volume, edge s = ∛V = 5.612 × 10⁻³ m = 5.61 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 5.61 mm.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in V = πr²L.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Took the square root rather than the cube root of the volume.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π from the cylindrical wire volume.

items.stem: In a head-on collision, a trolley of mass 0.25 kg hits a rubber stop at +32 m s⁻¹, stays touching for 10 ms, and rebounds back at 20 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for opposite signs of u and v in Δp = m(v − u).
Obtains J = -13.0 N s.
Divides |J| by contact time in seconds (0.01 s).
Obtains F_avg = 1.30 × 10³ N.
Uses ½m(v² − u²).
Obtains ΔE_k = -78.0 J.

parts.prompt: Taking the incoming direction as positive, calculate the signed impulse J delivered to the object.
Calculate the magnitude of the average contact force during the impact.
Determine the signed change in kinetic energy ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i.

items.stem: Measured with a high-resistance voltmeter across a bench battery, the open-circuit voltage is 10.5 V and the reading across a 12.0 Ω resistor is 9.00 V. Determine the voltage across a 4.00 Ω resistor replacing the 12.0 Ω resistor.
items.workedSolution: Unloaded voltmeter shows ε = 10.5 V. With R₁ = 12 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 0.7500 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 2.000 Ω. With R₂ = 4 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 7.000 V ≈ 7.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 2.00 Ω and computes V₂ = 7.00 V.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumed terminal potential difference stays unchanged when load resistance changes.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: Across a 9.00 V DC supply, an electrolysis cell takes a steady 1.25 A for 4 min.
items.workedSolution: Evaluate (a): One coulomb is defined as the charge flowing past a point in one second at one ampere. Evaluate (b): Q = It = 300.0 C, so N = Q/e = 1.875 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.88 × 10²¹ electrons. Evaluate (c): W = QV = 2.700 × 10³ J ≈ 2.70 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: States that one coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
Converts time to 240 s, computes Q = It = 300.0 C, and divides by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Correct electron count 1.88 × 10²¹.
Correct electrical work W = QV = 2.70 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Define the coulomb.
parts.expectedAnswer: The coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
workingSteps: Recall the SI definition linking electric charge, steady current, and time.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of conduction electrons passing through the device during the test.
workingSteps: Convert t = 4 × 60 = 240 s and I = 1.250 A.
Number of electrons N = Q / e = 300.0 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 1.875 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.88 × 10²¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total electrical work done by the supply during the test.

items.stem: A force of F = 18 N ± 0.4 N stretches a flat steel spring. Before loading, the ruler reads x₁ = 25 mm ± 0.5 mm; with the load, it reads x₂ = 105 mm ± 0.5 mm.

Obtains Δk = 7.81 N m⁻¹.

items.stem: A tension of 500 N at 60° to the path pulls a sled along flat snow at a steady 3 m s⁻¹. Driven by a tow motor drawing 1172 W, the pull lasts 25 s.

items.stem: Between its opposite 1.2 mm × 0.5 mm end faces, find the resistance of a rectangular carbon bar (60 mm long, 1.2 mm wide, 0.5 mm thick) of resistivity 2.50 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m.
items.workedSolution: End-face area: A = w × h = (1.2 × 10⁻³ m) × (0.5 × 10⁻³ m) = 6.000 × 10⁻⁷ m², and L = 60 × 10⁻³ m. Using R = ρL/A yields 2.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = w × h in m² and R = ρL/A to obtain 2.50 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used the wrong cross-sectional face for the current direction.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Failed to square the mm-to-m conversion factor for area.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted A and L in the resistance equation.

items.stem: Find the resistance of a car headlamp bulb at normal operating voltage if its label reads "12 V, 55 W".
items.workedSolution: Step-by-step: Using P = V² / R gives R = V² / P = 12² / 55 = 2.618 Ω ≈ 2.62 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies electrical power rating equations to obtain 2.62 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverted R = V² / P as P / V².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Used V / P instead of V² / P.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the rated current I = P / V rather than the resistance.

items.stem: A metal wire of original length 2.5 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 mm² extends elastically by 1.875 mm under a load of 270 N. The uncertainties are ±2% in stress and ±2% in strain.

markScheme.criterion: Converts area to m² (× 10⁻⁶) and extension to m (× 10⁻³).
Applies E = FL / (A ΔL) = σ / ε.
Obtains E = 2.40 × 10¹¹ Pa.
Sums percentage uncertainties to obtain 4.00%.
Obtains ΔE = 9.60 × 10⁹ Pa.

parts.prompt: Calculate the Young modulus E of the wire in pascals.

items.stem: A student plots current on the vertical axis against potential difference on the horizontal axis for an ohmic wire and a filament lamp. Which statement about finding resistance from these graphs is correct?
items.workedSolution: With current on the vertical axis the linear gradient equals the reciprocal of resistance while non ohmic resistance uses coordinate ratio.

markScheme.criterion: With current on the vertical axis the linear gradient equals the reciprocal of resistance while non ohmic resistance uses coordinate ratio.

options.label: A
options.text: Correctly interpreted, the straight line gradient equals resistance directly and the tangent gradient gives lamp resistance
options.distractorRationale: Commits both classic I–V traps: gradient is 1/R (not R), and curved static resistance is V/I (not tangent).

options.label: B
options.text: Correctly interpreted, a steeper ohmic line always indicates a larger electrical resistance
options.distractorRationale: When I is on the vertical axis, steeper slope means larger I/V, hence SMALLER resistance.

options.label: C
options.text: Correctly interpreted, with current on the vertical axis the linear gradient equals the reciprocal of resistance while non ohmic resistance uses coordinate ratio

options.label: D
options.text: Correctly interpreted, resistance of a filament lamp equals the area underneath the curve up to that voltage
options.distractorRationale: Area under an I–V curve does not equal resistance.

items.stem: Carrying a steady conventional current of 0.480 A from left to right, a cylindrical silver wire has free-electron density 5.70 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ and mean electron drift speed 8.55 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Solution: (a) A = 6.156 × 10⁻⁸ m² ≈ 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m². Then (b) d = 0.280 mm. Lastly, (c) Carrying negative charge, free electrons move against conventional current (right to left).

markScheme.criterion: Correct rearrangement A = I / (nve) with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Correct cross-sectional area 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m² (4 s.f. 6.156 × 10⁻⁸ m²).
Substitutes area into d = √(4A / π).
Correct final value 0.280 mm.
States electrons drift opposite to conventional current (from right to left).

parts.prompt: Calculate the cross-sectional area of the conductor in m².
workingSteps: Rearrange I = nAve to A = I / (nve).

parts.prompt: Determine the diameter of the conductor in mm.
workingSteps: Use A = πd²/4 so d = √(4A / π).

parts.prompt: State the direction of the mean drift velocity of the conduction electrons relative to the conventional current.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrons drift from right to left, opposite to conventional current.
workingSteps: Conduction electrons carry negative charge, so they move opposite to conventional current.

items.stem: Find the final speed in m s⁻¹ at the end of the 3.5 s. Moving at 144 km h⁻¹ on a straight level track, a commuter tram decelerates steadily at 1.5 m s⁻² for 3.5 s.

items.stem: Treating an atomic nucleus as a uniform sphere, its mass is 1.73 × 10⁻²⁵ kg and its diameter is 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.
items.workedSolution: (a) Density is mass per unit volume of a material. (b) r = 6.000 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, V = 9.048 × 10⁻⁴³ m³, producing ρ = 1.912 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.91 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Defines density as mass per unit volume.
Halves diameter to obtain radius r in metres.

parts.expectedAnswer: Density is mass per unit volume of a material.

items.stem: Running for 20 s at an input of 4083 W, a water pump raises 400 kg of salt water vertically by 15 m at steady speed. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

items.stem: A pressure sensor sits in a tall tank at depth h = 60 m ± 0.3 m in a liquid of density ρ = 900 kg m⁻³ ± 25 kg m⁻³. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ as exact. Calculate the gauge pressure p = ρgh at this depth in pascals.

options.label: B

items.stem: Containing 65% copper (density 8930 kg m⁻³) and 35% titanium (density 4510 kg m⁻³) by volume, a rectangular alloy block measures 7 cm × 3.5 cm × 3 cm. Find the mean density of the alloy in kg m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Volume V = (7 × 3.5 × 3) × 10⁻⁶ = 7.350 × 10⁻⁵ m³. Volume-weighted density ρ = (0.65 × 8930) + (0.35 × 4510) = 7383 kg m⁻³ ≈ 7.38 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Total mass m = ρ V = 0.5427 kg ≈ 0.543 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 7.38 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the volume fractions assigned to the two metals.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the harmonic mean formula, which applies to mass fractions rather than volume fractions.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses an incorrect geometric factor or lever-arm ratio.

items.stem: A student estimates the take-off speed of an adult in a standing vertical jump. They use $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and an estimated rise of $h = 0.50\text{ m}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.50} = 3.13\text{ m s}^{-1}$. (b) Since $3.13 < \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16$, the nearest order of magnitude is $10^0 = 1\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

workingSteps: Since $\log_{10}(3.13) = 0.496 < 0.5$, the nearest order of magnitude is $10^0 = 1\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

items.stem: A uniform metal wire is cut to half its original length at constant room temperature. Why does the resistivity of the shorter wire stay the same?
items.workedSolution: Resistivity is a material property independent of sample dimensions at constant temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Material property independent of sample dimensions at constant temperature.

options.label: A
options.text: Because resistivity is a dimension dependent quantity that halves whenever wire length halves
options.distractorRationale: Resistance halves when length halves, but resistivity stays constant.

options.text: Because resistivity is a material property independent of sample dimensions at constant temperature

options.label: C
options.text: Because cutting the wire doubles cross sectional area to cancel the reduced length
options.distractorRationale: Cutting a wire does not change its diameter or cross-sectional area.

options.label: D
options.text: Because resistance of a metal wire is completely independent of its length
options.distractorRationale: Resistance is directly proportional to length (R = ρL/A).

items.stem: A student converts the ohm into alternative SI derived and base unit expressions.
items.workedSolution: Step (a): Volt per ampere and joule second per coulomb squared. Step (b): Base unit form combines kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere squared. Key idea: resistance is potential difference divided by current.

markScheme.criterion: Volt per ampere and joule second per coulomb squared.
Links to principle: Resistance is potential difference divided by current.
Base unit form combines kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere squared.

parts.expectedAnswer: Volt per ampere and joule second per coulomb squared.

parts.prompt: State the SI base-unit combination corresponding to the ohm. [2]

items.stem: A small capsule is launched vertically upward at 15 m s⁻¹ with negligible air resistance. Take upward as positive and g = 9.8 m s⁻², and consider its motion at t = 1.8 s. Calculate its vertical displacement from the launch point at t = 1.8 s.
items.workedSolution: With upward positive, u = +15 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.8 m s⁻². Vertical displacement s = ut + ½at² = (15)(1.8) − 0.5(9.8)(1.8)² = 11.1 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses s = ut − ½gt² with g = 9.8 m s⁻² to obtain 11.1 m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses +g instead of −g when initial velocity is upward, adding ½gt² to ut.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 1/2 in the gravitational displacement term −½gt².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the motion as release from rest and omits the upward initial-velocity term ut.

items.stem: An accurate potential-divider experiment depends on choosing meters whose resistance does not disturb the circuit.
items.workedSolution: First, (a) Connected in parallel with infinite resistance. Next, (b) Infinite internal resistance ensures negligible current is diverted through the voltmeter. Key idea: parallel connection with infinite resistance draws zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Connected in parallel with infinite resistance.

items.stem: Find the root-mean-square voltage of the sinusoidal trace shown on a cathode-ray oscilloscope. The time-base is 2.0 ms div⁻¹ and Y-gain is 1.5 V div⁻¹. Each cycle covers 4.0 horizontal divisions with a vertical peak-to-peak height of 5.2 divisions.

items.stem: The wave speed v on a stretched rope obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ with a unit constant. The measured tension is 180 N ± 1.2 N and the mass per unit length is 6 g m⁻¹ ± 0.1 g m⁻¹. Use base units to find a and b, and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Matching SI base units: [v] = m s⁻¹, [T] = kg m s⁻², [μ] = kg m⁻¹. For kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, −2a = −1 ⇒ a = 0.5 and b = −0.5, so v = √(T/μ). With μ = 6 × 10⁻³ = 0.006 kg m⁻¹, v = √(180 / 0.006) = 173 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a = 1/2, b = −1/2, converts μ to 0.006 kg m⁻¹, and obtains v = 173 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Deduces v = √(T/μ) correctly but forgets to convert μ from g m⁻¹ into kg m⁻¹ (off by √1000).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses a = 1, b = −1 (computing T/μ with units m² s⁻²) without taking the square root required by dimensional homogeneity.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the dimensional ratio to √(μ/T), yielding s m⁻¹ instead of m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A test mass moves in a flat circle of radius r = 0.8 m ± 0.05 m at steady speed v = 12 m s⁻¹ ± 0.25 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r. Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δa in the centripetal acceleration.
items.workedSolution: Nominal acceleration a = v²/r = 12² / 0.8 = 180 m s⁻². Fractional uncertainty Δa/a = 2(0.25/12) + (0.05/0.8) = 0.104. Absolute uncertainty Δa = a(Δa/a) = 18.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Calculates a = v²/r and multiplies by 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) to obtain Δa = 18.8 m s⁻².

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to double Δv/v for the squared v² factor before multiplying by a.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts Δr/r instead of adding it when propagating uncertainty across a quotient.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes absolute uncertainties (Δv)² / Δr directly into the formula v² / r.

Obtains v = -26.2 m s⁻¹.

Obtains s = -23.5 m.

items.stem: A thin metal wire has circular diameter d = 0.5 mm ± 0.01 mm and supports a tensile load of F = 60 N ± 1.5 N. Calculate the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = π(0.5 × 10⁻³)² / 4 = 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m². Tensile stress σ = F / A = 4F / (πd²) = 3.06 × 10⁸ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 in m² to obtain σ = 3.06 × 10⁸ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses A = πd² instead of A = πd²/4 (treating diameter d as if it were radius r, off by a factor of 4).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter in millimetres directly without converting d² from mm² to 10⁻⁶ m².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by circumference πd instead of cross-sectional area πd²/4.

items.stem: Resting 18 m deep under open seawater (1030 kg m⁻³), a flat plate measures 1.8 m². Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Find the pressure increase Δp from the liquid column alone.
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1030 × 9.81 × 18 = 1.819 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 1.82 × 10⁵ Pa. Full pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 1.819 × 10⁵ = 2.829 × 10⁵ Pa = 282.9 kPa ≈ 283 kPa. Total force F = p_abs A = 2.829 × 10⁵ × 1.8 = 5.092 × 10⁵ N ≈ 5.09 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 1.82 × 10⁵ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds atmospheric pressure even though only the hydrostatic difference Δp = ρgh was asked.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to include g = 9.81 m s⁻².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gauge force instead of gauge pressure.

items.stem: Both mechanical work and the moment of a force multiply force by distance, yet moments are never written in joules. Why is the unit newton metre retained for a moment?
items.workedSolution: Moment is measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules.

markScheme.criterion: Measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules.

options.label: B
options.text: Because a moment uses distance parallel to the force whereas work uses perpendicular distance
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the geometry: work uses parallel displacement whereas moment uses perpendicular lever arm.

options.label: C
options.text: Because newton metre has completely different SI base dimensions from the joule
options.distractorRationale: Both share dimensions kg m² s⁻², yet they represent physically distinct vector/scalar concepts.

options.text: Because a moment is measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules

items.stem: For a metal cube tested using a digital balance and vernier callipers, the side length is 7.5 cm ± 0.06 cm. Its measured mass is 1140 g ± 1.5 g. Work out the percentage uncertainty in the bulk density.
items.workedSolution: Since ρ = m L⁻³, Δρ / ρ = Δm / m + 3(ΔL / L) = (1.5/1140) + 3(0.06/7.5). Converting to percent gives 2.53%.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Δρ/ρ = Δm/m + 3(ΔL/L) to obtain 2.53%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts percentage uncertainties in the quotient m / L³ instead of adding worst-case contributions.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Cubes the percentage uncertainty in L rather than multiplying the fractional uncertainty by 3.

items.stem: How does the internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas differ from that of a real liquid?

options.text: Specifically, internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on container volume and not on temperature

options.label: C

items.stem: A student explains rising gas pressure during heating only by citing the ideal gas law. Why does this explanation receive no credit?

items.stem: An electric truck travels along a flat tunnel at a steady speed of 108 km h⁻¹ against a resistive force of 2400 N. It draws 96000 W of electrical power for 45 s. Calculate the percentage efficiency of the motor system.
items.workedSolution: At constant velocity, tractive force F = 2400 N and v = 108/3.6 = 30 m s⁻¹. Useful power P_out = Fv = 2400 × 30 = 72000 W. Efficiency η = (72000/96000) × 100% = 75.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Converts speed to 30 m s⁻¹, computes P_out = Fv = 72000 W, and obtains η = 75.0%.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical power dissipated as heat rather than motor system efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by velocity (F/v) instead of multiplying P = Fv.

items.stem: Across all eight input combinations of $(A, B, C)$, how many rows produce $Q = 1$ for the five-gate network shown? Its Boolean function is $Q = ((A \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})) \cdot C$.

items.stem: Made from a cylindrical metal resistance wire of resistivity 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m, a heating element is 3.50 m long and 0.320 mm wide in diameter. It connects to a steady 36.0 V DC supply.
items.workedSolution: Evaluate (a): A = 8.042 × 10⁻⁸ m², R = 47.87 Ω ≈ 47.9 Ω. Evaluate (b): P = V²/R = 27.1 W. Evaluate (c): V = AL = 2.815 × 10⁻⁷ m³, so s = ∛V = 6.55 mm.

Correct resistance 47.9 Ω.

Correct cube edge length 6.55 mm.

items.stem: Approaching a flat wall at +12 m s⁻¹, a ball (mass 1.2 kg) collides head-on for 20 ms. It leaves in the opposite direction at 9 m s⁻¹ (final velocity −9 m s⁻¹). What is the signed kinetic energy change ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i for this bounce?
items.workedSolution: Direct evaluation: ΔE_k = ½m(v² − u²) = 0.5(1.2)((−9)² − 12²) = -37.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ½m(v² − u²) including negative sign to obtain -37.8 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes positive energy lost (E_k,i − E_k,f) instead of the signed change E_k,f − E_k,i.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates ½m(v − u)² instead of ½mv² − ½mu².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds the two kinetic energies because the velocity reversed sign, forgetting v² is always positive.

items.stem: On open circuit, an ideal voltmeter connected across a storage battery reads 12.6 V. Adding an 18.0 Ω load drops the reading to 11.3 V. Next, a 6.00 Ω load resistor replaces it.
items.workedSolution: Answers: (a) I₁ = 0.6300 A, so r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 2.000 Ω ≈ 2.00 Ω. Next (b) I₂ = 1.575 A, so V₂ = I₂R₂ = 9.450 V ≈ 9.45 V.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 0.630 A and substitutes into r = (ε − V₁) / I₁.
Correct internal resistance 2.00 Ω.
Uses V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) (or finds I₂ then I₂R₂).
Correct terminal potential difference 9.45 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.
workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 11.34 / 18 = 0.6300 A.
Internal resistance r = (ε − V₁) / I₁ = (12.6 − 11.34) / 0.6300 A = 2.000 Ω ≈ 2.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new terminal potential difference across the 6.00 Ω resistor.
workingSteps: New current I₂ = ε / (R₂ + r) = 12.6 / (6 + 2.000 Ω) = 1.575 A.
Terminal pd V₂ = I₂ R₂ = 1.575 A × 6 = 9.450 V ≈ 9.45 V.

items.stem: Running at 3.30 V, a data logger draws a constant 45 mA over a period of 12 min. Determine the electrical energy transferred over this interval.
items.workedSolution: Time in seconds: t = 12 × 60 = 720 s and current I = 0.04500 A. Charge Q = It = 32.40 C. Electrical work W = QV = 106.9 J ≈ 107 J.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 107 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert operating time from minutes into seconds.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omitted the mA-to-A prefix conversion (10³ error).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculated charge Q = It instead of electrical work W = QV.

items.stem: Find the percentage uncertainty in k = F / (x₂ − x₁) for a vertical coil spring, using Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx₁ + Δx₂. Readings are x₁ = 12 mm ± 0.5 mm, x₂ = 57 mm ± 0.5 mm, and F = 18 N ± 0.4 N.
items.workedSolution: Elongation e = x₂ − x₁ = 57 − 12 = 45 mm plus combined uncertainty Δe = Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 mm. Thus %Δk = (%ΔF) + (%Δe) = (0.4/18 + 1/45) × 100% = 4.44%.

markScheme.criterion: Finds e = 45 mm, Δe = 1 mm, and obtains %Δk = 4.44%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the uncertainty of a single ruler reading Δx rather than summing Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 2Δx for the difference x₂ − x₁.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx − Δx = 0 by subtracting absolute uncertainties in a difference.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides 2Δx by the final reading x₂ instead of by the extension e = x₂ − x₁.

items.stem: A heavy cart travels at steady speed 3 m s⁻¹ along a level rail for 25 s. It is pulled by an electric motor drawing 703 W, with 300 N in the cable at 60° to the rail. What is the percentage efficiency of this towing system?
items.workedSolution: Useful drive power P_out = F v cos θ = 300 × 3 × cos(60°) = 450 W. Overall efficiency η = (450 / 703) × 100% = 64.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates P_out = Fv cos 60° = 450 W and obtains η = 64.0%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses Fv sin θ instead of the component parallel to velocity Fv cos θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses un-resolved product Fv without multiplying by cos θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input power wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

items.stem: A steel wire of unstretched length 2.4 m and cross-sectional area 1.4 mm² stretches elastically by 2.4 mm under a tension of 168 N. The uncertainties are ±2.5% in stress and ±2% in strain. Calculate the absolute uncertainty ΔE in the Young modulus in pascals.
items.workedSolution: E = σ / ε = 1.20 × 10¹¹ Pa. Total percentage uncertainty %ΔE = 2.5% + 2% = 4.50%. Absolute uncertainty ΔE = E × (%ΔE / 100%) = 5.40 × 10⁹ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes E and multiplies by (2.5% + 2%) to obtain ΔE = 5.40 × 10⁹ Pa.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies percentage uncertainties instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: A semiconductor light-emitting diode is tested across both forward and reverse bias using a variable DC source.
items.workedSolution: Method: (a) Resistance is extremely high in reverse bias and below the forward threshold voltage so current is virtually zero. Second, (b) A protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction. Key idea: asymmetric threshold conduction defines a semiconductor diode characteristic.

markScheme.criterion: Resistance is extremely high in reverse bias and below the forward threshold voltage so current is virtually zero.
Links to principle: Asymmetric threshold conduction defines a semiconductor diode characteristic.
A protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction.
Above the forward threshold potential difference resistance falls sharply and current rises rapidly.

items.stem: What is the mean drift speed of electrons in a uniform aluminium wire of diameter 1.10 mm carrying 3.20 A? The free-electron density is 6.00 × 10²⁸ m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Wire diameter: d = 1.100 × 10⁻³ m. Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = 9.503 × 10⁻⁷ m². Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives v = I / (nAe) = 3.508 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 3.51 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 3.51 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in A = πr² (four times too large an area).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied by 4 instead of dividing by 4 in A = πd²/4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π when calculating the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: For 3 s, a lorry decelerates steadily at 1.5 m s⁻² along a straight road. Before braking, its speed was 108 km h⁻¹.

items.stem: Across a heating strip, the steady voltage is measured as V = 42 V ± 0.8 V. The component resistance is R = 25 Ω ± 0.2 Ω. Determine the absolute uncertainty ΔP in watts for this electrical power.
items.workedSolution: Dissipated power P = V² / R = 42² / 25 = 70.6 W. Adding fractional errors gives ΔP/P = 2(0.8/42) + (0.2/25) = 0.0461, which gives ΔP = 3.25 W.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates P = V²/R and multiplies by 2(ΔV/V) + (ΔR/R) to obtain 3.25 W.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses ΔV/V + ΔR/R without doubling ΔV/V for V².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts ΔR/R from 2(ΔV/V) in the quotient V²/R.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the fractional uncertainty by current V/R instead of power V²/R.

items.stem: Modelled as a uniform sphere, an atomic nucleus has mass 1.53 × 10⁻²⁵ kg and diameter 1.26 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Determine the average density of the sphere in kg m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Radius r = D / 2 = 6.300 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Volume V = (4/3)πr³ = 1.047 × 10⁻⁴² m³. Mean density ρ = m / V = 1.461 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.46 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Correct spherical density = 1.46 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter D instead of radius D/2 into (4/3)πr³, producing an 8× too-small density.

items.stem: A steel wire of circular diameter d = 1.2 mm ± 0.02 mm is held under a tension of F = 45 N ± 0.5 N. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the tensile stress σ = 4F / (πd²).
items.workedSolution: In σ = 4F / (πd²), the constant 4/π has zero uncertainty, so %Δσ = %ΔF + 2(%Δd) = (0.5/45 + 2 × 0.02/1.2) × 100% = 4.44%.

options.label: D

items.stem: A flat plate (area 3.2 m²) is held horizontally 30 m under the open surface of freshwater. Take liquid density 1000 kg m⁻³, atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, and g = 9.81 m s⁻². Find the total force pushing down on the plate.
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1000 × 9.81 × 30 = 2.943 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 2.94 × 10⁵ Pa. Net absolute pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 2.943 × 10⁵ = 3.953 × 10⁵ Pa = 395.3 kPa ≈ 395 kPa. Plate force F = p_abs A = 3.953 × 10⁵ × 3.2 = 1.265 × 10⁶ N ≈ 1.26 × 10⁶ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 1.26 × 10⁶ N.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides absolute pressure by area instead of multiplying F = p A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure, omitting atmospheric force.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes fluid mass instead of total downward force.

items.stem: Which statement accurately expresses the principle of moments?
items.workedSolution: The principle of moments states that for a body in equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot.

markScheme.criterion: For a body in equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot.

options.label: A
options.text: It states that for any accelerating beam the sum of clockwise forces equals the sum of anticlockwise forces
options.distractorRationale: Confuses moments with forces and applies equilibrium to an accelerating body.

options.label: B
options.text: It states that clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments only when taken about the physical hinge
options.distractorRationale: For a body in equilibrium, moments balance about ANY chosen pivot point, not only a physical hinge.

options.label: C
options.text: It states that for a body in equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot

options.label: D
options.text: It states that total upward force equals total downward force about any pivot
options.distractorRationale: Confuses translational force balance with rotational moment balance.

items.stem: How is the internal energy of a thermodynamic system defined?
items.workedSolution: Internal energy is the sum of random kinetic energies and intermolecular potential energies of all molecules.

options.distractorRationale: Internal energy sums BOTH kinetic and intermolecular potential energies over ALL molecules.

options.label: D

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mcΔT / (P_in t) × 100% = 85.0%.

options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical energy lost to the surroundings instead of the percentage retained.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides Q = mcΔT in joules directly by heater power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits sample mass m from Q = mcΔT.

items.stem: In freshwater of density 1000 kg m⁻³, a 6 kg wooden block of density 560 kg m⁻³ floats at rest (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Determine the percentage of the block's volume beneath the liquid surface.
items.workedSolution: Floating balance: ρ_fluid V_sub g = ρ_obj V g ⇒ V_sub / V = ρ_obj / ρ_fluid = 560 / 1000 = 0.5600 = 56.00% ≈ 56.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Percentage under water = 56.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the density ratio ρ_fluid / ρ_obj.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Halves the Archimedes density ratio.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage protruding above the waterline rather than under water.

items.stem: Photon energy is linked to frequency by $E = hf$. Which combination of coherent SI base units is equivalent to the unit of the Planck constant $h$?
items.workedSolution: Since $h = E/f = E T$, multiplying $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$ by $\mathrm{s}$ yields $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$. This confirms option D is correct: kilogram metre squared per second.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: kilogram metre squared per second.

items.stem: What is meant by the elastic limit of a ductile metal wire under tension?
items.workedSolution: The elastic limit is the maximum stress or load beyond which permanent plastic deformation occurs when unloaded.

markScheme.criterion: Maximum stress or load beyond which permanent plastic deformation occurs when unloaded.

options.label: A
options.text: It is the maximum stress or load beyond which permanent plastic deformation occurs when unloaded

options.label: B
options.text: It is the load at which the wire suddenly fractures into two separate pieces
options.distractorRationale: Confuses the elastic limit with the breaking or fracture point.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the point where extension stops increasing even when additional load is hung
options.distractorRationale: Beyond the elastic limit the wire extends even more easily via plastic deformation.

options.label: D
options.text: It is the minimum load required to initiate any measurable elastic extension
options.distractorRationale: Any non-zero load produces immediate elastic extension from the origin.

items.stem: A metal resistance wire is tested in a lab to check that it obeys Ohm's law.
items.workedSolution: Result (a): Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant. Result (b): Keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire. Key idea: limiting current prevents self heating from distorting a linear ohmic plot.

Keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.

items.stem: The wave speed v on a guy wire obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ (with constant 1). The tension is 320 N ± 1.5 N and the mass per unit length is 5 g m⁻¹ ± 0.15 g m⁻¹.

Converts linear density to 0.005 kg m⁻¹ and substitutes into √(T/μ).
Obtains v = 253 m s⁻¹.
Multiplies both %ΔT and %Δμ by 1/2 before adding.
Obtains 1.73%.
Obtains Δv = 4.39 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By equating SI base units on both sides of v = Tᵃ μᵇ, determine a and b and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: [T] = kg m s⁻² and [μ] = kg m⁻¹ ⇒ kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, so a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.

Determine the absolute uncertainty Δv in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A stone is thrown vertically upward with initial velocity +32 m s⁻¹ and negligible air resistance. Take upward as positive and use g = 9.81 m s⁻² at elapsed time 3.4 s. Calculate its signed vertical velocity at t = 3.4 s.
items.workedSolution: Using v = u + at with u = +32 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻² gives v = 32 − (9.81)(3.4) = -1.35 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds gt to u instead of subtracting gt when upward is defined as positive.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the mean vertical velocity u − ½gt rather than the instantaneous velocity u − gt.

Key idea: temperature tracks mean kinetic energy whereas latent heat alters intermolecular potential energy.

items.stem: A sealed rigid metal cylinder of helium gas is heated so its kelvin temperature rises. Using kinetic theory rather than the gas law, why does the gas pressure rise?
items.workedSolution: By kinetic theory and Newton's second law, faster molecules have a larger momentum change per wall collision. They also hit the walls more often, raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Faster molecules produce larger momentum change per wall collision and higher collision frequency raising average force per unit area.

options.label: A
options.text: Heating causes helium molecules to expand in physical volume so they pack tightly against the cylinder walls
options.distractorRationale: Individual gas molecules do not swell in volume; kinetic energy and speed increase.

options.label: B
options.text: Heating causes faster molecules produce larger momentum change per wall collision and higher collision frequency raising average force per unit area

options.label: C
options.text: Heating causes intermolecular repulsive forces to strengthen dramatically across the empty interior
options.distractorRationale: An ideal gas has negligible intermolecular forces between collisions.

options.label: D
options.text: Heating causes pressure to rise simply because pressure equals molar constant times temperature divided by volume
options.distractorRationale: Circular algebraic restatement of the gas law fails to provide a microscopic kinetic mechanism.

items.stem: A student models a glider of mass 80 kg travelling at 2 m s⁻¹ on a smooth horizontal air track. A steady 160 N pull acts at 53.13° above the horizontal over 4 s. Work out the horizontal distance moved in the 4 s.
items.workedSolution: Forward component F_x = 160 cos(53.13°) = 96 N, so a_x = F_x / m = 1.2 m s⁻². Using s = ut + ½a_x t² = (2)(4) + 0.5(1.2)(4)² = 17.6 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves F cos 53.13° to get a_x = 1.2 m s⁻² and obtains s = 17.6 m.

options.label: D

items.stem: Apply De Morgan's theorem to the three-gate circuit shown, which has output $Q = \bar{A} + \bar{B}$. Which single two-input logic gate gives the same output?
items.workedSolution: By De Morgan's law, $\bar{A} + \bar{B} = \overline{A \cdot B}$, which is a single two-input NAND gate.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that single two-input NAND gate.

items.stem: Drawn at constant volume so its diameter is halved to 0.175 mm, a cylindrical metal resistance wire originally had diameter 0.350 mm, length 5.00 m, and resistivity 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Calculate its new resistance.
items.workedSolution: Initial area A = πd²/4 = 9.621 × 10⁻⁸ m² and R = ρL/A = 75.35 Ω. Scaling diameter by factor k = 0.5 scales area by k² and length by 1/k² at constant volume, so R₂ = R / k⁴ = 1.206 × 10³ Ω ≈ 1.21 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 1.21 × 10³ Ω.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Only scaled area by k² and forgot that constant volume also changes length by 1/k².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumed resistance varies inversely with diameter rather than diameter to the fourth power.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted the scaling factor k⁴ when computing the redrawn resistance.

items.stem: An experiment uses a high-resistance voltmeter on a rechargeable battery. Open-circuit voltage is 7.50 V, dropping to 6.75 V with a 9.00 Ω load. Find the terminal potential difference after swapping that 9.00 Ω load for a 3.00 Ω resistor.
items.workedSolution: No-load reading yields ε = 7.50 V. With R₁ = 9 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 0.7500 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.000 Ω. With R₂ = 3 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 5.625 V ≈ 5.63 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 1.00 Ω and computes V₂ = 5.63 V.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: When used at its rated voltage, what resistance does a portable travel iron with rating "230 V, 920 W" have?

items.stem: In a uniform aluminium wire (free-electron density 6.10 × 10²⁸ m⁻³), the diameter is 1.60 mm. A steady conventional current of 4.40 A passes through it from left to right.
items.workedSolution: First, (a) A = 2.011 × 10⁻⁶ m² ≈ 2.01 × 10⁻⁶ m². Next, (b) v = 2.24 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. Finally, (c) Because electrons are negatively charged, they drift opposite to conventional current (right to left).

items.stem: Along a straight braking zone, a test trolley begins braking from 162 km h⁻¹. Uniform braking of 2 m s⁻² is applied for 4.5 s. How many metres does the test trolley travel during those 4.5 s?
items.workedSolution: Speed conversion: u = 162 / 3.6 = 45 m s⁻¹. With a = −2 m s⁻², s = ut + ½at² = (45)(4.5) − 0.5(2)(4.5)² = 182 m.

items.stem: A cast alloy of total mass 3.2 kg consists by mass of 40% zinc (7.14 g cm⁻³) and 60% magnesium (1.74 g cm⁻³). Take the final volume as the sum of both component volumes. What is the overall density of this alloy in kg m⁻³?
items.workedSolution: Masses: m₁ = 1.280 kg, m₂ = 1.920 kg. Volumes: V₁ = m₁/ρ₁ = 1.793 × 10⁻⁴ m³, V₂ = m₂/ρ₂ = 1.103 × 10⁻³ m³. Total volume V = V₁ + V₂ = 1.283 × 10⁻³ m³ (1283 cm³). Alloy density ρ = m / V = 3.2 / 1.283 × 10⁻³ = 2495 kg m⁻³ ≈ 2.49 × 10³ kg m⁻³ (2.49 g cm⁻³).

markScheme.criterion: Correct harmonic-mean alloy density = 2.49 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

options.label: A

options.distractorRationale: Averages the two densities equally regardless of mass percentages.

items.stem: The wave speed v along a metal wire obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ with a unit constant. The wire has tension T = 64 N ± 4 N and mass per unit length μ = 8 g m⁻¹ ± 0.08 g m⁻¹. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the wave speed v.
items.workedSolution: Dimensional homogeneity gives v = T^(1/2) μ^(−1/2). Hence %Δv = ½(%ΔT) + ½(%Δμ) = 0.5(4/64 + 0.08/8) × 100% = 3.62%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses exponents |1/2| and |−1/2| to obtain %Δv = 3.62%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Sums %ΔT + %Δμ without multiplying by the 1/2 power factor from the square-root exponents.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainties because μ appears in the denominator of √(T/μ).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the combined percentage uncertainty by 2 instead of 1/2 for a square-root power.

items.stem: A test mass moves in a flat circle of radius r = 0.5 m ± 0.03 m at steady speed v = 16 m s⁻¹ ± 0.2 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the centripetal acceleration a.
items.workedSolution: For a = v² / r, Δa/a = 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) = 2(0.2/16) + (0.03/0.5). Multiplying by 100% gives 8.50%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses %Δa = 2(%Δv) + (%Δr) to obtain 8.50%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainty of r from 2(%Δv) because r is in the denominator.

options.label: D

items.stem: Using g = 9.81 m s⁻² and atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, consider a flat plate of area 3 m² lying horizontally at depth 16.5 m in open salt water of density 1140 kg m⁻³. Find the total pressure in kPa acting on the plate.

items.stem: In the circuit shown, inverted inputs $\bar{A}$ and $\bar{B}$ enter an OR gate so that $Q = \bar{A} + \bar{B}$. How many of the four truth-table rows give $Q = 1$?
items.workedSolution: By De Morgan's theorem, $\bar{A} + \bar{B} = \overline{A \cdot B}$ (NAND), which is HIGH for $(0, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, and $(1, 0)$ — a total of 3 rows.

markScheme.criterion: Truth table has 3 HIGH rows.

items.stem: Connected across a steady 16.0 V DC supply, a heating element uses a cylindrical metal resistance wire. Its length is 2.80 m, diameter is 0.380 mm, and resistivity is 4.90 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.
items.workedSolution: Result (a): A = 1.134 × 10⁻⁷ m², R = 12.10 Ω ≈ 12.1 Ω. Result (b): P = V²/R = 21.2 W. Result (c): V = AL = 3.176 × 10⁻⁷ m³, so s = ∛V = 6.82 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates A = πd²/4 = 1.13 × 10⁻⁷ m² and substitutes into R = ρL/A.
Correct resistance 12.1 Ω.
Correct power P = V²/R = 21.2 W.
Computes conserved volume V = AL = 3.18 × 10⁻⁷ m³ and sets s³ = V.
Correct cube edge length 6.82 mm.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical resistance of the wire.
Calculate the thermal power output of the heating element at 16.0 V.
The wire is later melted down without loss and cast into a solid cube. Calculate the edge length of the cube in mm.
workingSteps: Volume conserved: V = AL = 1.134 × 10⁻⁷ m² × 2.8 = 3.176 × 10⁻⁷ m³.

items.stem: In a lab collision test, a metal puck of mass 0.4 kg hits a vertical wall at +28 m s⁻¹. It remains in contact for 16 ms and rebounds back at 12 m s⁻¹. Work out the average force magnitude on the metal puck across the 16 ms contact.
items.workedSolution: Taking incoming velocity as +28 m s⁻¹ and rebound velocity as −12 m s⁻¹, |Δp| = 0.4(28 + 12) = 16 N s. With Δt = 16 × 10⁻³ = 0.016 s, F_avg = |Δp| / Δt = 1.00 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Computes |Δp| = m(u + v_reb) and divides by 0.016 s to obtain 1.00 × 10³ N.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts speed magnitudes m(u − v_reb)/Δt instead of accounting for velocity reversal m(u + v_reb)/Δt.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides by contact time in milliseconds without converting ms to seconds (off by 10³).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the impulse magnitude |Δp| in N s and forgets to divide by contact time Δt.

items.stem: Using an ideal voltmeter, the open-circuit voltage of a battery pack is measured as 9.00 V. A 10.0 Ω load resistor lowers the reading to 7.50 V. A 4.00 Ω load resistor is then fitted instead.
items.workedSolution: Step (a): I₁ = 0.7500 A, so r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 2.000 Ω ≈ 2.00 Ω. Step (b): I₂ = 1.500 A, which gives V₂ = I₂R₂ = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 0.750 A and substitutes into r = (ε − V₁) / I₁.
Correct internal resistance 2.00 Ω.
Uses V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) (or finds I₂ then I₂R₂).
Correct terminal potential difference 6.00 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.
workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 7.5 / 10 = 0.7500 A.
Internal resistance r = (ε − V₁) / I₁ = (9 − 7.5) / 0.7500 A = 2.000 Ω ≈ 2.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new terminal potential difference across the 4.00 Ω resistor.
workingSteps: New current I₂ = ε / (R₂ + r) = 9 / (4 + 2.000 Ω) = 1.500 A.
Terminal pd V₂ = I₂ R₂ = 1.500 A × 4 = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V.

items.stem: In a lab test lasting 3.5 min, a small cooling unit draws 2.20 A from a 12.0 V supply. How many electrons pass a point in the circuit during this period?
items.workedSolution: SI time t = 3.5 × 60 = 210 s and current I = 2.200 A. Total charge Q = It = 462.0 C. Number of electrons N = Q / e = 462.0 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 2.888 × 10²¹ ≈ 2.89 × 10²¹.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 2.89 × 10²¹.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert time from minutes to seconds (factor of 60 error).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applied the wrong unit conversion factor for current or time.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied charge by e instead of dividing Q by e.

items.stem: Find the absolute uncertainty Δk of the spring constant, expressed in N m⁻¹, for a return spring. The unloaded reading is x₁ = 22 mm ± 0.8 mm, the loaded reading is x₂ = 82 mm ± 0.8 mm, and F = 36 N ± 0.5 N.
items.workedSolution: Net extension e = (82 − 22) × 10⁻³ = 0.06 m with Δe = 2(0.8) × 10⁻³ = 0.0016 m. Nominal k = 36 / 0.06 = 600 N m⁻¹. Fractional uncertainty Δk/k = 0.5/36 + 0.0016/0.06 = 0.0406, so Δk = 24.3 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines Δe = 2Δx with ΔF/F + Δe/e to obtain Δk = 24.3 N m⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes only one reading uncertainty Δx instead of 2Δx when evaluating Δ(x₂ − x₁).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts Δx₂ − Δx₁ = 0 on the extension difference, ignoring ruler uncertainty completely.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Leaves k in N mm⁻¹ instead of converting extension from millimetres to metres.

items.stem: Angled at 53.13° to the path, the rope applies 600 N to keep a sled moving along flat snow at 2.5 m s⁻¹ for 50 s. The input power is 1059 W. Find the energy lost to the surroundings during the 50 s.
items.workedSolution: Useful power P_out = Fv cos(53.13°) = 900 W. Wasted power = 1059 − 900 = 159 W. Over 50 s, E_wasted = (159)(50) = 7.95 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts Fv cos 53.13° from 1059 W and multiplies by 50 s to get 7.95 × 10³ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes wasted power in watts (P_in − P_out) and forgets to multiply by the time interval.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the useful mechanical work done Fvt cos θ instead of the wasted energy.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to resolve cable tension by cos θ before subtracting from input power.

items.stem: Across the opposite 1.2 mm × 0.8 mm end faces of a rectangular graphite bar, a steady potential difference of 12.0 V is applied. The bar has length 50 mm, width 1.2 mm, height 0.8 mm, and resistivity 4.50 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m.
items.workedSolution: Answers: (a) A = 9.600 × 10⁻⁷ m², so 2.34 Ω. Next (b) P = V² / R = 61.44 W ≈ 61.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates A = w × h = 9.60 × 10⁻⁷ m² and substitutes into R = ρL/A.
Correct value 2.34 Ω.
Substitutes V and R into P = V² / R.
Correct power dissipated 61.4 W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the cross-sectional area perpendicular to current flow and hence determine the resistance of the bar.
Calculate the electrical power dissipated in the bar at this potential difference.
workingSteps: Use P = V² / R with V = 12.00 V and R = 2.344 Ω.

items.stem: Find the current drawn by a stage projector lamp at rated voltage, given its rating "24 V, 150 W".
items.workedSolution: Computing directly: Using P = IV gives I = P / V = 150 / 24 = 6.250 A ≈ 6.25 A.

markScheme.criterion: Applies electrical power rating equations to obtain 6.25 A.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divided V by P instead of P by V.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculated working resistance R = V²/P instead of current I = P/V.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied power by voltage instead of dividing.

items.stem: A brass wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 mm² extends elastically by 1.5 mm under a load of 216 N. The uncertainties are ±2% in stress and ±3% in strain. Calculate the Young modulus E of the wire in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Tensile stress σ = F / A = 216 / (1.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.44 × 10⁸ Pa. Tensile strain ε = ΔL / L = (1.5 × 10⁻³) / 2 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁴. Young modulus E = σ / ε = 1.92 × 10¹¹ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates σ = F/A and ε = ΔL/L in SI units to obtain E = 1.92 × 10¹¹ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Converts mm² to m² using 10⁻³ instead of (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁶, underestimating stress and Young modulus by 10³.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets both mm² → 10⁻⁶ m² and mm → 10⁻³ m unit prefix powers properly.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies tensile stress by tensile strain (σ × ε) instead of dividing σ / ε.

items.stem: In a lab experiment, current is plotted on the vertical axis and potential difference on the horizontal axis.
items.workedSolution: Method: (a) Plotting current on the vertical axis against potential difference on the horizontal axis gives a straight line gradient equal to reciprocal resistance. Second, (b) For a curved non ohmic characteristic resistance at a point equals potential difference divided by current rather than inverse tangent gradient. Key idea: current over voltage is conductance which is the reciprocal of resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Plotting current on the vertical axis against potential difference on the horizontal axis gives a straight line gradient equal to reciprocal resistance.
Links to principle: Current over voltage is conductance which is the reciprocal of resistance.
For a curved non ohmic characteristic resistance at a point equals potential difference divided by current rather than inverse tangent gradient.
Therefore a steeper ohmic line corresponds to a smaller resistance.

parts.prompt: Explain how resistance is determined from a straight ohmic line on this graph and what a steeper slope indicates. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Plotting current on the vertical axis against potential difference on the horizontal axis gives a straight line gradient equal to reciprocal resistance.
workingSteps: Main point: Plotting current on the vertical axis against potential difference on the horizontal axis gives a straight line gradient equal to reciprocal resistance.
Key idea: Current over voltage is conductance which is the reciprocal of resistance.

parts.prompt: Explain how static resistance at a chosen point is found on a curved non-ohmic graph and why the tangent slope must not be inverted. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: For a curved non ohmic characteristic resistance at a point equals potential difference divided by current rather than inverse tangent gradient.
workingSteps: Explanation: For a curved non ohmic characteristic resistance at a point equals potential difference divided by current rather than inverse tangent gradient.
Avoid the common error of assuming the gradient of a current against voltage graph equals resistance directly.

items.stem: Electrons drift at a mean speed of 7.16 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ inside a cylindrical gold wire (free-electron density 5.90 × 10²⁸ m⁻³). The wire carries a steady current of 0.650 A. What is the diameter of this wire?
items.workedSolution: Using standard relations, using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the cross-sectional area is A = I / (nve) = 0.6500 A / (5.900 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ × 7.160 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 9.617 × 10⁻⁸ m². Since A = πd²/4, d = √(4A/π) = 3.499 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.350 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 0.350 mm.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reported the wire radius r = √(A/π) instead of the diameter d = 2r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Used A = πd² rather than A = πd²/4 when solving for diameter.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted the factor of π in the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: Initially travelling at 126 km h⁻¹ on a straight test road, an electric car applies its brakes for 4 s, giving a constant deceleration of 2 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Divides 126 by 3.6 to obtain u = 35 m s⁻¹ and applies v = u − |a|t.
Obtains v = 27.0 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½|a|t² or ½(u + v)t with SI units.
Obtains s = 124 m.
Obtains v_mean = 31.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Convert the initial speed into m s⁻¹ and calculate the speed at the end of the braking interval.
Calculate the distance travelled during the braking interval.
Determine the mean speed over this interval in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Connected to a constant supply, a fixed resistor receives V = 24 V ± 0.4 V. Its measured resistance is R = 8 Ω ± 0.4 Ω. Work out the absolute uncertainty ΔP in the electrical power (in watts).
items.workedSolution: Dissipated power P = V² / R = 24² / 8 = 72.0 W. Total fractional spread ΔP/P = 2(0.4/24) + (0.4/8) = 0.0833, so ΔP = 6.00 W.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates P = V²/R and multiplies by 2(ΔV/V) + (ΔR/R) to obtain 6.00 W.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses ΔV/V + ΔR/R without doubling ΔV/V for V².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts ΔR/R from 2(ΔV/V) in the quotient V²/R.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates (ΔV)² / ΔR directly instead of propagating fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: A flat washer-shaped ring of solid aluminium has outer diameter 36 mm and inner hole diameter 22 mm. Its thickness is 24 mm and density is 2700 kg m⁻³. What is the ring's mass in grams?
items.workedSolution: Outer radius R = 18 mm = 0.01800 m; inner radius r = 11 mm = 0.01100 m; thickness h = 0.02400 m. Volume V = π(R² − r²)h = 1.531 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (15.31 cm³). Mass m = ρ V = 0.04133 kg = 41.33 g ≈ 41.3 g.

markScheme.criterion: Correct mass = 41.3 g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses outer and inner diameters instead of radii in π(R² − r²), inflating area by 4×.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes π(R − r)² instead of π(R² − r²).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the washer as a solid cylinder and omits the central hole.

items.stem: Determine the percentage efficiency of a warehouse lift. At steady speed, it raises a crate of mass 400 kg by 20 m in 12 s using 9074 W (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Lift energy output ΔE_p = mgh = 400 × 9.8 × 20 = 7.84 × 10⁴ J. Supplied electrical energy E_in = 9074 × 12 = 108888 J. Efficiency η = (ΔE_p / E_in) × 100% = 72.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgh / (P_in t) × 100% with g = 9.8 m s⁻² to obtain 72.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits gravitational field strength g when computing gravitational potential energy mgh.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input energy wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides useful energy mgh in joules directly by input power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

items.stem: A pressure probe is lowered to depth h = 60 m ± 0.8 m in a lake of density ρ = 1020 kg m⁻³ ± 20 kg m⁻³. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ as exact.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into p = ρgh with g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.
Obtains p = 6.00 × 10⁵ Pa.
Adds percentage uncertainties in ρ and h.
Obtains 3.29%.
Obtains Δp = 1.98 × 10⁴ Pa.

parts.prompt: Calculate the hydrostatic gauge pressure p at depth h in pascals.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in p.
Hence state the absolute uncertainty Δp in pascals.

items.stem: A student examines a rectangular alloy block of size 8 cm × 3 cm × 3.5 cm. By volume, it is 50% copper (density 8930 kg m⁻³) and 50% aluminium (density 2700 kg m⁻³).
items.workedSolution: (a) A substance's density is its mass per unit volume. (b) ρ = 5815 kg m⁻³ ≈ 5.82 × 10³ kg m⁻³. (c) V = 8.400 × 10⁻⁵ m³, so m = 0.4885 kg ≈ 0.488 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Defines density as mass per unit volume.
Uses volume-weighted average ρ = f₁ρ₁ + f₂ρ₂.
Converts cuboid volume from cm³ to m³ (× 10⁻⁶) and multiplies by ρ.

parts.prompt: State the definition of density.
parts.expectedAnswer: Density is mass per unit volume of a material.
workingSteps: State density equals mass per unit volume.

parts.prompt: Calculate the overall density of this volume-mixed alloy in kg m⁻³.
Calculate the total mass of the cuboid ingot in kg.

items.stem: In a heating practical, an electric heater of power 64 W runs for 150 s and warms a copper block of mass 0.6 kg (c = 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 25 K. Work out the heat lost to the surroundings during the 150 s.
items.workedSolution: Electrical work input E_in = P_in t = 64 × 150 = 9600 J. Thermal energy retained by sample Q = mcΔT = 0.6 × 390 × 25 = 5850 J. Energy lost to surroundings = E_in − Q = 3.75 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mcΔT (5850 J) from P_in t (9600 J) to obtain 3.75 × 10³ J.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the thermal energy absorbed by the sample Q = mcΔT rather than the heat lost to the surroundings.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the total electrical energy supplied P_in t instead of subtracting mcΔT.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the rate of heat loss in watts without multiplying by the heating time t.

items.stem: A student hangs an 18 kg solid copper block of density 8930 kg m⁻³ on a spring balance and lowers it fully into seawater (1025 kg m⁻³) without hitting the bottom. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the upthrust exerted by the liquid on the block?
items.workedSolution: Solid volume V = m / ρ_obj = 18 / 8930 = 2.016 × 10⁻³ m³. Upthrust F_B = ρ_fluid V g = 1025 × 2.016 × 10⁻³ × 9.81 = 20.27 N ≈ 20.3 N. Measured weight W_app = m g − F_B = 176.6 − 20.27 = 156.3 N ≈ 156 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value = 20.3 N.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports apparent weight instead of upthrust.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes displaced mass in kg without multiplying by g = 9.81 m s⁻².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses object density instead of fluid density, recovering the object's own weight.

items.stem: The target diagram shows six repeated readings of a resistor value made with a digital ohmmeter that had a non-zero lead resistance. Which description best classifies this dataset?
items.workedSolution: Tightly grouped dots indicate high precision (small spread about the mean). The constant offset from the centre shows a systematic zero error and low accuracy. Hence option A is correct: high precision with systematic error and low accuracy.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: high precision with systematic error and low accuracy.

items.stem: A tensile testing machine plots tensile stress on the vertical axis against tensile strain on the horizontal axis for a steel rod. How is Young's modulus determined from the plot?
items.workedSolution: Young's modulus equals the gradient of the initial straight line region of a stress against strain graph.

markScheme.criterion: Equals the gradient of the initial straight line region of a stress against strain graph.

options.label: A
options.text: Young's modulus equals the gradient of the initial straight line region of a stress against strain graph

options.label: B
options.text: Young's modulus equals the total area enclosed beneath the stress against strain graph up to fracture
options.distractorRationale: Area under stress–strain gives strain energy per unit volume (toughness), not Young's modulus.

options.label: C
options.text: Young's modulus equals the reciprocal of the gradient of the linear region of the graph
options.distractorRationale: Gradient is stress divided by strain, which is directly Young's modulus (not its reciprocal).

options.label: D
options.text: Young's modulus equals the highest stress coordinate reached near necking
options.distractorRationale: Maximum stress coordinate is the ultimate tensile strength.

items.stem: The wave speed v along a steel cable obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ (k = 1). A sensor measures T = 75 N ± 2 N for a cable of mass per unit length μ = 8 g m⁻¹ ± 0.2 g m⁻¹. Use base units to find a and b, and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Matching SI base units: [v] = m s⁻¹, [T] = kg m s⁻², [μ] = kg m⁻¹. For kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, −2a = −1 ⇒ a = 0.5 and b = −0.5, so v = √(T/μ). With μ = 8 × 10⁻³ = 0.008 kg m⁻¹, v = √(75 / 0.008) = 96.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a = 1/2, b = −1/2, converts μ to 0.008 kg m⁻¹, and obtains v = 96.8 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Deduces v = √(T/μ) correctly but forgets to convert μ from g m⁻¹ into kg m⁻¹ (off by √1000).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses a = 1, b = −1 (computing T/μ with units m² s⁻²) without taking the square root required by dimensional homogeneity.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the dimensional ratio to √(μ/T), yielding s m⁻¹ instead of m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A cyclist rides around a flat circular bend of radius 5 m ± 0.03 m at speed 24 m s⁻¹ ± 0.4 m s⁻¹. The centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the centripetal acceleration a.
items.workedSolution: For a = v² / r, Δa/a = 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) = 2(0.4/24) + (0.03/5). Multiplying by 100% gives 3.93%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses %Δa = 2(%Δv) + (%Δr) to obtain 3.93%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 on the fractional uncertainty of v despite v being squared in v²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainty of r from 2(%Δv) because r is in the denominator.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the percentage uncertainties instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: A small sphere is launched vertically upward from a platform with initial velocity +15 m s⁻¹. Neglect air drag, take upward as positive with g = 9.81 m s⁻², and consider its motion 2.6 s later. Calculate its vertical displacement from the launch point at t = 2.6 s.
items.workedSolution: With upward positive, u = +15 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻². Vertical displacement s = ut + ½at² = (15)(2.6) − 0.5(9.81)(2.6)² = 5.84 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses s = ut − ½gt² with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 5.84 m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses +g instead of −g when initial velocity is upward, adding ½gt² to ut.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 1/2 in the gravitational displacement term −½gt².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the motion as release from rest and omits the upward initial-velocity term ut.

items.stem: A steel piano wire has diameter d = 1.5 mm ± 0.01 mm and experiences a tension of F = 75 N ± 0.6 N. Calculate the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = π(1.5 × 10⁻³)² / 4 = 1.77 × 10⁻⁶ m². Tensile stress σ = F / A = 4F / (πd²) = 4.24 × 10⁷ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 in m² to obtain σ = 4.24 × 10⁷ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses A = πd² instead of A = πd²/4 (treating diameter d as if it were radius r, off by a factor of 4).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter in millimetres directly without converting d² from mm² to 10⁻⁶ m².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by circumference πd instead of cross-sectional area πd²/4.

items.stem: In an open tank of seawater (density 1025 kg m⁻³), a flat horizontal plate sits 22.5 m below the surface. Its area is 2 m². Take atmospheric pressure as 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the pressure difference Δp due to the liquid alone.
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1025 × 9.81 × 22.5 = 2.262 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 2.26 × 10⁵ Pa. Combined pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 2.262 × 10⁵ = 3.272 × 10⁵ Pa = 327.2 kPa ≈ 327 kPa. Overall downward push F = p_abs A = 3.272 × 10⁵ × 2 = 6.545 × 10⁵ N ≈ 6.54 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 2.26 × 10⁵ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to include g = 9.81 m s⁻².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gauge force instead of gauge pressure.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds atmospheric pressure even though only the hydrostatic difference Δp = ρgh was asked.

items.stem: Which description correctly identifies purely scalar physical quantities?
items.workedSolution: A scalar quantity is completely specified by magnitude alone such as mass energy speed or temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Scalar quantity is completely specified by magnitude alone such as mass energy speed or temperature.

options.label: A
options.text: A scalar quantity includes displacement, velocity, force, and linear momentum
options.distractorRationale: Every listed example is a vector possessing spatial direction.

options.label: B
options.text: A scalar quantity is completely specified by magnitude alone such as mass energy speed or temperature

options.label: C
options.text: A scalar quantity includes weight, acceleration, moment, and electric field strength
options.distractorRationale: All four listed quantities are directional vectors.

options.label: D
options.text: A scalar quantity requires a direction angle whenever energy or mass is recorded
options.distractorRationale: Scalars have magnitude only and carry no spatial direction.

items.stem: During a 20 s vertical lift at steady speed, an electric lift moves a load of mass 500 kg upward by 15 m. Its input power is 4598 W (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). How much energy is wasted over the 20 s period?

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mgh from P_in t to obtain 1.84 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the gravitational potential energy gained mgh instead of wasted energy.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates wasted power in watts without multiplying by duration t.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to multiply mass and height by g when subtracting useful work from P_in t.

items.stem: Checking a metal alloy cube in a lab practical yields a mass of 164 g ± 2.5 g. Every side measures 4.5 cm ± 0.06 cm. Determine the density of the cube, using SI units (kg m⁻³).
items.workedSolution: In SI base units: m = 164 × 10⁻³ = 0.164 kg and L = 4.5 × 10⁻² = 0.045 m. Volume V = L³ = (0.045)³ m³. Bulk density ρ = m / L³ = 1.80 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Converts mass to kg and cubed edge length to m³ to obtain ρ = 1.80 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates density in g cm⁻³ without applying the factor of 1000 needed to convert g cm⁻³ into kg m⁻³.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass in kilograms by a single edge length in metres instead of cubing the converted length.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the centimetre prefix 10⁻² once rather than cubing it to (10⁻²)³ = 10⁻⁶ when converting cm³ to m³.

items.stem: Phase-change materials store thermal energy during solid–liquid transitions.
items.workedSolution: Answers: (a) Specific latent heat is the thermal energy required per unit mass to change state at constant temperature. Key points: Thermal energy needed per unit mass to convert between solid and liquid or liquid and vapour. State change occurs completely at constant temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Thermal energy needed per unit mass to convert between solid and liquid or liquid and vapour.
State change occurs completely at constant temperature.

parts.prompt: Define specific latent heat. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: Specific latent heat is the thermal energy required per unit mass to change state at constant temperature.
workingSteps: Key idea: Latent heat changes molecular potential energy without changing temperature.
Include both points: Thermal energy needed per unit mass to convert between solid and liquid or liquid and vapour and state change occurs completely at constant temperature.

items.stem: A student wants to compress trapped dry air inside a metal syringe so that the compression closely follows Boyle's law. Which experimental condition best ensures an isothermal change?
items.workedSolution: To keep temperature constant, compress slowly inside a thin conducting wall so thermal energy transfers to surroundings keeping temperature constant.

markScheme.criterion: Compress slowly inside a thin conducting wall so thermal energy transfers to surroundings keeping temperature constant.

options.label: A
options.text: The student should compress rapidly inside thick foam insulation so no heat escapes to the room
options.distractorRationale: Rapid insulated compression is adiabatic and raises the gas temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: The student should heat the syringe continuously while pushing the piston inward quickly
options.distractorRationale: Adding heat raises temperature further and violates Boyle's constant-temperature requirement.

options.label: C
options.text: The student should compress slowly inside a thin conducting wall so thermal energy transfers to surroundings keeping temperature constant

options.label: D
options.text: The student should open the syringe valve slightly so gas leaks out as volume shrinks
options.distractorRationale: Allowing gas to escape violates the fixed-mass requirement of Boyle's law.

items.stem: An electric boat travels at a steady speed of 36 km h⁻¹ across a calm lake against a drag force of 2400 N. Its motor draws 28571 W for 60 s. Calculate the percentage efficiency of the motor system.
items.workedSolution: At constant velocity, tractive force F = 2400 N and v = 36/3.6 = 10 m s⁻¹. Useful power P_out = Fv = 2400 × 10 = 24000 W. Efficiency η = (24000/28571) × 100% = 84.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Converts speed to 10 m s⁻¹, computes P_out = Fv = 24000 W, and obtains η = 84.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies drag force in N by speed in km h⁻¹ without dividing speed by 3.6 to obtain watts.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical power dissipated as heat rather than motor system efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by velocity (F/v) instead of multiplying P = Fv.

items.stem: A steady force of 187.5 N at 36.87° to the horizontal pulls a sled (mass 50 kg) along smooth flat ice for 8 s, without lifting it off the ice. Its initial speed is 1.5 m s⁻¹. What is its horizontal speed after 8 s?
items.workedSolution: Track-direction force F_x = 187.5 cos(36.87°) = 150 N ⇒ a_x = 3 m s⁻². New speed v = u + a_x t = 1.5 + (3)(8) = 25.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a_x = 3 m s⁻² via F cos 36.87° / m and obtains v = 25.5 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the vertical component F sin θ instead of F cos θ to compute horizontal acceleration.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies F/m directly without resolving the angled force vector horizontally.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the velocity change Δv = a_x t and forgets to add the initial speed u.

items.stem: Two binary inputs A and B feed the five-gate logic circuit shown, giving $Q = (\bar{A} \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})$. Out of all four rows in the truth table, how many input pairs give output $Q = 1$?
items.workedSolution: $Q = (\bar{A} \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})$ is HIGH for $(A, B) = (0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ only, giving 2 HIGH rows.

markScheme.criterion: Exactly 2 input combinations yield $Q = 1$.
