items.stem: A cylindrical metal resistance wire of resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m is 2.00 m long with diameter 0.280 mm. Redrawing it at constant volume leaves the diameter doubled to 0.560 mm. What is the new resistance?
items.workedSolution: Initial area A = πd²/4 = 6.158 × 10⁻⁸ m² and R = ρL/A = 12.34 Ω. Scaling diameter by factor k = 2 scales area by k² and length by 1/k² at constant volume, so R₂ = R / k⁴ = 0.7714 Ω ≈ 0.771 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 0.771 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Only scaled area by k² and forgot that constant volume also changes length by 1/k².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumed resistance varies inversely with diameter rather than diameter to the fourth power.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted the scaling factor k⁴ when computing the redrawn resistance.

items.stem: An 8 ms impact with a flat metal plate sends a steel block (0.25 kg) straight back at 9 m s⁻¹ after arriving at +24 m s⁻¹. Find ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i, the signed change in kinetic energy during the collision.
items.workedSolution: Applying the relation: ΔE_k = ½m(v² − u²) = 0.5(0.25)((−9)² − 24²) = -61.9 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ½m(v² − u²) including negative sign to obtain -61.9 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes positive energy lost (E_k,i − E_k,f) instead of the signed change E_k,f − E_k,i.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates ½m(v − u)² instead of ½mv² − ½mu².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds the two kinetic energies because the velocity reversed sign, forgetting v² is always positive.

items.stem: A student tests a battery pack with a high-resistance voltmeter and reads 12.0 V on open circuit. Across a 10.0 Ω load, the voltage falls to 10.0 V. Calculate the terminal potential difference after replacing the 10.0 Ω load with a 6.00 Ω resistor.
items.workedSolution: Open-circuit reading gives ε = 12.0 V. With R₁ = 10 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 1.000 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 2.000 Ω. With R₂ = 6 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 9.000 V ≈ 9.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 2.00 Ω and computes V₂ = 9.00 V.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumed terminal potential difference stays unchanged when load resistance changes.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: Powered by a 24.0 V DC source, a lab heater draws 1.85 A steadily over 2.5 min. Find the electrical work done by the supply.
items.workedSolution: Change time t = 2.5 × 60 = 150 s and current I = 1.850 A. Charge Q = It = 277.5 C. Electrical work W = QV = 6.660 × 10³ J ≈ 6.66 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 6.66 × 10³ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert operating time from minutes into seconds.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omitted the mA-to-A prefix conversion (10³ error).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculated charge Q = It instead of electrical work W = QV.

items.stem: Measurements on a spring balance give an initial mark x₁ = 20 mm ± 0.5 mm. Hanging a weight of F = 18 N ± 0.4 N moves the pointer to x₂ = 65 mm ± 0.5 mm. Work out the percentage uncertainty in k = F / (x₂ − x₁), using Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx₁ + Δx₂.
items.workedSolution: Stretch length e = x₂ − x₁ = 65 − 20 = 45 mm with absolute uncertainty Δe = Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 mm. Thus %Δk = (%ΔF) + (%Δe) = (0.4/18 + 1/45) × 100% = 4.44%.

markScheme.criterion: Finds e = 45 mm, Δe = 1 mm, and obtains %Δk = 4.44%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the uncertainty of a single ruler reading Δx rather than summing Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 2Δx for the difference x₂ − x₁.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx − Δx = 0 by subtracting absolute uncertainties in a difference.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides 2Δx by the final reading x₂ instead of by the extension e = x₂ − x₁.

items.stem: Find the percentage efficiency when an electric motor uses 1067 W for 25 s to move a heavy cart along a level rail at 2 m s⁻¹. The cable pulls with 500 N at 36.87° to the rail.
items.workedSolution: Output power delivered P_out = F v cos θ = 500 × 2 × cos(36.87°) = 800 W. Overall efficiency η = (800 / 1067) × 100% = 75.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates P_out = Fv cos 36.87° = 800 W and obtains η = 75.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses Fv sin θ instead of the component parallel to velocity Fv cos θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses un-resolved product Fv without multiplying by cos θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input power wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

items.stem: With dimensions 30 mm long, 0.6 mm wide, and 0.3 mm thick, a rectangular metal-oxide bar has resistivity 1.80 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m. What is the resistance between its opposite 0.6 mm × 0.3 mm end faces?
items.workedSolution: Normal face area is A = w × h = (0.6 × 10⁻³ m) × (0.3 × 10⁻³ m) = 1.800 × 10⁻⁷ m², and L = 30 × 10⁻³ m. Using R = ρL/A yields 3.00 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = w × h in m² and R = ρL/A to obtain 3.00 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used the wrong cross-sectional face for the current direction.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Failed to square the mm-to-m conversion factor for area.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted A and L in the resistance equation.

items.stem: The rating plate on a microscope lamp states "6 V, 18 W". Determine its resistance at rated voltage.
items.workedSolution: Quick calculation: Using P = V² / R gives R = V² / P = 6² / 18 = 2.000 Ω ≈ 2.00 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies electrical power rating equations to obtain 2.00 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverted R = V² / P as P / V².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Used V / P instead of V² / P.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the rated current I = P / V rather than the resistance.

items.stem: A brass wire of length 2.5 m and cross-sectional area 0.8 mm² extends elastically by 1.875 mm under a load of 168 N. The uncertainties are ±2% in stress and ±4% in strain. Calculate the absolute uncertainty ΔE in the Young modulus in pascals.
items.workedSolution: E = σ / ε = 2.80 × 10¹¹ Pa. Total percentage uncertainty %ΔE = 2% + 4% = 6.00%. Absolute uncertainty ΔE = E × (%ΔE / 100%) = 1.68 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes E and multiplies by (2% + 4%) to obtain ΔE = 1.68 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts percentage uncertainties |%Δσ − %Δε| in the quotient E = σ / ε.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses 10⁻³ m² instead of 10⁻⁶ m² when converting area from mm² to m².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies percentage uncertainties instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: Which description accurately summarizes the current–voltage behaviour and safe wiring of a semiconductor light-emitting diode?
items.workedSolution: An LED shows negligible current in reverse bias and below forward threshold followed by rapid current rise requiring a protective series resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Negligible current in reverse bias and below forward threshold followed by rapid current rise requiring a protective series resistor.

options.label: A
options.text: A diode exhibits negligible current in reverse bias and below forward threshold followed by rapid current rise requiring a protective series resistor

options.label: B
options.text: A diode exhibits a straight line through the origin in both quadrants requiring a parallel shunt resistor
options.distractorRationale: Describes an ohmic resistor rather than an asymmetric threshold diode.

options.label: C
options.text: A diode exhibits steady current in reverse bias and infinite resistance above the forward threshold
options.distractorRationale: Reverses forward and reverse conduction states completely.

options.label: D
options.text: A diode exhibits steadily rising resistance above threshold so no series protective resistor is needed
options.distractorRationale: Above threshold, diode resistance drops sharply so current surges dangerously without a series limiter.

items.stem: A copper wire of uniform diameter 1.40 mm conducts 4.20 A of steady current. Its free-electron density is 8.40 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Find the mean drift velocity magnitude of the free electrons.
items.workedSolution: Diameter in metres: d = 1.400 × 10⁻³ m. Conductor cross-section A = πd²/4 = 1.539 × 10⁻⁶ m². Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives v = I / (nAe) = 2.030 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 2.03 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 2.03 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in A = πr² (four times too large an area).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied by 4 instead of dividing by 4 in A = πd²/4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π when calculating the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: During a 4.5 s braking check on a straight wet road, a tow truck slows at a uniform rate of 2.4 m s⁻² from 72 km h⁻¹. Calculate the speed in m s⁻¹ at the end of the 4.5 s braking interval.

markScheme.criterion: Converts u to 20 m s⁻¹ and obtains v = 9.20 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts |a|t in m s⁻¹ directly from u in km h⁻¹ without converting units.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds |a|t instead of subtracting |a|t during braking deceleration.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the average velocity ½(u + v) over the interval instead of the final velocity.

items.stem: A student notes R = 16 Ω ± 0.2 Ω for a school lab resistor when connected to a steady DC voltage V = 36 V ± 0.3 V. Using P = V² / R, determine the percentage uncertainty in the electrical power.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2(%ΔV) + (%ΔR) = 2.92%.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

items.stem: A rocky dwarf planet can be treated as a uniform sphere of diameter 13000 km and mass 7.40 × 10²⁴ kg. Calculate its mean density in kg m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Radius r = D / 2 = 6.500 × 10⁶ m. Volume V = (4/3)πr³ = 1.150 × 10²¹ m³. Mean density ρ = m / V = 6433 kg m⁻³ ≈ 6.43 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Correct spherical density = 6.43 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides sphere volume incorrectly by a factor of 2.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 4/3 factor in the sphere volume formula.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter D instead of radius D/2 into (4/3)πr³, producing an 8× too-small density.

items.stem: With g = 9.8 m s⁻², a hoist check shows an electric winch drawing 817 W for 20 s while lifting a cage of mass 80 kg vertically through 15 m at steady speed. Work out the total energy wasted in these 20 s.
items.workedSolution: E_in = 817 × 20 = 16340 J and ΔE_p = 80 × 9.8 × 15 = 1.18 × 10⁴ J. Dissipated waste = E_in − ΔE_p = 4.58 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mgh from P_in t to obtain 4.58 × 10³ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the gravitational potential energy gained mgh instead of wasted energy.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates wasted power in watts without multiplying by duration t.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to multiply mass and height by g when subtracting useful work from P_in t.

items.stem: A tall tank holds oil of density ρ = 1100 kg m⁻³ ± 10 kg m⁻³ to a depth of h = 6 m ± 0.3 m. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ with negligible uncertainty. Calculate the gauge pressure p = ρgh at this depth in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure p = ρgh = 1100 × 9.81 × 6 = 6.47 × 10⁴ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates p = ρgh = 6.47 × 10⁴ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes ρh and omits gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reports the numerical value in kilopascals while labelling the unit as pascals.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides ρg by depth h instead of multiplying ρgh.

items.stem: By mass, a 1.2 kg alloy sample contains 70% gold of density 19.3 g cm⁻³ and 30% copper of density 8.93 g cm⁻³. Assume total volume equals the sum of the separate volumes. Find the density of the cast block in kg m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Masses: m₁ = 0.8400 kg, m₂ = 0.3600 kg. Volumes: V₁ = m₁/ρ₁ = 4.352 × 10⁻⁵ m³, V₂ = m₂/ρ₂ = 4.031 × 10⁻⁵ m³. Total volume V = V₁ + V₂ = 8.384 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (83.84 cm³). Alloy density ρ = m / V = 1.2 / 8.384 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.431 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.43 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ (14.3 g cm⁻³).

markScheme.criterion: Correct harmonic-mean alloy density = 1.43 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses an incorrect geometric factor or lever-arm ratio.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the density in g cm⁻³ instead of converting to kg m⁻³.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies the arithmetic weighted mean w₁ρ₁ + w₂ρ₂, which is only valid for volume fractions.

items.stem: A 20 K warming of an aluminium block of mass 0.5 kg (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) takes 120 s using a heater rated at 100 W. What percentage of the supplied electrical energy heats the aluminium block?
items.workedSolution: Q = mcΔT = 0.5 × 900 × 20 = 9000 J and E_in = 100 × 120 = 12000 J. Fraction kept as heat η = (Q / E_in) × 100% = 75.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mcΔT / (P_in t) × 100% = 75.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical energy lost to the surroundings instead of the percentage retained.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides Q = mcΔT in joules directly by heater power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits sample mass m from Q = mcΔT.

items.stem: By mass, salt water of density 1068 kg m⁻³ contains 9% dissolved salt. To collect 3 kg of solid salt, a student evaporates the liquid. Calculate the volume of salt water, in litres, that must be evaporated.
items.workedSolution: Total liquid mass m_sol = 3 / (9 / 100) = 33.33 kg. Volume V = m_sol / ρ = 33.33 / 1068 = 0.03121 m³ = 31.21 L ≈ 31.2 L.

markScheme.criterion: Correct solution volume = 31.2 L.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by the mass fraction instead of dividing by it.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the volume in m³ instead of converting to litres (× 1000).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Ignores the solute mass percentage completely.

items.stem: A steel spring obeys Hooke's law $F = k\Delta L$. What is the unit of the spring constant $k$ in SI base units?
items.workedSolution: Using $k = F/\Delta L$, the newton is $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$, so dividing by $\mathrm{m}$ cancels length to leave $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}$. Hence option B is correct: kilogram per second squared.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: kilogram per second squared. Reject N m⁻¹ when SI base units are explicitly demanded.

items.stem: A metal wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit and then unloaded slowly to zero load.
items.workedSolution: Evaluate (a): Maximum force or stress a material can bear and still return completely to its original length upon unloading. Evaluate (b): Exceeding the elastic limit leaves a permanent extension due to plastic deformation. Key idea: elastic behaviour means complete recovery of original dimensions on removing load.

markScheme.criterion: Maximum force or stress a material can bear and still return completely to its original length upon unloading.

Exceeding the elastic limit leaves a permanent extension due to plastic deformation.

Avoid the common error of equating the elastic limit with the breaking point where fracture occurs.

items.stem: The wave speed v along a steel cable obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ (k = 1). A sensor measures T = 320 N ± 2.4 N for a cable of mass per unit length μ = 3 g m⁻¹ ± 0.3 g m⁻¹. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the wave speed v.
items.workedSolution: Dimensional homogeneity gives v = T^(1/2) μ^(−1/2). Hence %Δv = ½(%ΔT) + ½(%Δμ) = 0.5(2.4/320 + 0.3/3) × 100% = 5.37%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses exponents |1/2| and |−1/2| to obtain %Δv = 5.37%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Sums %ΔT + %Δμ without multiplying by the 1/2 power factor from the square-root exponents.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainties because μ appears in the denominator of √(T/μ).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the combined percentage uncertainty by 2 instead of 1/2 for a square-root power.

items.stem: A lab flywheel rotates so a point on its rim at radius r = 2.5 m ± 0.08 m moves at speed v = 20 m s⁻¹ ± 0.3 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r. Calculate the fractional uncertainty Δa / a in the centripetal acceleration.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) = 0.0620.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the exponent multiplier 2 on Δv/v for the v² term.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts Δr/r from 2(Δv/v) in the quotient v²/r.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Confuses percentage uncertainty with dimensionless fractional uncertainty (off by a factor of 100).

items.stem: A small probe is thrown vertically upward with initial velocity +22 m s⁻¹. Neglect air resistance, take upward as positive, and use g = 9.81 m s⁻² over 4.2 s. Calculate its vertical displacement from the launch point at t = 4.2 s.
items.workedSolution: With upward positive, u = +22 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻². Vertical displacement s = ut + ½at² = (22)(4.2) − 0.5(9.81)(4.2)² = 5.88 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses s = ut − ½gt² with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 5.88 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses +g instead of −g when initial velocity is upward, adding ½gt² to ut.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 1/2 in the gravitational displacement term −½gt².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the motion as release from rest and omits the upward initial-velocity term ut.

items.stem: In a school lab practical, a student measures a wire of diameter d = 1 mm ± 0.01 mm under a tension of F = 24 N ± 2 N. Calculate the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = π(1 × 10⁻³)² / 4 = 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². Tensile stress σ = F / A = 4F / (πd²) = 3.06 × 10⁷ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 in m² to obtain σ = 3.06 × 10⁷ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses A = πd² instead of A = πd²/4 (treating diameter d as if it were radius r, off by a factor of 4).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter in millimetres directly without converting d² from mm² to 10⁻⁶ m².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by circumference πd instead of cross-sectional area πd²/4.

items.stem: With density 1020 kg m⁻³, open seawater sits to a depth of 31.5 m above a flat horizontal plate of area 2 m². Use 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa for atmospheric pressure and g = 9.81 m s⁻². Determine the overall downward force exerted on the plate.
items.workedSolution: Liquid gauge pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1020 × 9.81 × 31.5 = 3.152 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 3.15 × 10⁵ Pa. Total absolute pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 3.152 × 10⁵ = 4.162 × 10⁵ Pa = 416.2 kPa ≈ 416 kPa. Plate force F = p_abs A = 4.162 × 10⁵ × 2 = 8.324 × 10⁵ N ≈ 8.32 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 8.32 × 10⁵ N.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes fluid mass instead of total downward force.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure, omitting atmospheric force.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides absolute pressure by area instead of multiplying F = p A.

items.stem: Which statement correctly defines the moment of a force about a pivot?
items.workedSolution: The moment of a force is the product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force.

markScheme.criterion: Product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force.

options.label: A
options.text: The product of force and distance measured straight along the beam from the pivot to the point of application
options.distractorRationale: Omits the essential perpendicular condition when the force acts at an oblique angle.

options.label: B
options.text: The product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force

options.label: C
options.text: The ratio of force to the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action
options.distractorRationale: Divides by perpendicular distance instead of multiplying.

options.label: D
options.text: The product of mass and perpendicular distance from the pivot to the centre of gravity
options.distractorRationale: Uses mass instead of gravitational force (weight).

items.stem: An input power of 766 W is supplied to a warehouse lift as it lifts a crate of mass 150 kg by 10 m vertically. At steady speed, this takes 30 s (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Determine the percentage efficiency of the lift.
items.workedSolution: Useful GPE gain ΔE_p = mgh = 150 × 9.81 × 10 = 1.47 × 10⁴ J. Motor input energy E_in = 766 × 30 = 22980 J. System efficiency η = (ΔE_p / E_in) × 100% = 64.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgh / (P_in t) × 100% with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 64.0%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits gravitational field strength g when computing gravitational potential energy mgh.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input energy wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides useful energy mgh in joules directly by input power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

items.stem: In a class record sheet for a solid plastic cube, the side length is 3.2 cm ± 0.04 cm and the mass is 147 g ± 1.5 g. Determine the percentage uncertainty in the calculated density.
items.workedSolution: Since ρ = m L⁻³, Δρ / ρ = Δm / m + 3(ΔL / L) = (1.5/147) + 3(0.04/3.2). Converting to percent gives 4.77%.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Δρ/ρ = Δm/m + 3(ΔL/L) to obtain 4.77%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds the percentage uncertainty in edge length once instead of multiplying it by the power exponent 3 for L³.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts percentage uncertainties in the quotient m / L³ instead of adding worst-case contributions.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Cubes the percentage uncertainty in L rather than multiplying the fractional uncertainty by 3.

items.stem: Why is the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water much larger than its specific latent heat of fusion?
items.workedSolution: Specific latent heat of vaporisation exceeds fusion because intermolecular bonds are completely broken and work is done expanding against atmospheric pressure.

markScheme.criterion: Specific latent heat of vaporisation exceeds fusion because intermolecular bonds are completely broken and work is done expanding against atmospheric pressure.

options.distractorRationale: Both melting and boiling take place at constant temperature.

options.label: C
options.text: Because steam has a much higher density than liquid water requiring extra gravitational work
options.distractorRationale: Steam is far less dense than liquid water, expanding dramatically on vaporisation.

options.label: D
options.text: Because melting breaks covalent bonds inside molecules whereas boiling only warms the container
options.distractorRationale: Neither melting nor boiling breaks intramolecular covalent bonds; intermolecular forces are overcome.

items.stem: A student plots volume against Celsius temperature at constant pressure. How can this straight-line graph be used to estimate absolute zero?
items.workedSolution: At constant pressure, extrapolating the volume against Celsius line back to zero volume locates absolute zero.

markScheme.criterion: Extrapolating the volume against Celsius line back to zero volume locates absolute zero.

options.label: A
options.text: It works because extrapolating the volume against Celsius line back to zero volume locates absolute zero

options.label: B
options.text: It works because the vertical volume intercept at freezing point directly equals absolute zero
options.distractorRationale: The vertical intercept gives the gas volume at zero Celsius, not absolute zero temperature.

options.distractorRationale: The gradient gives expansion rate per degree rather than the zero-volume temperature intercept.

items.stem: An electric ferry travels at a steady speed of 72 km h⁻¹ across calm water against a drag force of 800 N. Its motor draws 18182 W of electrical power for 50 s. Calculate the percentage efficiency of the motor system.
items.workedSolution: At constant velocity, tractive force F = 800 N and v = 72/3.6 = 20 m s⁻¹. Useful power P_out = Fv = 800 × 20 = 16000 W. Efficiency η = (16000/18182) × 100% = 88.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Converts speed to 20 m s⁻¹, computes P_out = Fv = 16000 W, and obtains η = 88.0%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies drag force in N by speed in km h⁻¹ without dividing speed by 3.6 to obtain watts.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical power dissipated as heat rather than motor system efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by velocity (F/v) instead of multiplying P = Fv.

items.stem: Suppose a low-friction trolley of mass 25 kg moves along a flat bench at 1 m s⁻¹. Over 8 s, a string pulls steadily with 50 N at 36.87° to the horizontal. Calculate the horizontal speed at the end of the 8 s.
items.workedSolution: Horizontal component F_x = 50 cos(36.87°) = 40 N ⇒ a_x = 1.6 m s⁻². Final speed v = u + a_x t = 1 + (1.6)(8) = 13.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a_x = 1.6 m s⁻² via F cos 36.87° / m and obtains v = 13.8 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the vertical component F sin θ instead of F cos θ to compute horizontal acceleration.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies F/m directly without resolving the angled force vector horizontally.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the velocity change Δv = a_x t and forgets to add the initial speed u.

items.stem: Why do circuit designers often build combinational logic using NAND gates alone, even when extra gates are needed?

options.distractorRationale: NAND gates are purely digital switching elements.

options.label: D
options.text: NAND gates eliminate the need to obey De Morgan's laws.
options.distractorRationale: De Morgan's laws are the exact tool used to convert circuits to NAND-only form.

items.stem: What is the new resistance when a cylindrical titanium wire (length 6.00 m, diameter 0.500 mm, resistivity 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) is drawn at constant volume so its diameter is halved to 0.250 mm?
items.workedSolution: Initial area A = πd²/4 = 1.963 × 10⁻⁷ m² and R = ρL/A = 12.83 Ω. Scaling diameter by factor k = 0.5 scales area by k² and length by 1/k² at constant volume, so R₂ = R / k⁴ = 205.3 Ω ≈ 205 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 205 Ω.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Only scaled area by k² and forgot that constant volume also changes length by 1/k².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumed resistance varies inversely with diameter rather than diameter to the fourth power.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted the scaling factor k⁴ when computing the redrawn resistance.

items.stem: What is the signed kinetic energy change ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i when a small cart of mass 0.5 kg hits a spring bumper at +30 m s⁻¹ for 4 ms and rebounds straight back at 16 m s⁻¹?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ½m(v² − u²) including negative sign to obtain -161 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes positive energy lost (E_k,i − E_k,f) instead of the signed change E_k,f − E_k,i.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates ½m(v − u)² instead of ½mv² − ½mu².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds the two kinetic energies because the velocity reversed sign, forgetting v² is always positive.

items.stem: What is the new terminal potential difference if a 5.00 Ω resistor across a battery pack is swapped for a 2.00 Ω resistor? On open circuit, a high-resistance voltmeter reads 6.00 V, and with the 5.00 Ω resistor it reads 5.00 V.
items.workedSolution: No-load reading yields ε = 6.00 V. With R₁ = 5 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 1.000 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.000 Ω. With R₂ = 2 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 4.000 V ≈ 4.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 1.00 Ω and computes V₂ = 4.00 V.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumed terminal potential difference stays unchanged when load resistance changes.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: A steady current of 520 mA flows through a small electric pump for 5 min across a 15.0 V supply. How many electrons pass a point in the circuit during this period?
items.workedSolution: SI time t = 5 × 60 = 300 s and current I = 0.5200 A. Total charge Q = It = 156.0 C. Number of electrons N = Q / e = 156.0 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 9.750 × 10²⁰ ≈ 9.75 × 10²⁰.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 9.75 × 10²⁰.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert time from minutes to seconds (factor of 60 error).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applied the wrong unit conversion factor for current or time.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied charge by e instead of dividing Q by e.

items.stem: In a bench test of a metal spring in a lab press, the loaded reading is x₂ = 118 mm ± 1 mm for F = 60 N ± 0.3 N. The zero-load reading was x₁ = 18 mm ± 1 mm. What is the absolute uncertainty Δk of the spring constant in N m⁻¹?
items.workedSolution: Net extension e = (118 − 18) × 10⁻³ = 0.1 m with Δe = 2(1) × 10⁻³ = 0.002 m. Nominal k = 60 / 0.1 = 600 N m⁻¹. Proportionate error: Δk/k = 0.3/60 + 0.002/0.1 = 0.0250, so Δk = 15.0 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines Δe = 2Δx with ΔF/F + Δe/e to obtain Δk = 15.0 N m⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes only one reading uncertainty Δx instead of 2Δx when evaluating Δ(x₂ − x₁).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts Δx₂ − Δx₁ = 0 on the extension difference, ignoring ruler uncertainty completely.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves k in N mm⁻¹ instead of converting extension from millimetres to metres.

items.stem: A steady 300 N pull at 53.13° above the ground keeps a log sled moving along flat ground at 5 m s⁻¹ for 25 s. The electric winch draws 1059 W of electrical power. What is the percentage efficiency of this towing system?
items.workedSolution: Effective power delivered P_out = F v cos θ = 300 × 5 × cos(53.13°) = 900 W. Efficiency η = (900 / 1059) × 100% = 85.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates P_out = Fv cos 53.13° = 900 W and obtains η = 85.0%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses Fv sin θ instead of the component parallel to velocity Fv cos θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses un-resolved product Fv without multiplying by cos θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input power wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

items.stem: What is the resistivity of silicon if a rectangular bar (40 mm long, 1 mm wide, 0.4 mm thick) has resistance 2.80 Ω along its 40 mm length?
items.workedSolution: End-face area: A = w × h = (1 × 10⁻³ m) × (0.4 × 10⁻³ m) = 4.000 × 10⁻⁷ m², and L = 40 × 10⁻³ m. Using R = ρL/A yields 2.80 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = w × h in m² and R = ρL/A to obtain 2.80 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Chose the side face (L × w) instead of the end cross-section (w × h).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Converted mm² to m² using 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁶.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Rearranged resistivity wrongly as ρ = R L / A.

items.stem: Labelled "230 V, 1840 W", a laboratory kettle element is switched on at its rated voltage. Calculate the current drawn.
items.workedSolution: Applying the relation: Using P = IV gives I = P / V = 1840 / 230 = 8.000 A ≈ 8.00 A.

markScheme.criterion: Applies electrical power rating equations to obtain 8.00 A.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divided V by P instead of P by V.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated working resistance R = V²/P instead of current I = P/V.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied power by voltage instead of dividing.

items.stem: An alloy wire of length 2.5 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 mm² extends elastically by 1.875 mm under a pulling force of 225 N. The uncertainties are ±2% in stress and ±2% in strain. Calculate the absolute uncertainty ΔE in the Young modulus in pascals.
items.workedSolution: E = σ / ε = 2.00 × 10¹¹ Pa. Total percentage uncertainty %ΔE = 2% + 2% = 4.00%. Absolute uncertainty ΔE = E × (%ΔE / 100%) = 8.00 × 10⁹ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes E and multiplies by (2% + 2%) to obtain ΔE = 8.00 × 10⁹ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses 10⁻³ m² instead of 10⁻⁶ m² when converting area from mm² to m².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Includes only the stress uncertainty and ignores strain uncertainty.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the quantity through an algebraic factor-of-two slip.

items.stem: Why is a fixed resistor connected in series with an LED when testing its forward current–voltage graph?
items.workedSolution: Above threshold the LED resistance drops sharply, so a protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction.

markScheme.criterion: A protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction.

options.label: A
options.text: In the test circuit, a protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction

options.label: B
options.text: In the test circuit, a protective series resistor is included to raise the reverse breakdown voltage of the diode
options.distractorRationale: A series resistor does not alter the internal semiconductor junction breakdown rating.

options.label: C
options.text: In the test circuit, a protective series resistor is included to make the diode behave as an ohmic conductor
options.distractorRationale: The diode itself remains non-ohmic; the resistor prevents excessive current above threshold.

options.label: D
options.text: In the test circuit, a protective series resistor is included to prevent the voltmeter from drawing charge
options.distractorRationale: Voltmeter loading is avoided by high voltmeter resistance, not the LED safety resistor.

items.stem: A steady current of 3.60 A flows in a cylindrical zinc wire. Free-electron density is 6.60 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, and the mean electron drift speed is 2.78 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. Determine the wire's diameter.
items.workedSolution: Direct evaluation: Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the cross-sectional area is A = I / (nve) = 3.600 A / (6.600 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ × 2.780 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 1.226 × 10⁻⁶ m². Since A = πd²/4, d = √(4A/π) = 1.250 × 10⁻³ m = 1.25 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 1.25 mm.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reported the wire radius r = √(A/π) instead of the diameter d = 2r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Used A = πd² rather than A = πd²/4 when solving for diameter.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted the factor of π in the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: From 108 km h⁻¹ on a straight road, a lorry applies steady brakes giving 3 m s⁻² over 4 s. Calculate the speed in m s⁻¹ at the end of the 4 s braking interval.
items.workedSolution: u = 108 / 3.6 = 30 m s⁻¹. Terminal speed here v = u + at = 30 − (3)(4) = 18.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Converts u to 30 m s⁻¹ and obtains v = 18.0 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts |a|t in m s⁻¹ directly from u in km h⁻¹ without converting units.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds |a|t instead of subtracting |a|t during braking deceleration.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes the average velocity ½(u + v) over the interval instead of the final velocity.

items.stem: Resistance checks on a heater element give R = 10 Ω ± 0.2 Ω. A steady supply provides V = 8 V ± 0.3 V across it. Find the percentage uncertainty in the electrical power given by P = V² / R.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2(%ΔV) + (%ΔR) = 9.50%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the exponent factor 2 on %ΔV for the squared V² term.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts %ΔR from 2(%ΔV) because R is in the denominator.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the percentage uncertainties instead of adding them.

items.stem: From a 1.2 kg block of solid titanium (density 4510 kg m⁻³), a uniform wire of diameter 1.8 mm is drawn with no metal lost. Instead, the same metal could be cast into a solid cube. Calculate the side length of the cube in cm.
items.workedSolution: Volume V = m / ρ = 1.2 / 4510 = 2.661 × 10⁻⁴ m³ (266.1 cm³). Wire cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = 2.545 × 10⁻⁶ m² ⇒ L = V / A = 104.6 m ≈ 105 m. Recast cube edge s = ∛V = 6.432 cm ≈ 6.43 cm.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value = 6.43 cm.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Misplaces a decimal factor during m to cm conversion.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides the volume by 3 instead of taking its cube root.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Takes the square root of volume instead of the cube root.

items.stem: Electrical input to a crane is 3267 W. In 25 s, it raises an engine block of mass 200 kg by 30 m straight up at constant speed (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). How much energy is wasted over the 25 s period?

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mgh from P_in t to obtain 2.29 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the gravitational potential energy gained mgh instead of wasted energy.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates wasted power in watts without multiplying by duration t.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to multiply mass and height by g when subtracting useful work from P_in t.

items.stem: A pressure gauge sits at depth h = 24 m ± 0.3 m in a deep water tank of density ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ ± 20 kg m⁻³. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ as exact. Calculate the gauge pressure p = ρgh at this depth in pascals.
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure p = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 24 = 2.35 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates p = ρgh = 2.35 × 10⁵ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes ρh and omits gravitational field strength g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reports the numerical value in kilopascals while labelling the unit as pascals.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides ρg by depth h instead of multiplying ρgh.

items.stem: A rectangular metal block has dimensions 11 cm × 4.5 cm × 2.5 cm. Its composition by volume is 75% copper (8930 kg m⁻³) and 25% aluminium (2700 kg m⁻³). What is the alloy density in kg m⁻³?
items.workedSolution: Volume V = (11 × 4.5 × 2.5) × 10⁻⁶ = 1.238 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Volume-weighted density ρ = (0.75 × 8930) + (0.25 × 2700) = 7372 kg m⁻³ ≈ 7.37 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Total mass m = ρ V = 0.9123 kg ≈ 0.912 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 7.37 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses an incorrect geometric factor or lever-arm ratio.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the volume fractions assigned to the two metals.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the harmonic mean formula, which applies to mass fractions rather than volume fractions.

items.stem: Heated for 200 s by a heating coil at 605 W, 1.2 kg of water shows an 18 K temperature rise. Specific heat capacity is c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Work out the heat lost to the surroundings during the 200 s.
items.workedSolution: Supplied electrical work E_in = P_in t = 605 × 200 = 121000 J. Thermal energy retained by sample Q = mcΔT = 1.2 × 4200 × 18 = 90720 J. Escaped heat = E_in − Q = 3.03 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mcΔT (90720 J) from P_in t (121000 J) to obtain 3.03 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the thermal energy absorbed by the sample Q = mcΔT rather than the heat lost to the surroundings.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the total electrical energy supplied P_in t instead of subtracting mcΔT.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the rate of heat loss in watts without multiplying by the heating time t.

items.stem: Using g = 9.81 m s⁻², find the percentage of volume below the surface for a wooden block (mass 10.5 kg, density 680 kg m⁻³) floating freely in seawater of density 1025 kg m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Equating weight and upthrust: ρ_fluid V_sub g = ρ_obj V g ⇒ V_sub / V = ρ_obj / ρ_fluid = 680 / 1025 = 0.6634 = 66.34% ≈ 66.3%.

markScheme.criterion: Percentage under water = 66.3%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage protruding above the waterline rather than under water.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses an incorrect geometric factor or lever-arm ratio.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the density ratio ρ_fluid / ρ_obj.
